THE NEW YEAR. As glad New Year upon the world shall dawn, When dies the old, and midnight melts in morn, Fair and unsullied as the virgin snow That falls on mountains when the wind is low. A happy year when first his dawn we view, Welcomed with jay by young, fair, brave and true; May truth and kindness mane by justice strong. O'ercome base selfishn.ss, deceit and wrong. May discord, poverty, and vice grow lesr, And smiling plenty with abnndance bless, The world advancing towards her s miner finds Bright hopes have been great blessings to mankind. What priceless gems upon thy temples shine, Rich heritage of all past years is thine, The sage's thlughts and hero's noble life. A web of beanty woven out of strife Oh messenger of vast eternity. Nearer poetic dreams thy destiny, When truth and love mankind on earth shall bless. And discord be diszolvcd in happiness. Warrington, December, 18;33
B. REV YON.

Perseverance cannot be counterfeited. It is the afterwards that tests all our actions. Piety and virtue are not subject to circumstances. Doing good is the only certainly happy action of a man's life.—Sitiney. In a hundred ells of contention there is not au inch of lovs.—G•2,irge Herbert. A man v, rvi has tried it says that all the short cuts to wealth are overerav!Pd. Deal has at girl pilot only seventeen years old. Knows all the boys in the Downs. A gentleman said, when a pretty girl trod on his toes, that he had received the stamp of beauty. So far as we are concerned, style is no object. We would just as lief walk to a cemetery as ride in a hearse. An Aberdonian recently bought a horse by photograph, thus literally getting the carte before the horse. Gold can buy pretty nearly everything in the world ex- cept that which a man wants most—viz., happiness. lie is a very ordinary man who never finds fault with himself, and a very extraordinary one who never has reason to do so. "It is a curious fact," says some entomologist, "that it is the female mosquito which torments us." A bachelor thinks it is not at all curious. "Viii you dake something ?" said a German teetotaller to a friend, while standing near a tavern. "I don't care if I do," was the reply. "Veil, den, let us dahe a valk." A Levant paper says they are cultivating sponges with success. We have a great variety of indigenous "sponges" in this country, but we never think of boasting about them. . "Who," said a member of the Canadian House of Com- mons to the members who were trying to choke him off— "Who brayed there 2" • "It was an echo," retorted a mem- ber, amid a yell of delight. "Illustrated with cuts!" said a mischievous urchin, as he drew his knife across the leaves of his grammar. "Illus- trated with guts!" repeated the teacher, as he laid his cane across the back of the mischievous urchin. Two servants of a coquette are discussing the visitors of the house. "It seems to me," says the first, "that now-a days we never see Monsieur—tdonsieur—what is his name —the straw-coloured beard." " Ah, yes. The Deluge" "Why do you call him the Deluge?" "Because he reigned forty days." Poetical Jones said :—" The profusion and colour of he hair would lead one to think it was sigin by the nimble fiwrers of the easy hours as they glided through bright June days, whose sunny rays of light had been caught in the meshes and were content to go no farther?' Smith ex- presses the same thing by saying, "Her hair was awfully • red."

REDUCTION OF RENT.—At Lord Bolton's rent audit just held at Kingsclere (Hants), his lordship liberally allowed his tenants a reduction of ten per cent. An extensive creamery has been established in Tullamore, King's County, Ireland, and immense quantities of high- class butter are manufactured daily, the process of churn- ing and butter-making being performed with the newest and , man improved systems, the hands not touching the butter. ' Are INFURIATED BULL.—An exciting scene took place last week at the Christmas sale of fat cattle at the Inverness Auction Mart. The sale ring was crowded with dealers, when an enraged ball suddenly got loose and dashed into the ring, knocking several persons down and trampling upon them. Mr. Macrae, butcher, Dingwall, was tossed in the air, and thrown against the barricade with great violence. He was very much bruised and stunned. Mr. Conn, Keith; Mr. M`Gandale, Inverness, and others were knocked down and trampled upon, all escaping, however, with only slight bruises. Owing to the crowded state of the market it was a difficult matter to get oat, and many persons had to cling to the rafters until the animal was secured. "THOSE HEAVY WILDEYES."—It may be worth noticing that the heaviest shorthorn costrs in the Agricultural Hall was by a Wildeyes bull, bred at Holker, whilst a cow (full sister in blood to that bull) was, a year or twe ago, the heaviest cow present on that occasion. This fact saould direct attention to the value of this Wildeyes *ibe for its ability to confer size, on females especially. Sir J. H. Greville Smyth's heifer (which won both at Reading and York) is really by a Wildeyes sire, although, in the report in the Royal Agricultural Society of England's Journal for 1883, she is erroneously described as having been "sired by an Oxford bull." The bull, "Duke of Beaufort," which (bred at Dunmore) has begotten such admirable crosses for Lord Lovat is another instance of the usefulness of the Wildeyes as beef-makers. PREHISTORIC APPLES.—Jast as the New Zealanders, in precolonial days, were wont to gather vast stores of wild fruits, so the prehistoric savages, likewise unacquainted with the use of metals, who dwelt in villages constructed on piles in the lakes and swamps of North Italy, Savoy, and Switzerland, at some indeterminate period, probably not more than four or five centuries c., made abundant use of apples. They split the fruit lengthwise, and dried them as provisions. Recent researches among these lacustrine re- mains have brought to light large stores of these fruit, many of them charred by the confl tgrations which seem to have been so common in these villages. A German archaeologist has distinguished at least two species of apple, one, when charred, resembling in size an English crab-apple; the other of larger dimensions, akin to those of an apple found to this day in orchards in the German-speaking cantons of Swit- zerland, under the name of campaner. The quantities stored have suggested to some archeologists the idea that the trees were cultivated. Intermixed with the apples oc- cur a few small wild pears dried in like manner. MODERN FARMING.—A letter on this subject by Sir J. B. Lewes recently appeared in The Times. Market price, he says, is modifying farm practice. Even " Wheathamp- sted " is giving up wheat-growing. The estates around are being gradually grassed over, and milk and butter and meat are becoming more and more the dependence of the farmer In a district where wheat will probably continue to be grown as long as anywhere in this country. Bat an im- mensely larger capital is needed for stock farming than for grain crops. Why is it not forthcoming? The reason ob- vionsly is that the risk is too great to be incurred. Capital invested in live stock is liable at any moment to destruction by imported disease. There is no reason why protection from this great universal risk, against which the farmer cannot protect himself, should not be . provided, when we see that Parliament has gone out of its way to provide pro- tection for the farmers' capital against risks which he could always avoid if he chose, and which at worst are the rarest I exceptions to ordinary experience. Sir J. B. Lewes has lately bought a frozen New Zealand sheep, and can testify to the quality of its mutton. Why should we not trust our meat supply to the carcass importer, and forbid live stock importation from infected countries once for all. "If a law were passed that after a certain date no imports of live stock should take place, it would tend greatly to revive agriculture, and would tempt a large amount of capital into the business of farming; and I am by no means certain," says Sir John, "that the result would not be a redaction, rather than an increase in the price of meat." ALLEGED CURE FOR SHEEP ROT.—At the end of last March I discovered that a part of my breeding flock, con- sisting of 94 Cosswold ewes, which had been put on land which was flooded in the summer of 18S2, had contracted the rot, although previous to their being turned ul5Oll after the flood the land was sown with salt. As the whole of these ewes passed safely through the lambing season, and produced a fairly good fall of lambs, I hoped they were all right; but upon the sadden death of one at the above period an examination of its liver showed the presence of number- less flukes, and as in a few days after many more of the flock showed by bottling they were rotten, my hopes were quite disappointed. I consulted with my bailiff, and we decided to commence at once to give them a liberal supply ef crashed oilcake, beans, and oats, and to send to Messrs. Wells and Co. for four bags of their vegetable charcoal. By some means it was delayed in transit, and some ten or twelve days elapsed before it arrived. Daring this time I lost three more ewes, all their livers being full of flukes, and the others became more emaciated. Upon the arrival of the charcoal the prescribed quantity for 100 ewes was mixed with their daily allowance of corn and cake, and all ate it excepting one, which was so emaciated that it could .scarcely walk. She lingered for about ten days longer and died, her liver being infested with live flukes. The ewes in general showed but little sign of improvement till the four bags were nearly finished, when another ewe died, her liver containing flukes, many of them dead. After this the sheep began to improve rapidly. By the beginning of July many were fit for the butcher, and no one from their appearance would have sus- pected they were ever flaked. I now commenced drafting for market, and by August 8 was cleared off. Oat of the last lot one died, and one I had slaughtered; neither of these had any flakes, but their livers showed unmistakable signs of having been sorely affected by them. I have not com- municated with Messrs. Wells and Co. on the subject, but I am of opinion that their charcoal will destroy flukes in the livers of sheep, and if given before the ravages of the disease have affected the heart and lunge, wonld prevent loss from flake.—E. itiontxy, Brize Norton, Oxon.—Agricultural Gazette. ENSILAGE.—Many persons have been making experiments on ensilage during the present year; but nearly all have tried it with a view to seeing whether green forage would keep sound in an air-tight and water-tight pit, duly weighted on the surface, in default of being absolutely closed. That it would keep under such conditions ought to have gone without asking. What ensilage does is to (1) increase the nutritive powers of green forage; (2) to obviate waste; (3) to save time (4) to increase the productive powers of the soil. It does the first, if in no other way, by making the forage more digestible; the second by saving a crop from deterioration by exposure to weather; the third by putting the least possible time between cutting and storing; the fourth, as a sequence of the third, by enabling the farmer to cut a double crop yearly, by giving him op- portunity for enlarging his stock of cattle, and by enor- mously increasing the value and amount of manure. I know from the correspondence which I have had (at one time nearly that of a department in a Goverment office) that the construction of silos is going on on the new plan, practised in the United States, and sketched in my little book on the subject, in India and Australia, as well as generally in Europe. A day or two ago I gave leave to a correspondent to translate my book on ensilage into Swedish. Most Eng- lish silos of which I have read are made in too shallow masonry. It stands to reason that this increases the ex- pense per cubic yard. They should be made from 20 to 25 feet deep, if they are to be made in the cheapest way. I believe that my friend Mr. Samuel Whitebread has made the best hitherto constructed in England. The main object of ensilage is to get two crops a year off the same land. Silos are profitable if they obviate loss; most gainful when they increase produce. I should add, however, that cattle need cleanliness and ventilation as much as human beings do; and I do not wonder at disease being prevalent in English herds, and for the matter of that in flocks, when I see the dark filthy dens in which they are generally housed, and the wasteful way in which they are exposed to weather. Our forefathers kept their sheep under cover from November to April. Had silos been common in England, millions of pounds worth of fodder would have been saved last summer, and not much less worth of aftermath would be saved now. I should have thought that this was the time in which Eng- lish agriculture could not afford to neglect small esonomies, let along great ones.—,l. E. Thorold Rogers, Oxford.

THOSE WRETCHED CHRISTMAS "WAITS! .7 —The " wait " between the roast beef and the pudding when the hostess is trembling lest the latter should "turn out" a failure. The " wait " at the cabstand on a wet Christmas morning, when all the cabs are engaged. The "wait" at your friend's dinner-table, in consequence of the said dearth of cabs and your non-arrival. The" wait" which young ladies have to endure before the young gentlemen get bold, and mistle- toe practice begins. The " wait " at the pit entrance on Boxing .night, when you have somebody's elbows in each rib, somebody's bag of oranges on your shoulder, and some- body else's child kicking at the small of your back. The " wait" at your door on the part of the lamplighter, bell- ringers, turncock, &c., while your servant has gone to ask you for a Christrhas box. "1 have a suite tooth ! "Now, gentlemen," said a nobleman to his guests, as the ladies left the room, "let us understand each other; are we to drink like men or like beasts?" The guests, somewhat indignant, exclaimed, "Like men!" "Then," he replied, "we are going to get jolly drank, for brutes never drink more than they want." FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.

The death of Count Graday, the Hungarian Minister of National Defence, from an affection of the throat, is announ- ced from Vienna, where he had been staying for medical treatment. It is reported from St. Petersburg that dissensions have broken out amongst the Socialists in that city preventing the publication for some weeks past of the organ represent- ing their views. According to the latest accounts, 19 children and a teacher perished in the fire at the Jewish school at Galata. The loss of life was greatly increased by the circumstance of the staircase taking fire. LARGE COTTON FAILURE IN AMERICA. MEIER'S. A. D. Smith and Co., of Providence, Rhode Island, have failed, with liabilities $1,000,000. The firm owned five cotton mills, and employed 10,000 men. The failure is attributed to bad management. A telegram from Alexandria contradicts some reports which have been published relative to the cost of the army of occupation. The total cost to Egypt for the current year amounts to £480,000. In the last three months the amount was under £72,000. CLOSE OF THE HAYTIAN INSURRECTION. Intelligence received at Paris from the French Legation, in Hayti, states that the town of Jeremie capitulated on the 18th instant, and Miragoane had offered to submit. The despatch adds that the insurrection may be regarded as virtually at an end. ARREST OF A SPY IN FRANCIE.—On Saturday, at Bel- fort, the gendarmes arrested a stranger who gave his name as Deutschel, and is believed to be a spy. He said he was a land surveyor at present unemployed. In his possession were found the uniform of an officer of the Austrian Army, a passport for three years, and two plans. A fatal labour riot is reported from Lida in the Russian Government of Minsk. The contractors and their overseers seem to have been too exacting in their demands upon the workpeople, who struck in a literal sense for shorter hours, killed one of their overseers, and maltreated several others. The ringleaders of the riot wereearrested, and order was promptly restored. The Pope delivered his customary address to the cardinals on Christmas Eve. It consisted of a series of complaints against the implacable hatred of the enemies of the church; that the pilgrims to the Vatican had been grossly insulted; he objected to the tone of the Italian Press on the Luther Commemoration; and he deplored dangerous writings which aggravated the present situation, the allusion being under- stood to be Father Curci's book. ALLEGED PLOT AGAINST THE SULTAN.—A Turkish officer at the Yddiz Kiosk has been murdered by a soldier of the helped:el Guard. Revenge is said to be the motive of the crime; but rumours prevailed in Constantinople that the murder is not unconnected with another Palace plot against the Sultan, and great excitement consequently prevails. The newspapers received strict injunctions from the police authorities to abstain from all camment on the affair. DYNAMITE IN RUSSIA.—A chief depot for the manufac- ture and storage of dynamite has been discovered in Little Russia, one of the provinces in the Czar's dominions, which has been supposed to be hitherto untainted by the plots of the Nihilists. Many arrests have been made, some of which are thought to be of great importance, as the prisoners are supposed to be prominent heads of the conspiracy. The seizure included weapons as well as explosives. THE SOUDAN : REPORTED ADVANCE OF THE MARDI ON KHARTOUM.—A despatch from Cairo on Wednesday states that nothing is known there confirming the rumour published by the Paris papers that the False Prophet was advancing OR Khartoum, nor has any information been received in confirmation of the statement published by a London morn- ing paper that insurgent bands were close to that place. According to the latest intelligence the Mandi was still at El Obeid. M. de Lesseps, lecturing at Abbeville on the subj,ct of ship canals, seems to have made a great " hit " by remark- ing that "no Englishman had dared to say that the Suez Canal would be taken by England." M. de Lessens would have been more correct and friendly if he had said that no Englishman imagined that England would " take " the Canal. He assured the meeting that the increased traffic through the Canal which would follow upon the reduction of dues would compensate for any immediate loss of revenue. The Russian Government is contemplating an important scheme for the development of its political and commercial interests in Central Asia. A railway is projected to connect Turkestan with Khiva and Bokbara. The ostensible pur- pose of the line is, of course, to "promote Russian trade with Central Asia," but its military importance must be ob- vious. It would add enormously to the power of Russia in the neighbourhood of Afghanistan. The project is at present "in the clouds," and it cannot be realised for some years to come. Arrustpz TO ABDUCT THE QUEEN OF MADAGASCAR.—A letter has arrived at Zanzibar from the French Admiral Galiber announcing that on the night of November 16 the Roves made an attempt to carry off the Queen of the Sake- lavas fro n Majunga. The attempt was foiled by the fire of the French gunboat Pique and by a party of riflemen from the Forfeit, under the command of Midshipman Ducrest. The sanitary condition of the French forces is described as everywhere satisfactory. The negotiations with the Hovas had been resumed. ACCIDENT TO GENERAL GRANT. General Grant, OR alighting from his carriage at his residence on Monday evening last, slipped, and fell on his left side, seriously in- juring his leg about four inches below the hip joint. He was immediately assisted to bed, where he has since re- mained, lying in one position on his back. The surgeons say that no bones are broken, but it is supposed that a bruise has been sustained to the sciatic nerve. They do not anticipate anything serious ' • still they predict that several weeks must elapse before the general will be able to leave the house. THE ATTACK ON SONTAY. The French Minister of Marine has received particulars from Admiral Courbet of the losses in the taking of Sontay. The number killed was 85 and the number wounded 240. A private despatch says the Black Flags, when they saw that all the exterier de- fences of the fortress had fallen into the hands of the French, did not wait for the attack on the citadel, but slipped out quietly and escaped up the river in the direction of Laokai and the mountains. It is stated, however, that information has reached Hongkong that the French were subsequently defeated at Sontay and the fortress retaken. THE IMPRISONED NlHlLlSTS.—According to a Nihilist print published in Switzerland, the Nihilist agitator Net- shajeff, who was extradited by the Swiss Government in 18i2, and sentenced by the Russian authorities to 20 years' penal servitude in the Siberian mines, was never sent to Siberia, but has been imprisoned ever since in the fortress of Alexef Ravelin, near St. Pe•ersburg. A letter which he managed to smuggle out of his prison appears in the news- paper. Netshajeff gives most harrowing descriptions of his prison life, especially with respect to the extortion and neglect cf the officials. He states that the prisoners are fed on horseflesh, and that since the assassination of Alexander 11. they have been deprived of their daily half-hour's exer- cise in the open air. THE ILBERT BILL.—The Calcutta Englishman states that a concordat has been arranged between the Indian Government and the Anglo-Indian Defence Association, ac- cording to which no native, other than a district judge or magistrate, shall exercise criminal jurisdiction over Euro- pean British subjects. The latter will be entitled as ef right to trial by jury, the majority of jurors being Europeans. This right will be conferred even in non-jury districts, and will apply in every case tryable by district magistrates even when the latter may be European British subjects. The Calcutta Englishman declares that this arrangement has permanently established the principle that the rights and liberties of Europeans will be safeguarded by the verdict of men of their own race. TERRIBLE FIRE AT A So:more—Early on Sanday morn- ing a fire broke out on the premises occupied by the Ger- mano-Israelite School, Constantinople. The flames, which were first seen in the basement of the building, spread with such rapidity as to prevent most of the children from effect- ing their escape by the ordinary means of egress. Many were thrown or leaped out of the windows of the upper floors into blankets which were held in the street, and in the course of their descent several were more or less seriously injured. Nineteen charred bodies have been found, but it is feared that more have perished, as 30 children in all are missing. On Sunday night the directrees of the school, seized with fright, threw herself out of a window into the street, and was killed on the spot. THE SOUDAV DISASTER —There appears to be even yet no thoroughly decisive information to be had as to the manner in which Hicks Pasha and his army were destroyed. The Khedive has received telegrams from the Governors of Dongola and Berber, the former stating that Hicks Pasha and 3,000 of his mese were killed, but that an Egyptian officer, with the remainder of the army, is encamped in a position where he is receiving supplies. The latter tele- gram gives information of a still more cheering character, but no reliance can be placed upon it. The bazaar rumours at Khartoum before the disaster referred to some dissension between Hicks Pasha and the Egyptian officer (Aladeen Pasha) mentioned in the telegrams. It was said that the English gentleman separated himself aod a large portion of the army from Aldeen, who refused to march because the water failed, and pushed on, finally reaching a defile where he fell into an ambush and was slain. Hicks Pasha was known to be a daring officer, but he would scarcely be so rash as to play the part imputed to him in the Arab reports.
A SHORT ROAD TO HEALTH AND WEALTH.—ltiStilad Of bottle of champagne every day at dinner, drink a bottle of CAMMACK'S sparkling POMMETTE.—Advt.

DISTRIBUTION OF PRESCOT CIIARITIES.—OD Monday last these charities were distributed, at the Town Hall, to a number of deserving door. The recipients, 83 in number, each received the sum of 5s Henry Cross, Esq., attended as treasurer, with the vicar and churchwardens, who for the time being are the trustees of the above charities. THE ALEXANDRA DIVIDING SOCIETY, SUTTON—The annual meeting of this society was held on Friday last week, in the Alexandra Hotel, Sutton. The balance sheet was read, and copies distributed to the members. It was shown that the income of the society during the year amounted to 282 as 9i, of which £lO7 16s 4d has been paid to sick members, and £8 for one death; and after paying rent, salaries, doctor's account, and other sundry expenses, there was a sum of £lO2 15s 2d appropriated in dividends, at the rate of 12s id per full member, and a balance of .£l7 93 4d reserved in hand. The total number of !members during the year was 178, a gain of 19 during he year.

div.head: POLITICAL.
div.p: POLITICAL.

Sir Richard Cross was on Saturday chosen assessor of the St. Andrews University. Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Fawcett will visit Brighton early in the new year, this being looked upon as an offset to the recent visits of Mr. E. Clarke and Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett to this town in the Conservative interest. MR. HERBERT GLADSTONE AT OLDHAM.—Speaking at Oldham, on Saturday, Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., said he hoped the Government, whatever the House of Lords might do, would not dissolve Parliament until they had passed all their reform measwes. He charged the Parnellites an 4 Tories with combining to obstruct Liberal legislation. Ha regarded Sir Staffosd Northcote's visit to Ireland as one of the greatest politiesi blunders ever made, as the effect of Sir Stafford's speeches, moderate though they were, seemed to have been to inflame the minds of the orange party in Ireland.

M. JOSEPH COWEN AT NEWCASTLE.—Speaking at New- castle ou Saturday evening, Mr. Jos,ph Cowen, M.P., al- luded to the new rules of procedure, and said he did not see why the work of Parliament should not be further divided, nor why it should not meet in November like the law courts. In regard to Egypt, he expressed the opinion that we never should have gone there, but now that we were there we would be obliged to remain, or chaos would return. He believed that the franchise should be brought to the front next session, and • that the question of redistribution should wait.

A LIBERAL VIEW OF TORY HOSTILITY.-Mr. Medley, one of the Liberal candidates for Devonport, having brought to Mr. Bright's notice some criticisms by Mr. Puleson, M.P., the right honourable gentleman, in reply, says—" I pay no attention to Tory hostility of this kind. I was always in favour of legi4ation for the protection of children in fac- tories and elsewhere. I was against it when it interfered with adults. lam so now. A large section of the Tories voted for the Factory Bill to revenge themselves upon manufacturers who were opposing the Corn Laws, and the few Whigs who supported it as a means of injuring the Government of Eir Robert Peel."

MR FORSTER AND EGYPTIAN SLAVERY. Mr. W. E Forster, writing on the subject of Ez,yptian slavery, urges that support should be given to the project for establishing a home for freed women at Cairo. The right hon. gentle- man denounces the abominable traffic in slaves with his ac- customed energy. He has long been convinced, he says, that the slave trade for the supply of the Oriental markets is as destructive of human life and as productive of human misery as was the American traffic. He would not attempt to reconquor the Soudan for the purpose of stopping the trade, but would attack the evil in Lower Egypt, where there is a great "demand" for slaves. Mr. Clifford Lloyd has, however, informed him that he dare not press the Khedivial Government to enforce their present emancipation laws until provision has been made for the welfare of the large num- ber of women and girls who would be turned out of the Egyptian harems. LORD LYTTON ON "BRITISH PRINCIPLES AND IN- TERESTS."—In the Whitehall Review there appears a letter written by Lord Lytton in response to an invitation to at- tend a dinner to be given by the Southwark Working Men's Conservative Asssociation. In his letter the noble Lord says :—" Had it been in my power to attend your annual dinner it would have given me the greatest possible pleasure to exchange greetings and encouragement with the South- wark Working Men's Association in that cause which will, I think, long continue to unite us, especially at a time when almost every part of our empire is suffering from reckless disregard of those British principles and interests which have so long coastituted the strength and glory of it, and which I believe to be essential to its preservation. Private ' circumstances, however, have compelled me to decline all public engagements this year."

LIBERAL WORKING MEN AND MR. GLADSTONE. - Mr. Gladstone was on Saturday presented with a handsome des- sert service of Crown Derby porcelain, which had been sub- scribed for by the Liberal working men of Derby. The deputation was introduced by Sir William Harcourt, who spoke of the services which, during the present half century, had been rendered to the country by the Premier. Mr. Gladstone, in reply' thanked the deputation for their present and kind wishes. It was a peculiar and great thing for England to be able t 6 say that at present she stood at the head of the porcelain-producing countries of the world. Referring to public affairs, Mr. Gladstone said there was no subject more important than how to economise the time of Parliament, in order to overtake the enormous increase in the business of the country. Many important subjects would have to wait, but there was one which the Government were pledged to submit to her Majesty at a suitable period for preposal to Parliament, and that was the extension of the franchise. There was no cause now for the fears and the apprehensions which naturally were felt previous to the first Reform Bill. They might approach the extension of the franchise not only with a good conscience but with a light heart, knowing it would strengthen the Constitution, the Throne, and the law.

They err who tell us politeness has fled, as witness the following postscript to a letter received by the Duke of X from the steward of one of his estates :—" I beg that your grace will excuse me for having taken the liberty of writing this letter in my shirt sleeves, but the excessive heat has compelled nig to be guilty of this apparent dis- respect." •

..•.vo sound nerves and good health without using Hop Bitters ostrengthen the stomach, purify the blood, and keep the liver and kidneys active, to carry off all the poisonous and waste mattnr of the ystem. See Advt.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

In consequence of a strike of labourers at the Limerick gasworks, the Lord Lieutenant has ordered soldiers to work in their stead, pending the settlement of the dispute. ALLEGED SHOCIIII4G MATRICIDE.—A man named Caul- field was arrested at Newry, on Thursday, for killing hie. mother. It is alleged that he knocked her down and jumped upon her.

MR. PARNELL, M.P.—Mr. Parnell, M.P., is at present staying at his residence, at Avondale, county Wicklow. He purposes starting extensive aaw mills there, as well as open- ing quarries for granite paving setts. A BOARD OF GUARDIANS IN DIFFICULTIFS.—AII Irish correspondent states that the National Bank of Ireland has refused to cash cheques for the Loughrea Guardians, £l,OOO being overdrawn. It is found impossible to collect the rates, owing to the prevailing poverty. On Saturday the bank manager was urgently requested to advance £lOO only, and it was stated at the meeting of the guardians that when his was anent they wonld have to close all out-door relief. FACTION FIGHT IN THE CURRAGH CAMP.—Christmas-day was observed in the Carragh Camp with the usual festivi- ties, but the pleasure of the day was somewhat marred by I an unfortunate encounter which occurred in the course of the afternoon between the men of the 2nd Battalion Royal Scots and those of the 2nd Batt Ilion Rifle Brigade. The timely arrival of armed pickets quickly restored order, but not before one or two men had received rather severe cuts about the head and face. A line 'of armed sentries was p'aced between the combatants, who were confined t) their respective quarters for the rest of the day. TERRIBLE Creists.—A. man named M‘Connatty has been committed for trial for the murder of his wife near Roberts- town, in county Kildare. The crime, according to the nar- rative of the prisoner's daughter, a child nine years old, has perhaps seldom been exceeded for ferocity. The prisoner appears to have heard something said to his wife's detri- ment, and going home he dragged her to the ground by the hair, kicked her violently about the head and neck, and knelt upon her and tried to choke her, then inflicted a ter- rible wound upon her head with an iron implement and dragged and kicked her about the yard, and finally dealt her a further blow on the head, this time with a pail, and in- flicted another wound. Death resulted from the injuries caused by the prisoner's savagery. THE GALWAY MURDER.—The inquest on the body of Moylan, the Galway farmer who was shot dead while in the company of his wife one night last week, has resulted in an open verdict. Mrs. Moylan and her brother were among the witnesses examined. Their evidence was strangely at variance in an important particular. The woman stated with regard to the piece of writing alleged to have been left on the body of the deceased that she told her brother of it while they were on the way to the scene of the murder, whereas the brother said he never heard of the paper until his sister showed it to him OR the spot. On the man stating in evidence th t he did not know any reason why Moylan should be shot, the Coroner told him he lid not believe him. Mrs. Moylan and two men are in custody on suspicion.
ST. HELENS NEWS. SOLTRD AT LesTi—What Mr. Bradlaugh was always doing at the "bar" of the House.—Drinking °AMUCK'S SODA WATER.—Ad 4.

44We are pleased to state that Mr. J. Birtles, of the Pres- cot Board Schools, has been appointed maater of the Downall Green Church schools, Ashton. Tlr_re were IS7 applicants for the post. Sr. HELENS SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE —The ordinary monthly meeting of this committee was to be held on the 21st inst., but owing to their not being a quorum of members present no business was done. The only mem- bers present were Messrs. T. Cook and Massey. THE CIRCUS, Sr. HELENS.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, Mr. Mearns applied on behalf of the proprietor, Mr. Culeen, for a music license for the circus. Mr. Hart, the borough surveyor, in ansWer to the Bench, said he thought the circus was in a perfectly safe condition, and could b 3 emptied in a very short time in case of neces- sity. The license was granted. THEFTS FROM THE MARKET.—At the St. Helens Pollee Court. on Monday a lad named William Hill, 13 years of age, was convicted of having stolen a pair of trousers from a stall in the Market-place on Saturday night, and was ordered to have 12 strokes with a birch rod.—Sarah Pennington, a middle-aged married woman, who lives in Glover-street, was convicted of having stolen a pair of boots from a market stall, and was fined £l.

PRESCOT SCHOOL BOARD.—An adjourned meeting of this Board was held on Friday last, far the purpose of electing an assistant mistress of the girls' department. Three applicants had been selected to appear before the Board. The success- ful one was Miss A. E. Sayer, of Newtown, Montgomery- ehire, who commences with the salary of £4O per annum. The members present were Messrs. L, Evans (chairman), T. P. Hewitt, J. T. Hale, and H. Fogg. DEFRAUDING THE RAILWAY COMPANY. Thos. Elland an elderly man, was, on Friday, charged at the St. Helens Police Court with having travelled by railway from Earles- town to St. Helens without a ticket.—Mr. Preston, junr., prosecuted on behalf of the London and North-Western Railway. The defendant, on arriving from Earlestown at St. Helens Junction, told the station-master that he had lost his ticket and had no money, but if he were allowed to go on to St. Helens he would there find money. On arriving at St. Helens, however, he told ;he ticket collector that he had not come by train, and passed out. The guard of the train from St. Helens Junction, however, brought him back. —He was fined 20s. and costs. MANIFESTING A SEASONABLE SPlRlT.—•Thomas Walsh was charged, on remand, at St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, with having unlawfully wounded a man named Haywood at St. Helens Junction mil the 15th inst.—Sup- erintendent Johnson read a doctor's certificate, which certi- fied that Haywood, one of whose legs had been broken, would not be able to appear at court for two or three weeks yet, and asked for a further remand.—Mr. J. 0. Swift, who appeared for the prisoner, read a letter signed by Haywood stating that he did not wish to press the case.—Superinten- dent Johnson was of opinion that it was an improper note— Mr. Swift thought it was a very proper note at the time of the year, and manifested a very seasonable spirit.—Anothisr remand for a week was granted, bail of one £4O and two £2O being accepted. ALLEGED ATTEMPT TO DEFRAUD, THE LONDON AND NORTH-WESTERN —A middle-aged man named John Hamp- son, said to live in Ashcroft-street, Parr, was on Monday charged at the St. Helena Police Court with having travelled by rail from St. Helens Junction to St. Helens without a ticket on Saturday night. It seemed that the prisoner had gone from Rainhill to St. Helens Junction, and there given up his ticket to that place. Being in a drunken condition he was refused a ticket for St. Helens, but man- aged to get into the train, and came to St. Helens where he was detained. The Bench decided that they could not con- vict, as the prisoner had been refused a ticket, and had shown no intention to defraud. If he was drunk, they considered he ought not to have been allowed to get into , the train.

KICKING A WIFE AT ST. HELENS.—Jos. Gre,pty, of 27, Crab-street, was, on Wednesday, charged at the St. Helens Police Court with having assaulted his wife.—From the statement of Supt. Johnston, who applied for a remand owing to the complainant not being able to appear, it seemed that on Christmas Eve the prisoner's wife had pro- vided him with tea about seven o'clock, and then gone out. She returned about 11 o'clock, when the prisoner asked her for some supper, upon which an altercation seems to have taken place between them. In stepping out of the way of her husband the complainant fell, and he then, it is said, kicked her so eavagely about the body that she became in- sensible, and was thought to be dead, for about three hours. She, however, came round, and is now recovering.—The re- mand was granted till Friday, bail being accepted. CHRISTMAS AT PRESCOT UNION WORKHOUSE.—The usual Christmas treat was given to the inmates of the above by the Guardians of the Union. The dinner took place in the large dining-room of the building, which was decorated very profusely and adorned with mottoes which. together with the roast beef and plum pudding, must have caused a feeling of joy and gladness throughout the whole house. The Guardians present were Mr. J. T. Hall, chair- man of the Workhouse Committee; Mr. J. Leatherbarrow ; Dr. Hall, the Union medical officer, was also present. Mr. James Berry, who we believe has attended on similar occa- sions for the past seven or eight years, and Mr. Flint per- formed the arduous task of carving for nearl 500 appetites. The master and matron very ably superintended the whole of the arrangements, which were admirably carried out. After justice had been done to the good things provided, on the motion of Mr. Berry, three lusty and hearty cheers were given for the guardians for providing such an excel- lent dinner. In the evening the hall had been cleared out and provision made for dancing. Messrs. Welsby's noted band supplied suitable music, and the: light fantastic toe was tripping till half-past 12 o'clock in the morning. After according a well-deserved hearty vote of thanks to the master and matron, the company separated.

THE QUEEN'S ARMS DIVIDING SOCIETY. SUTTON.—The annual meeting of this society was held at the Queen's Arms Hotel, Sutton, On Christmas Eve, when the dividend of 15s. (31. per full member was paid, after which upwards of 40 sat down to a substantial dinner which gave great satisfaction. A meeting was afterwards held, Mr. Kilgour (the president) occupying the chair. He proposed the usual loyal toasts. The secretary was then called on to read the balance sheet. "The town and trade of St Helens, and our representatives in council" was given by the vice- president (Mr. Wilscn), and responded to by Coun. Hanson, who thought there was a large trade being done by the manufacturers of St. Helens, if they might judge from the traffic, which had been great for some time. It was encouraging to the community that the signs of things generally indicated a good outlook for progress. The work of the Town Council, which had been spoken of, was not always smooth and easily executed. In complying with the Government requirements as to sanitary arrangements, some improvements were being adopted for the preservation of health. The recent establishment of a borough bench in St. Helens was shown to be an a4vantage, and the credit for this was to be attributed to the exertions of their senior representative, Councillor Massey. (Applause.) He con- gratulated the society on the progress in numbers, which were nearly doubled in a year. He also gave a few practical hints, which appeared to be appreciated. He also spoke of the advantages of a public library.—After a patriotic toast. Mr. Hanson proposed "The Trustees," and complimented the society on having such practical gentlemen to take the responsibility of the important office.—Mr. J. Whittaker (contractor) responded. Songs were given by various gentlemen, and, after a compliment Iry toast to the host and hostess, the proceedings terminated with the singing of ths, National Anthem,

The amendment was then put to the meeting, nine voting for and six against. ' D. its.T,EELE drew attention to the fact that several peresms tiresentilad not voted, and he thought they ought to leave the room. (Laughter.) Dr. MACDOUGALL : That's cutting it too fine. Mr. SHAW: Dr. Steele considers he is at a meeting of the Commissioners. (Renewed laughter.) The CHAIRMAN declared the amendment to be carried. Mr. COLEBURN said he found that six of the candidates were in connection with the Parish Church, four in connec- tion with Trinity, five nominattd by the Wesleyans, and two independent candidates—Mr. Pritchard and Mr. Hand- ley—besides the Rev. Father Fennelly. He had put to Dr. McDougall alone—(laughter)—but he believed he had now become a Churchman. (Dr. McDougall: "No, no.") He therefore suggested that as they had representatives in the room from the different bodies they should say what mem- bers they would like to serve on the Board. If this was done they could proceed to business. Dr. STEELE moved that the retiring members of the I Board be re-elected; Mr. G. S. Hazlehurst being substituted
for Mr. Simpson. Mr. Klfivrrox seconded the motion. Hitherto their elections had been conducted on denominational lines. Three of the members of the Board were Churchmen, and

he prestuned the Church party would keep them there. Two were Wesleyans, and considering the educa- tional work which that body had done in the town; he thougut they were fairly entitled to them. Personally he should be glad to see undenominational education in the country, but they had not got it, and whatever they might say if it came to an election it would be conducted on de- nominational lines, and would not be a ratepayers' so much _ . _ _
as a sectarian question, and much bad feeling and bitterness would be engendered. Mr. WATSON proposed as an amendment that Mr. Handley take the place of Mr. Simpson.

Mr. LEACH thought the whole matter lay in a nutshell. The church had three members, and if it went to an election there was no doubt they would carry them. The Weslevans would carry two, and so far as he could see the remaining seat lay between Mr. Pritchard and Mr. Handley. The Rev. W. PRESTON supported Dr. Steele's motion. Mr. CARTWRIGHT seconded Mr. Watson's amendment. Mr. HANDLEY before the amendment was put wished to say a few words. He considered at the first that it was a mistake to make the formation of the School Board a

denominational question. (Dr. McDougall: A terrible mis- take.) His opinion was still unaltered, and he believed they were not then trying to arrive at a result in accordance with the Elementary Education Act, which did not recognize one sect or the other. The Act was a matter for the rate- payers entirely. It was manifest this was so, for the money that was found was not intended for the furtherance of denominational schools. The primary cause of the Act be- ing passed was to educate the children of the country, and for that purpose the public purse was to be drawn upon. The public purse was the ratepayers' purse, and in some sense the ratepayers ought to be represented cn the Board. The Board had been parcelled out in a family way, being divided amongst the different churches and chapels. Mr. Leach, very kindly no doubt, was trying to pit him (Mr. Handley) against Mr. Pritchard,but he should be sorry to see Mr. Pritchard removed from the Board by any act of his. , (Hear, hear.) He said it without fear of contradiction, or without making any invidious comparisons, that no better member had been on the School Board for the ratepayers of Runcorn outside denominational lines than Mr. Pritchard— (hear, hear)—and they did not look upon him as a denomi- nationalist. It then being purely a ratepayers' question to find not £l2O but £4OO a year, he thought it was right that the ratepayers, either by contest or in some proper way, should have a full voice in the election of their members. This could only lee done effectively by a contest, though he (Mr. Handley) did not wish to force one. What was to be done? Were they to go on denominational lines or on the broader principle of the education of the children? The chairman had given them his opinion, and it was the opinion of other outside the School Board, that before long they woud have to provide additional accommodation. If there was now a lack of accommodation to the extent of $OO, in three or four months more they would have to provide accommation for three or four hundred more children through the alteration in the boundaries of the township. If the denominations were going to find the money, he would have no objection to their parcelling it out as had been suggested, because they who paid the piper had a right to choose the tune. His nomination had been sent in twice over, and in an informal way three times, and to his nomination there had been affixed the names of more Chnrchmen than Nonconformists; , but it had not been on Nonconformist or on Church lines that he was nominated, but simply that he might be a rate- payers' representative. He left it to the meeting to pass ' whatever resolution they pleased, but he reserved his right I of private judgment. Mr. Smog said before the vote was put to the meeting'he I might say that his time was so much taken up with other matters that he had no intention of devoting any to the education of the children of Runcorn, and he intended to ' withdraw.

Mr. Farm said he did not know whether the Wesleyans present were willing to forego the usual number of candi- dates. For his own part, although a Wesleyan, he did not care so long as they got candidates who would do their duty. He therefore had pleasure in supporting Mr. Handler.

Mr. KNIVETON said be happened to know the feeling of many Wesleyans on the subject, and he believed they were very anxious that Mr. Hazlehurst should take the vacant seat. He endorsed every word that Mr. Handley had said. He thought the conducting of the election on denominational principles was not in harmony with the Education Act at all. Still such was the fact they had to face, and if there was an election it would be on denominational lines, and the result would be an amount of bitterness that it was de- sirable to avoid. It would be a denominational election and they knew that the result would be as it had been for the past three years. Mr. HANDLEY : I understand from Dr. McDougall that Mr. Hazehurst had withdrawn to avoid a contest. Dr. MCDOUGALL read the following telegram, which he had received from Mr. Hazlehurst :—" Have pleasure in ac- cepting nomination but not for contest." The amendment to the effect that the six retiring members should be re-elected, Mr. Handley being sub- stituted for Mr. Simpson, was then put and lost by eleven votes to six. Several of the candidates then present then withdrew their nominations if a contest could thereby be avoided. After some conversation as to the most expedient course to be pursued, the members of the Wesleyan denomination present, at the suggestion of the meeting, withdrew for private conference. On returning, Mr. SHAW announced that the gentlemen who had retired were quite willing to accept a s their candi- dates Mr. Pritchard, Mr. Norman, and Mr. Wil ham Hand- ley, and that they would get Mr. Hazlehurst to withdraw with the other Nonconformists. They thought the best way would be by arranging a time to meet on Monday, when all the withdrawals could be delivered by a person to be appointed to Mr. Linaker. The CHAIRMAN: Of course if the withdrawals are not here the others don't withdraw. Mr. SHAW was understood to say that if all the with- drawals were not in time to be delivered then none would be sent in and there would be a contest.

It was then decided that Mr. Kniveton should meet the Rev. Canon Barclay at one o'clock on Monday afternoon, for the purpose of receiving the withdrawals and conveying them before four o'clock on the same afternoon to the offices of Mr. H. Linaker, Frodsham.
The proceeding; then terminated. A COMPROMISE EFFECTED.

The arrangement come to on Saturday night was some- what unexpectedly upset on Monday, and had not one of the candidates been willing to sacrifice a position to which he was justly entitled a contest must have taken place. It seems that on Sunday Dr. McDougall, who was Mr. Hazleharst's nominee, communicated with that gentleman by telegram, stating that Mr. Shnpson's seat rested between himself and another, and asking him to forward his with- drawal to the proper quarters. We understand that Mr. Hazlehurst on Monday replied that he would decide his course of action on learning the name of the gentleman chosen to fill the seat. He also asked to be informed whether the candidate was a Wesleyan. A hurried meeting of candidates was held in the Commis- sioners' Board-room, and it was agreed that the only way in which a contest could be avaided would be to ask Mr. Handley to withdraw. A general feeling prevailed that Mr. Hazlehurst's withdrawal would come in due course, but in- asmuch as he would then be a member of the new Board it was understood that he should resign his seat in favour of Mr. Handley. This arrangement met with the approval of the Church of England representatives and the Wealeyans present, and Mr. Fisher and Mr. Kniveton were directed to proceed to Dutton Workhouse, where Mr. Handley was attending as a Guardian, and inform that gentleman of the decision which had been arrived at. They were accom- panied by Mr. Thomas Handley, who was the bearer of a telegram of which we give an exact copy :---" From G. S. Hazlehurst, Banbury, to W. Handley, Bridge-street, Run- corn.—l cannot possibly consent to only one Wesleyan on the School Board. Trust you will see reasonableness of this, and • not contest. Any change in constitution of Board will lead to endless disputes. Please wire reply." Mr. Handley at once wrote out his withdrawal and forwarded it with the others, which were in readiness, to Frodsham, where they were lodged within the specified time, and a contest averted. The Rev. Canon Barclay and Mr. T. Norman were, we may state, in favour of the arrangement which the candidates had come to at Runcorn. The new Board will thus be constituted of three Church of England representatives, two Wesleyan,one Presbyterian, and one Roman Catholic, the names being as follows :—The Rev. ; Canon BaTclay, the Rev. Father Fennelly, Messrs. R. Lea, . P. Briscoe, T. Norman, Geo. S. Hazlehurst, and James Pritchard. If Mr. Hazlehurst decides to carry out the arrangement which his friends have made for him, Mr. Handley will, of course, be elected his successor.

fEARLESTOWN NEWS. THE GOSPEL MISSION CHOIR.—The Gospel Tempe- nce Mission conducted in the Co-operative Hall is leaking satisfacne y progress, and those in charge of the mission deserve thanks for the efforts they have put forth. On Christmas Eve the members of the choir and a few fr:eeds met by arrangement and proceeded carol-singing at the residences of Mr. J. W. Emmett, Mr. Harwood, the Rev. H. E. Smith (curate of Earlestown), and other gentlemen and , friends. The singers separated about six o'clock on Christ- mas morning after doing a good work in the early hours of the morning. CROW-LANE CATHOLIC SCHOOL—A very pleasant and enjoyable gathering was held in St. Mary's Catholic Hall, Crow-lane, on Christmas Day. About 100 members of the congregation and friends were present, and thoroughly en- joyed themsAves in dancing, singing, and ether similar ways. Among those present were the Rev. Fattier Lennon, who briefly addressed the assembled company, congratu- lating them upon their enjoyment, and wishing them the compliments of the season. Refreshments were provided for the party, who spent a very pleasant evening. CHRISTMAS AT EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON. Another Christmas has come and gone, and once again the advent of a new year is at hand. The proverbial "snow covered fields" have hitherto been conspicuous by their absence during the present season, at least, so far as this neighbour- hood is concerned. The weather has been exceedingly mild for the time of the year, and Christmas Day was ushered in with a somewhat gloomy and watery atmosphere. Rain fortunately held off, however, and pleasure-seekers were well favoured in that respect. After the closing of the public- houses at eleven o'clock on Christmas Eve many persons were to be met with in the streets, while numerous bands of carol-singers were to be seen and heard. As a rule the people were well behaved and orderly, and comparatively few disorderly persons troubled the police officers. The day was, of course, observed as a general holiday, and a goodly number of persons left the town. The Vulcan Ironfoundry, and the printing works of Messrs. Geo. McCorquodale and Co., resumed work on Wednesday morning, while the Viaduct Waggon Works were stopped until Thursday morning. Special services were preached in several places of worship in the forenoon, while the Primitive Methodists of Earles- town held their annual tea party in the afternoon. ST. PETER'S CHURCH, NEWTON.—The Rev. J. C. Clore (curate) preached in St. Peter's Church, Newton, on Christ- mas Day forenoon, when a special service was held, at which there was a moderately large congregation. The in- terior of the edifice was very pleasingly and tastefully decorated for the occasion by Miss Pearson, Miss Birley, Miss MeCorquodale, Miss Gillespie, Miss Devereux, Mr. W. Birley, and others, who bad evidently spared no pains in making an attractive display. The bottom of the window behind the chancel was bordered with holly and berries, with a star of beautifully white amaranths in the centre, and a vase of flowers in each corner. Beneath was the text, "Unto you is born this day a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord." The front of the choir stalls was bedecked with leaves, berries, Sic., with the following words conspicuous, " Hark the herald angels sing, glory to the new-born King." The pulpit was very neatly decorated—the holly leaves and berries being most artistically arranged round the edges and sides, while on each panel was a carefully-formed device of cotton wool. The reading desks and lantern did not escape the attention of the decorators, and the fent at the opposite end of the church was far from being the least attractive of the decorations. It was undoubtedly a skilfully worked framework by which it was almost covered, and it formed one of the principal attractions. EXTRAORDINARY DEATH AT EARLESTOWN: DROWNED IN SIX lercuEs or WATER. A shocking discovery was made in Fairclough-street, Earlestown, on Christmas Day forenoon, when Mr. John Hatton, grocer, discovered the dead body of a man (afterwards ascertained to be Thomas Burke, a labourer, lodging in E+rle-street), in an old lime pit situate a little from the road, straight opposite the entrance to the Liberal Club. The pit contained no more than about six inches of water, and the deceased was found lying face downwards therein at a quarter to eleven in the forenoon. The news quickly spread, and a large number of persons visited the spot during the day, and the 1 fact that the deceased had a -wound on his forehead caused many statements to be circulated, some of which were to the effect that 131.rke had been murdered, and the body thrown into the pit. It has, however, since been ascertained that the deceased was in a very drunken state early on Christmas morning—so drunk indeed that he could hardly stand. He was last seen alone by a boy named Donoughoe shortly after one o'clock, and nothing; further was heard of him until he was found under the cir- cumstances narrated. An inquest on the body was held at the Oddfellows' Arms,Legh-street, on Wednesday afternoon, before Mr. Rowbottom, deputy coroner. Evidence to the foregoing effect was given by Mrs. Jennings, lodging at the same house as the deceased, Mrs. Galligkan, the boy Donoughoe, and Mr. John Hatton, grocer.— P.C. Lloyd stated that after receiving informa.tien of the discovery he went to the place indicated, and found the body of deceased lying on the bank of the lime pit. It was conveyed to deceased's lodgings in Legh-street, when he (witness) searched his clothes, and found over ss. in his pockets. He also examined the body, and found no nuirks of violence with the exception of a slight cut on the fore- head, which might have been caused by deceased falling into the pit, which contained several pieces of brick and slates.—The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased was "Accidentally drowned." EARLESTOWN PRIMITIVE METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL: ANNUAL TEA MEETING—TiIe annual tea meeting in con- nection with the Earlestown Primitive Methodist School was held in the schoolroom, Legh-street, on Christmas Day, and proved to be a very successful and enjoyable gathering. The room had been tastefully decorated by several of the teachers, numerous pieces of holly, coloured papers, and seasonable mottoes being pleasingly displayed. About 130 persons sat down to an excellent tee, after which the chair was occupied by the Rev. F. N. Shimmin, minister, who was supported by Mr. Woods, superintendent of the Sunday school. After devotional exercises, the rev, chairman ex- pressed the appreciation of the committee at the numerous attendance, and heartily wished the congregation the compliments of the season, trusting that their happiness would be derived from pure sources. Those who took part in the entertainment which followed were— Messrs. Jas. Worslev, C. Kelly, F. Begnall, John Potter, John Worsley, W. \Vorsley, James Henry Woods, John Richard Clarke, George Clarke, Alfred Clarke. J. W. Banton, Jos. T. Banton, Albert Banton, Alfred Morris, Richard Sephton, Joseph Hodgkinson, J. W. Auetin, John Pendrey ; and Miss Woreley, Miss Woods, Miss Martha Massey, Miss Alice Massey, Miss Mary E. Whittaker, Miss Nelly Thompson, Miss Elizabeth Clarke, Miss Harrison, and Miss Thompson. A capital stlectien of music was given by the choir, ably led by Mr. Banton; and Mr. Austin ac- companied on the harmonium. Miss Dickens sang the solo " When the mists are rolled away ;" and Mr. R. Sprostien effectively gave "Where is my wander- ing -boy to-night." Dialogues, entitled "The good old times," " The gospel ship," "Fault finding," and " The trials of a patient woman," were excellently gone through, while the recitations were given in a very satisfactory man- ner. At the close of the meeting Mr. Woods moved a hearty vote of thanks to the cliei:reen, ladies who presided at the tea tables, the choir, reciters, and all who had assisted, which was seconded by Mr. Thomas Cl irks, and accorded with acclammation.—On the evening of the following day (Wednesday) the annual treat to the scholars and children was given, About 200 attended and were regaled with tea, bread and butter, currant bread, Sm. At the subsequent pro- ceedings Mr. Woods (superintendent) presided, and the scholars gave a nice selection of recitations. Various games were afterwards indulged in, all present thoroughly enjoy- ing themselves. _
CHARGE OF ASSAULT AGAINST A COLLIERY MANAGER.

Robert Turner, a colliery manager under Messrs. Bourne and Robinson, was on Friday charged at the St. Helens Policct Court with having assaulted William Hayes, a lad who lives with his parents in Warrington New-road.—Mr. Malkin prosecuted, and Mr. J. 0. Swift defended.—Mr. Malkin stated that on. Monday, the 10th inst., Hayes was engaged in Sherdley mine when Turner and an underlooker named Thomas Williams came to where he was. Williams asked him why he was not "pushing down," and he re- plied he csuld not dot do that, as he was alreasiy doing two ,lads' work. Turner said he must do it, and on Hayes saying again that he could not, the defendant struck him on the ankle with a stick he had in his hand. Hayes fell to the ground, when the defendant, not content with what he had done, got hold of him by the collar and inflicted certain blows on his left side. Hayes got up and ran into another portion of the pit closely pursued by defendant, but no fur- ther blows were struck, and ultimately be was sent out of the pit. On getting home his mother examined his ankle, and found it in a very bad state. . She undressed and put him to bed, and then sent for Dr. Hayes, who, however, did not come. Finding the complainant getting worse, she sent for Dr. Ricketts, and he would tell the bench that he found the lad suffering from bruises on the ankle and body which must have arisen from blows. The complainant had not been able to go to work since.—ln defence, it was admitted that Turner had struck the complainant with a small stick, being irritated by several instances of culpable neglect, but it was contended that the hurt to the ankle had been caused by a fall, or by the attempts of Hayes to kick Turner.— Before the evidence for the defence was called, the Bench intimated that they did not look upon the matter as being serious, and would simply impose a fine of 108 and costs.

PRESCOT PARISH CHORCH.—Tuesday last b eing Christ- mas Day, the Parish Church was decorated in honour of the great religious festival. Services were held, and attended by large congregations. The musical part of the service was effectively rendered by the very efficient choir. FATAL EFFECTS FROM THE UPSET TING OF A PARAFFIN LAMP.—An inquest was held at the :Nlans Arms, School- brow, on Monday,.before Mr. Barker, coroner, on the body of Benjamin Jolley, carrier, of Back William-street, who died under painful circumstances on the previous morning. Tke deceased was 67 years of age, and from the evidence adduced it appeared that he was reading in his house some weeks ago when he was seized with a "fainting bout," to which he was accustomed. In falling he upset a varaffin latrp, and was so severely burnt that he died at half-past nine on Sunday morning last. He had been at- tended by Dr. Joseph. There was, the widow of the de- e tsed stated, no one in the house at the time of the acci- e,at, and every attention was paid to hint, not only by the cl ctor but by herself. The itry returned a verdict of "Accidental death."
A MILITARY BURGLAR AT WARRINGTON.

John Patric a O'Brien, a private in the East Yorkshire Regiment of Foot, was charged at the Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, with burglarously breaking and entering the vaults and dwelling-house of Sherwood Wiseman, the Manx Arms, School Brow, between a quarter to twelve on Friday, and six on the morning of Saturday, and stealing 1 pint bottle of rum, 14 half-ounce packets of twist tobacco, and a clay pipe of the value of 35. 91—The prisoner, it appears is a native of Glasgow, and a private in the East Yorkshire Regiment of Foot, but had been absent from his regiment since the 10th inst. Shortly after nine o'clock on Friday night, he entered the Manx Arms, and had two or three glasses of beer between then and twenty-five minutes to eleven. The landlord and several customers conversed with prisoner, who at length asked to be shown to the rear of the premises. He came back, drank his beer, and left at twenty-five minutes to eleven. The landlord fastened the house up at eleven o'clock, but sat smoking till shortly before twelve, when he retired to bed, leaving his pipe on the mantelpiece. Between three and four o'clock in the morning the landlady, Mrs. Wiseman, beard some one astir, as she thought, on the landing or stairs, and she shouted out, thinking it to be the servant, "Annie, Annie, what are you doing ? " She heard nothing more, however, and went to sleep. Mrs. Wiseman rose about half-past six, and on going downstairs she noticed one or two drawers oat of the dresser, and which appeared to be ransacked. She thereupon called her husband, who went to the till, and dis- covered that although the lock had been tampered with and the counter cut about, the thief had not succeeded in his pur- pose. Several knives had been displaced, and a quantity of twist tobacco, some rum, and other things were missed. The burglary was reported to the police, and suspicion fell on the prisoner. During Saturday it was ascertained that the prisoner about five o'clock that morning had surrendered himself to the sergeant on duty at Orford Barracks as a deserter, and several ounces of twist tobacco were found In his overcoat. Sergeants Berry, Cox, Spinks, and other officers instituted inquiries which ended -in peisoner being brought to the lock-up, and then some more tobacco was discovered on his being searched, and which corresponded to that sold by prosecutor. A square in the window at the back of the public-house was smashed, and by this means prisoner had obtained ingress and egress, and when Mrs. Wiseman heard the noise referred to it was doubtless caused through prisoner smashing the glass.—Prisoner pleading not guilty, was committed for trial at the next Liverpool Assizes.

A FARMER'S ADVENTURE AT WARRINGTON. A CHRIS TMAS EVE EPISODE. At the Warrington Borough Court, on Wednesday, Patrick Thomas O'Brien, labourer, 6, Jones' Buildings—a powerful looking fellow—was charged with being gunk in Butter- market-street on Christmas Eve, and with absaulting Henry Wolfe, farmer, Rixton Hall. Wolfe was also charged with being drunk in Buttermarket-street whilst in charge of a horse and trap and with assaulting O'Brien.—The Chief- Constable, in stating the facts of the case, said they were of a somewhat intricate nature. It seemed that ahout a quar- ter past eleven on Monday night Mr. Wolfe was proceeding along Sankey-street, driving a rather spirited horse. When at Market Gate, however, there being a crowd of people, he slackened his speed. In passing through however, he was I stopped by Inspector Berry, who noticed the horse's trace I was broken off at the side and called Mr. Wolfe's attention to this. Mr. Wolfe was apparently much irritated at the delay thus caused, but he shortly afterwards continued his journey, driving down Buttertnarket-street at a gentle pace, and when opposite the Pelican pablic-house he found a group of men, O'Brien being one of them. Mr. Wolfe's horse's head touched the arm or shoulder of O'Brien, who thereupon turned round and struck the animal violently on the neck. Mr. Wolfe, who was very much annoyed, said to O'Brien, " If you strike my horse once I will strike you twice," and he did strike, and no time was lost in one, two, or three blows being returned by O'Brien, who subsequently knocked Mr. Wolfe to the ground and kicked him a number lof times. Although the crowd assembled was a mixed one the majority appeared in favour of Mr. Wolfe, as was shown in the help they aforded the police in getting O'Brien to the lock-up. Mr. Wolfe drove on aeaing, but had not gone far before his vehicle nnfortunately came in con- tact with a cart belonging to iMr. John Por- i ter, fishmonger, tine and the traps bacame loceed and it was with great difficulty they were cleared. A gentleman narnedllyam,who was with Mr. Wolfe,was thrown out on the ground and lay insensible tor some time. Mr. Wolfe, it appeared, became very excited and defiant, and he was at length taken to the station house on the charge of drunkenness, and his troubles for that day concluded by be— ing lodged in a cell, but he was liberated on bail on Chriet- mae morning.—Evidence was then adduced. Inspector Singleton said he had known Mr. Wolfe for 25 years, but never heard of drunkenness or furious driving on his part before.—Mr. Wolfe stated that he was fearfully abused in, , Buttermarket-street by O'Brien, and his horse became ex- ceedingly restive. He could not control the animal as he would liked ti have done, and she had quite her " metal " up when she entangled the vehicle with that of Mr. Porter's. —The prisoner O'Brien said with regard to his complaint against Mr. Wolfe, that when the latter was driving down , the street he (O'Brien) had his back to them. The horse's head came over his shoulder, and thinking he would receive a bite or be run ever he hit the animal , with his open hand. Mr. Wolfe than said "If anybody strikes my horse once I will strike him twice" I and standing up in the trap he struck him two blows with the whip. Mr. Wolfe then got out, wishing to continue the ! scrimmage, and afterwards what he (O'Brien) did was in • self-defence. He admitted having had a drop," but if he ; had been perfectly sober he would have defeuded himself in the same way.—ihe magistrates retired for consideration, • and on their return the Mayor seid they were of opinion ; that the else of drunkenness against O'Brien was clearly ; proved, and for that offence he would be fined Sc. and costs 7 or seven days. They also thought that the assault csne- mitted on Mr. Wolfe was proved, aed for which they in- •flicted a fine of £1 and costs. On the other hand they con- sidered that Mr. Wolfe ought not to have assaulted O'Brien with the whip in the roa.un-r described, but he did so, and • they Ynust fine Mr. Wolfe 103. and costs. The charge of drunkenness, however, against Mr. Wolfe was open to great doubt and they would give him the benefit of it in dismie- sing it. The Mayor added that it was a pity Mr. Wolfe took the law into his own hands in any way.

div.head: DEATH OF MRS. MATTHEWS, OF EARLESTOWN.
div.p: DEATH OF MRS. MATTHEWS, OF EARLESTOWN.

It is with the deepest regret we have to-day to record the. sudden death of Mrs Matthews, wife of the Rev. T. R. Matthews, vicar of Earlestown, which sad event took place at the Vicarage, early yesterday (Thursday) morning. The painful news could scarcely be credited in many qutrters, but when its truth became known a very general feeling of sincere sorrow and sympathy was Expressed for Mr. Mat- thews and his family in their bereavement. The death came as a shock upon Mrs. Matthews' more intimate friends—and they were many—and it is fervently hoped that the differ- ence in church matters will now be entirely dropped. Mrs. Matthews had not been very well for some considerable time, Lut it was only about a fortnight or three weeks ago that she was noticed to be more than usually indisposed. It was deemed advisable to call in Dr. Handyside, and since then he has attended her. Notwithstanding all medical skill could do, however, she gradually declined. She was not confined to bed until Wednesday last. She then seemed to be cheery ond happy, but about six o'clock in the evening, she became insensible and never recovered consciousness. Dr. Hanclyside was immediately sent for, and his assistant, Jr. Foulson, attended, but Mrs. Matthews was past recovery, and the apoplectic seizure she was then suffeiing from proved fatal about two o'clock on thn follow- ing morning. The deceased lady was married to the Rev. T. R. Matthews 27 years ago, and she leaves three children—two daughters and a sou—to mourn her loss. She was 48 years of age at the time of her death. During the seven years she has lived in Earlestown she formed a wide circle of friends, and on her demise becom- ing known, the Rev. Canon Whitley and other friends visited the Vicarage for the purpose of sympathising with the bereavei family. The sad event has been a severe blow to Mr. Matthews, and we are sorry to learn that that geitie- man was confined to his bed yesterday (Thursday). It is almost needless to add that the usual weekly service held on Thursday nights was dispensed with last evening in conse- quence of Mrs. Matthews' death.

NINTH LANCASHIRE (WARRINGTON) RIFLE VOLUNTEERS' DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES. - On Saturday afternoon the prizes given by the tradesmen of Warrington to the mem- bars of this corps were distributed in the Drill Hall by Cap- tain Litton and Captain Ridgway, there being also present Captain Thompson and Lieutenant Buckton, in addition to a good muster of the men. Captain Litton said it had baen his happy lot for several years to present them with the prizes so kindly given by the tradesPenple of Warnngtou. It showed that the services of the Volunteers were appre- ciated by their fellow-townsmen, and, happily, this year they had to thank the tradesmen for a much larger number as well as more baluable prizes that they had ever had. He thought it was a matter for congratulation to the Volunteers that their services were so much appreciated. The prizes he was about to distribute numbered 194. There were 529 members efficient that year, which he was pleased to say was an increase on the previous year, and the capitation grant earned amounted this year to £937 sq, which was also an adavnce upon the previous year.—Captain Ridgway, in a few remarks said he was very glad to see the prize com- mittee had done their duty so well. He thought all the shooting men ought to be proud of the manner in which that had been done. He was sure they would all accord their hearty thanks to the tradesmen of Warrington for having so liberally responded to their call for Christmas privs. In looking iver the Bat he was pleased to find that the B Company Um own) had turned up so well, no less than 35 men having taken prizes. He did not consider they were a shooting company, but still he was pleased to find that the men were gradually coming to the front in this spect. (Applause.)—The prizes having been distributed. I a usual vote of thanks were accorded, and the proceedings t,
