TEE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, DECEMBER 29, 1883.

The year which is just closing has been a comparatively uneventful one so far as Great Britain is concerned. We have not been en- gaged in any warlike operations, and our relations with foreign countries have been of the most amicable character. At home we have been able to turn our attention to domestic matters; and but for the fact that trade has been dull, and that we have been threatened with extinction b) the disciples of the "gospel of dynamite "—many of which threats have not, however, been carried out know of nothing which has disturbed the even tenour of our ways. Ireland has for years been a source of trouble, but happily during the past twelve months there have not been wanting signs of contentment in the sis- ter isle, and a growing disposition to live on more friendly terms with us We earnestly hope that this feeling may be cultivated in the coming year on both sides of the Channel.

The legislative efforts of the year may be briefly told. Parliament met on the r sth February,haVing held a session in the autunin previous for the reform of the rules of pro- cedure. The debate on the Address to the Throne occupied eleven nights, in many previous years it has not occupied more than one, and there is no reason why this year it should have absorbed so much time. The Address out of the way, quite a multitude of questions were as usual discussed, prominent amongst these being the Egyptian embroglio, in the course of the debates on which it was elicited that the cost of the Egyptian expedi- tion had been £4 500,000, of which the British Treasury defrayed £3,360,000, and the remainder fell upon India. What is known as the " Kilmainham Treaty" gave rise to a bitter controversy again and again renewed; but the question appears now to have been set at rest without any appreciable advantage to the Opposition. One of the most important measures which came before the House was the Affirmation Bill, the second reading of which, we regret to think, was rejected by a majority of only:three,-292 voting in its favour, and 289 against. This would not have occurred had Liberal members remained loyal to their principles, instead of allowing themselves to be governed by prejudice in their voting. One of the most satisfactory features of the Parliamentary Session was the Budget statement of Mr. CHILDERS, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, which provided for the introduction of six- penny telegrams, the reduction of the railway passenger duty, and a reduction also of the income tax to sd. in the pound. On the other hand, one of the most unsatisfactory features was the commotion caused by Mr. GLADSTONE'S agreement with " the Suez Canal Co., which agreement was in deference to public clamour abandoned. The House of Commons again endorsed Sir W. LAW- SON'S metion in favour of local, option regarding the traffic in drink; and on the Contagious Diseases (Women's) Act it passed a resolution by 182 to Iro against compul- sory • examination. The House passed a Bankruptcy Bill, a Patents Bill, an Agricul- tural Holdings Bill for England and another for Scotland, all excellet measures, besides many other bills of less importance. The House likewise passed an Explosive Bill, which greatly increases the penalty for employing destructive explosives against pro- perty, and gives extensive powers to the police to search for explosive materials The rapidity with which this Act was passed proved that the House can, when it chooses to apply itself, get through its work expediti- ously. Irish affairs attracted a great deal of attention, and the Home Rulers lost no opportunity of violently attacking the Govern- ment policy in Ireland. Mr. PARNELL'S Land Bill was lost by the large majority of 187, the numbers being zso for and 63 against. This surely was decisive enough. Amongst the measures which the House was obliged to drop was the bill for establishing a Court of Appeal in Criminal Cases, Lon- don Municipality Bill, Irish Sunday Closing Bill, Ballot Perpetuation Bill, &c. The Lords were, as usual, again at their foolish work. On the second reading they passed the bill legalising marriage with a deceased wife's sister, but changed their mind on the third reading, and threw the bill out. They also rejected a resolution in favour of opening the national museums on the Sunday; and they threw out the Scotch Local Government Bill, which had passed the Commons. It is need- less to say that, in addition to those already mentioned, many other subjects were dis- cussed in both houses of Parliament. -

Amongst the domestic and social events of the year may be mentioned the birth of a daughter to the Duke and Duchess of ALBANY. On the 17th March the QUEEN met with a slight injury to her knee, the result of slipping on the stairs, and it was at one time feared the accident would prove serious, but HER MAJESTY has now happily quite re- covered. In connection with Royalty we ought here to chronicle the dtath - on the 27th

March of JouN BROWN, HER MAJESTY'S faithful personal attendant, and which event cast for a time a gloom over the Royal House- hold. Considerable sensation was caused in the early part of the year by the suicide at Hounslow of a Dr. EDWARDES, partner to Dr. WHITAIARSPI, in consequence of charges brought against him by a wicked designing woman, and it transpired at the inquiry on the body of the deceased that his partner ;had been in league with the accuser, evidently from selfish motives. About the same time .the prosecution of Messrs. FOOTE, RAMSAY, and KEMP for a blasphemous libel in the Freethinket attracted much attention; whilst no little amusement was created by the ap- pearance of Mr. BIGGAR, M.P., in an action for breach of promise, the plaintiff coming off victorious with a verdict for £4OO. The attempt to blow up the Gas Works in Glasgow and the explosions at the Government offices in Westminster and the Times office in Print- ing House Square demonstrated that there were in this country believers in the "gospel of dynamite," and extraordinary precautions had therefore to be taken for the protection of public buildings as well as of our leadingpublic men; but the raid made by the Birmingham Police upon a dynamite factory there, and the startling disclosures which subsequently fol- lowed, enabled a check to be placed upon the evil designs of the dynamitards. It was found necessary, however, to make the law Telating to explosives more stringent, and accordingly the Hors SECRETARY ran through Parliament a bill with that object—at a speed said to be " unparalelled since the 'passing of the Habeas Corpus Act in 1866." A great many of the dynamitards were as we know brought to justice and severely punished. The mysterious explosions on the London underground railway, and the discovery only recently of a plot by some German Socialists to blow up the German Embassy, combined with rumoured attempts on the life of the -PRIME MINISTER and other members of the Cabinet, have caused considerable uneasiness amongst metropolitan and local police authorities; but it is hoped we have at length heard the last of these wicked conspiracies. Should they be matured, we are sure the law is powerful enough to cope with the emer- -gency, and to punish offenders. The calamities at sea during the year include the collision in the Mersey between the City of Brussels and the Kirby Hall; the wreck of .H.M S Lively, which had on board the Skye Crofters Commission on their tour of inquiry; the wreck of the St. Germaine, bouna for New York, in the English Channel, by which 18 lives were lost; and also the loss of the Daphne on being launched from the Clyde shipbuilding yard. It is not yet exactly known how many lives were lost; but 150 children were left fatherless by this last dis- aster. During the year there have been colliery explosions at Tyldesley and Barnsley; but the most serious is that which took place at Moorfield, near Accrington, whereby 68 persons were killed and 30 injured. Amongst other notable events of the year are the alleged attempt on the life of Lady FLORENCE DIXIE, which has been since proved a delusion; the success of Mr. BRAD- -LAUGH in the cause of CLARKE V BRAD- LAUGH; the outrage in St. Paul's Cathedral, .for which a man named CAmproN was fined Ls, with the alternative of a month's imprison- went; the distribution of honours to the troops uho served in the Egyptian campaign; the unveiling of the BEACONSFIELD statue in Westminster by Sir S. NORTHCOTE ; the estab- lishment of a new decoration for nurses, to be known as the Royal Red Cross; the open- ing of the International Fisheries Exhibition, one of the most successful schemes of the kind ever carried out; the barbarous proposal to exhume the remains Of SHAKESPEARE in order to ascertain the shape of the Poet's skull ; the establishment of the parcels post, which has proved to be of great service; the fire in a private lunatic asylum at Southwell Park, in which the doctor perished in at- tempting to save some of the patients; the establishment of a Land Nationalisation Society; the cruise of Mr. GLADSTONE in company with the poet TENNYSON in the Pembroke Castle, and of Sir S. NORTHCOTE in the Pandora; and what was called the " bombardment " of Woolwich by an acci- dental explosion of rockets. In literary cir- cles more especially surprise has been gener- ally expressed at the POET LAUREATE accept- ing a Peerage, which HER MAJESTY has just expressed her desire to confer upon him The year is also memorable in consequence of the great Reform demonstration at New- castle, at which so 000 persons attended; the Reform conference at Leeds; the proposal toteduce wages in the cotton trade: and the shocking accident at the Victoria Hall, Sun- derland, by which 120 childreh who attended a magical and ventriloquial entertainment there were killed. We ought not to omit to chronicle the death of MAR- WOOD, the executioner, and the fact that the Sheriffs of London and Middlesex received something like r .zoo applications by telegrams and otherwise for A_lARwoD's place. Irish events have again attracted a con- siderable amount of attention during the year. On the 2nd January Mr. BIGGAR was com- mitted for trial for using inflammatory language calculated to disturb the peace, but the prosecution was afterwards dropped. In the same month Messrs. HEALY, DAVITT, and QUINN were sent to prison for six months for violent speeches. Subsequently Mr. WILLIAM O'BRIEN, editor of United Ireland, was committed for trial for publishing a seditious libel in his journal; and two days afterwards he was elected member for Mal- low by a majority of 72 votes over MT. NAISH, the Government candidate. At a later period of the year the :Kerry Sentinel was seized, in consequence of printing a seditious handbill. The trial of the Invincibles, with its horrible details of the hair-breadth escapes of Mr. FoRsTER, and the way in which the murders of Lord FREDERICK CAVENDISH and Mr. BURKE were planned. it is unnecessaryto dwell upon. Sufficient it is that the Invincibles, with their "inner circle" of sworn assassins, have been found out and made to pay the penalty of their cowardly crimes with their lives There is to us but one regret, and that is that so many of the informers should have escaped the gallows. One, indeed the most infamous of the lot, JAMES CAREY. met his death on the high seas at the hands of O'DONNELL, who, there is ground for the be- lief, was sent after the notcrious Informer to take his life. This last was one of the great- est sensations of the year. What is known as the Sligo conspiracy, in which four men were indicted for having planned the demoli- tion of a portion of Weston House, in county Galway, with dynamite, has been unearthed, and the conspirators brought to justice. It seems that this diabolical outrage was planned because the agent of the property was unpopular. The detection of these and other crimes reflects credit on the Irish con- stabulary; but it is also in a great measure

due to the firm and energetic manner in which the provisions of the Crimes Act have been inforced by the LORD LIEUTENANT (Earl SPEN- CER) and the CHIEF SECRETARY (Mr.TREVEL- YAN). Unmistakeable evidence of dr.; benefits arising from recent legislation for Ireland was shown during the year. On the Ist May thetimeallowed to Irish tenan s to take advan- tage of the Arrears' Act expired. "It was then announced that about 136,000 holders made application, and the State contributed £Blo,ooo to wipe out arrears to the amount of two and a half millions sterling. In over 1,000 cases tenants applied for loans amoun- ing to the extent of £32,000 to be applied to the payment of rent arrears. The actual payments on account of arrears exceeded £250,000, while payment orders amounting to £500,000 were issued." This is very satis- factory, but in addition we have the test nony of Mr. Parnell that the Fisheries, the Tram- ways, and the Labourers' Acts of last session are "second in value only to the Land and Arrears Act." Mr. PARNELL'S position in the House of Commons has been strength- ened during the year by the election of Mr HEALY for County Monaghan and Mr. REDMOND for Wexford. Speaking of the former contest Mr. PARNELL said it would "prove as memorable in the annals of Ireland as the victory of O'CONNELL at Clare." The only other events worth men- tioning so far as Ireland is concerned are the opening of the Irish Lace Exhibition in June, which is found to have given an impetus to the trade in lace for which Ireland is noted; and the presentation of nearly Lq.0,000, the national tribute to Mr. PARNELL, this amount being subscribed by Irishmen at home and, abroad, and in opposition to the discourage- ment given to the movement at the Vatican. Trade, we regret to say, has not been good during the year, nor are there any signs of a speedy revival. The few sentences quoted below will convey a very clear conception of how matters have stood commercially :--"The economic history of the year is, for the most part, a record of disappointed hopes in the trading world. From time to time symptoms seemed to be presented that a business revival was in the course of sure though. slow development, and these indications, which found expression in the business reports issued' from various districts, encouraged a belief that the recovery which began at the end of 1879, and which had progressed with a few minor breaks until the autumn of had acquired a firm footing, and would not encounter any serious check. The rapidity with which the political struggle in Egypt was terminated, and the ingathering of a good harvest, had much to do with the fostering of this view, and for a time it actually served to re-awaken the previous activity. The movement was, however, short- lived. It was bred of a feeling of hopeful- ness that was to prove without solid founda- tion in actual existing conditions. Here and there complaints of slackness and despon- dency began to be heard; but it was some time before they embraced any really wide area of trade. Indeed, many branches which had previously felt the pinch of stagnation were yet buoyed up .by an expectation that t}-1 political quiet looked for from the Egyp"^ settlement, the subsidence of the French financial crisis, and the amelioration , in the affairs of the agricultural classes fol- 'owing on a favourable harvest, would prove the turning point in their careers, and they were content to ignore the past, to treat as a short state of probation the present, and to count on the immediate future as the sure haven for which they had so long struggled.l After a while the evidence became unmis- takeable that a real and definite recoil in the general trade current had set in, and that '! nothing short of a fortuitous set of conditions I would again make it resume its previous ' direction." The failure of Mr. MORRIS RANGER, of Liverpool, with liabilities esti- mated at £900,000, is perhaps the most notable event in the commercial world. Turning from our own to other countries, , we find that France during the past twelve months has been pursuing the same aggres- sive policy that has characterised her actions during the past few years. In 188 z Tunis . was the scene of her operations; in 1882 she I first laid hands on Madagascar, and she has not let go her hold yet; and this year, in consequence of her determination to prac- tically anne& the kingdom of Annam, she has been obliged to enter upon a war with China. , The Chinese seem determined to resist the i advance of the French on their southern dominions. Latest accounts point to a dis- position on the part of the two Powers to ac- cept the mediation of England, but should i this be cast aside we may look forward to a , long and sanguinary strugole. The deaths of M. GAMBETTA and the COMTE DE CHAM- BORD are two of the chief events of the year of a social character to be noted in France. In Egypt, the work of reform has proceeded slowly but surely, and our troops have been withdrawn according as circumstances allowed; but the recent sad disaster in the Soudan, resulting in the annihilation of HICKS PASHA and his army, will, we fear, disturb Egyptian affairs for some time to come. Our influence there, however, is still maintained. In Turkey, we note there has been a revival of the agitation for reforms in Armenia, and, as usual, the SULTAN has ordered a Commission to inquire into the grievances of the Armenians, which only means a shelving of the question. In Mon- tenegro, we notice a closer intimacy between PRINCE NICHOLAS and the SULTAN, the latter being at one time considered the inveterate foe of the former; in Bulgaria, there are signs of jealousy on the part of both Eastern Roumelians and Bulgarians at Russian domi- nation; whilst Servia shows an increased cordiality to Austria. A great calamity has befallen Italy this year in the disaster on the island of Ischia, by which 2,000 persons lost their lives. Spain has suffered from the operations of secret societies, but happily the conspiracy seems to have been in a great measure rooted out. In Germany, PRINCE BISMARCK'S influence is still potent, though there are not wanting indications that it is on the wane. The great event here has been the festivities in honour of the silver wedding of the CROWN PRINCE and PRINCESS. in Austria, the Socialist movement has come prominently to the front during the year Twenty-nine of these Socialists were tried, but only two were condemned to fifteen years' penal servitude, five were discharged for want of evidence, and the remainder were acquitted. In Russia, the all-absorbing event has been the Imperial Coronation. In America, we discern the feeling in favour of free trade is spreading, and we hope the Prin- ciple will soon be adopted. In our Indian possessions, we have pleasure in noting a steady development of the railway enterprise, which is destined to do so much good there. The Ilbert Bill has given rise to much bitter- ness. not only in India, but elsewhere ; we are glad, however, to find that a compromise has now been arrived at on this matter. The

div.head: EXANINEII, SATURDAY, DECEMBER O. 1883.
div.p: THE EXANINEII, SATURDAY, DECEMBER O. 1883.
OUR LONDON LETTEL.

CHRISTMAS IN LONDON-THE THEATRES- LOITA-THE KENDALS-SIR CHAS. DILKE'S PROGRAMME FOR HORRIBLE LONDON - CHURCH DECORATIONS-WESTMINSTER ABBEY -THE TOMB OF CHARLES DICKENS-A NEW FASHION IN CHRISTMAS CARDS-THE PAN- DORA'S LOG-TO LEEWARD.
LONDON, THIIRSDAY.

This season of Christmas has been in many respects a strange one. London has been enormously full, but I don't think it has been very festive. The drapers have had it all their own way; but in the commodity of beef there has been a falling off. Whether all the articles about horrible Londen or the sensation descriptions if bow the poor live have effected the rich, I do not know, but the display if beef has been wonderfully meagre. Last year and the year before the supply overflowed from the butchers' shops ea to the pavements in such abundance that the carcases could not be housed during the night, and for a couple of even- ings in Christmas week watchmen were up till dawn guard- ing sides and quarters, saddles and sirloins, from hungry wayfarers or hungrier dogs. After dusk the shops were illuminated and a crowd would collect and look on with wonder. Indeed, it was difficult for an Englishman to con- template so much beef without emotion. This year ex- travagance has been cut down, and neither butchers nor poulterers have glorified their shop fronts with the accus- tomed gas jets flaring over colossal carcases. Indeed, a spirit of economy has pervaded the whole tribe of London shopkeepers. It is very noticeable in how few instances holly and ivy has been used to decorate the windows. I remember when certain thoroughfares in Kensington and South Kensinon looked like groves of shrubs, the greenery covering everything. On the other hand the fancy goods warehouses have been busier than usual. There has been an extension of the baz,ar principle. In many cases large drapers have hired contigu- ous empty. shops, stuffed them choke full of Christmas goods, and done a roaring trade in small trifles. But the reaction has come to-day, and in the languid trace which follows festivity even bargains are at a discount. A damp Christmas has made turkeys cheap, and tradesmen are generally congratulating themselves that they " hedged " against bad weather.

The same rule seems to apply in the case of theatrical management. There has been a wonderful lack of novelty. Cattle show week is really for the manager what Christmas week is for the shopkeeper. We have one or two of the necessary pantomimes, but otherwise things are flat. I think the only ; noveltyf, has been Lotta, at the Opera Comique. She is a frolicsome, kittenish, droll little child of about 15, till you use your opera-glass, and then— you regret that you used it. The Americans tell us that she is typical of their country, and I think she is. Nothing can be more unlike English acting. Her present piece has been a failure, chiefly owing to the badness of the play. It could not well be stupider or more un- intelligible. But I fancy Lotta is the same in every piece. She is very dainty with beautiful little feet and ankles, ugly large hands—curiously enough Minnie Palmer shows the same contrast—and a quite audacious way of bundlingfup her petticoats and kicking her feet forwards and backwards, while she gesticulates with her big hands in a way quite unknown to the English stage. Her drollery, naivette, and daring frankness, make the other actors in the piece look quite at disadvantage— slow, prosaic, and stilted. I hear she is great in a version of Little Dorrit, in which she takes the part of the Marchion- ness. At the Olympic there is the American play of the Crimes of Paris. It comes from across the Thames, and I think the audiences have followed it. It is very strange to find in a West End Theatre the familiar story of the forger and the murderer, the wicked nobleman, the heroic and undaunted detective, the outraged woman who takes her revenge, vice punished and virtue triumphant. The villain of the piece is hissed with great sincerity, and the play acts like a play of a hundred years ago. Since I last wrote they have brought out a revival at St. James's Theatre. It is the favourite "Scrap of Paper," in which the Kendal's won such deserved praise when tkey played it at the Court some years ago. I suppose there is no play in which that com- pany appear to such advantage; and beyond doubt, for modern comedy, it is the best company in London. At the last production Mr. Hare took the boy lover's part. This actor always likes an extreme of age. This time he takes the part of a dried np old mummy of a doctor, and his get- up was so perfect that the first night most of the audience, remembering him in the boy's part at previous perfor- mances, failed to recognise him for some time.

Sir Charles Dilkes tour of the Landon slums has come to an end. He has gathered up a large amount of practice information. He can speak not from blue books and statistics, but fl:om what he has seen and heard. Something of what he intends to do he has shadowed forth. We are to have no spasmodic or sensational legislation. The law as it exists is adequate—only that law must be applied— and it will be applied. Two methods of application are already annonnced. Overcrowding will be remedied. The exact number of inmates which a house ought to hold will be settled. More than that number will not be allowed to inhabit it. Of course something more must be done. This is only getting rid of a lot of rubbish by digging a hole and burying it. We shall probably see in the course of nex year many rows of houses built for the poor with State money. The evil cries for an immediate remedy which it must receive. The existing houses are there, and—as I have said—they are not to be over-crowded. That is the positive check to disease and demoralisation. The prudential check will also be applied. The houses will be supplied with all proper sanitary arrangements. Water freely laid on, and drainage thoroughly seen to. There are some diseases that are always hovering over London, seeking a lodgment, and when they obtain one very slow to leave. In this branch of relief of the poor the whole salubrity of the capital will be benefited. I have spoken already of the deficiency of holly and ivy in shop decorations this season. No doubt it is a spirit of economy which has prompted this result. But I was sur- prised to find the same dearth of greenery in the London Churches on Christmas Day. Here at least the cause can neither be the cost of the material nor the 'price of the la- bour. The former costs little and has hitherto been very freely subscribed. The latter, chiefly furnished by the young ladies of the parish, costs nothing at all. About five years ago a fashion was introduced of nicely ' decorating the chancel. Everything was ,concen- trated on the choir stalls, and the pulpit and -lectern, and the rest of the building was left bare. It was very noticeable yesterday at Westminster Abbey that no- thing at all was done to relieve the grey:gloom of the great building; and yet the services were well attended, and the Christmas sermon was preached by the Dean. But the me- mory of one great preserver of Christmas mirth, and kindly preacher of Christmas good-will and charity, was at least kept green and fresh in the minds of many. After the service I joined the little throng who had collected round • the grave of Charles Dickens. If there was no wreathing of of pulpit or lectern or choir-stalls round about, it at least had not been forgotten. On the grey tombstone on which his name was carved a crown of holly had been placed side by side with the immortelles which all through the year are constantly renewed.'

If Chrismas cards have brought with them no novelty in design this year, and I think rather a falling off in beauty, one new fashion has at least come up with the present season. It is the sending the day after Christmas a receipt for the card delivered the day before. It certainly sounds rather commercial ; but then the charm of the thing lies hi the way in which it is done. The card is like the old- fashioned wedding card, the edge is bevelled and silvered. The corner is out off, and the silver rim run in, so as to look as if the corner had been turned down. On this angle is printed in bold silvered script the figures 1884. Then there is the name on the card in the usual place, and a little message of thanks above it, all printed in ; silver. They are to be sent any time after Christmas not later than New Year's Day, and are, in fact, but an adop-

death of Sir SALAR JUNG on the Bth February "removed one of the most eminent native administrators that have been seen during our tenure of India." Turning to our colonies, we find that in Canada the Marquis of LORNE has been succeeded in the Governor General- ship by the Marquis of LANSDOWNE ; we have to record a growing desire on- the part of the Au._; ralian colonists for the annexation of New Guinea; we observe that a "vigorous social pro&) ess " is going on in New Zea- land; and 'le year has been notable for a civil war in Zululand, consequent upon the return of CETEWAYO to his native country.

During the year death has removed from literary circles Dr. WILLIAM CHAMBERS, the head of the well-known firm of Messrs. W. and R. CHAMBERS, and Mr. SPOTTISWOODE, President of the Royal Society. The Church has to mourn the loss ofißishop COLENSO, Dr. BOYD (Dean of EXETER), and the Bishop Of LLA.NDOFF ; art will miss GUSTAVE DORE ; and music RICIIARD WAGNER, one of the great- est composers. Dr. MOFFATT, the famous missionary, has passed away during the year full of years and full of honours; LORD JUSTICE DEASEY and Sir GEORGE BONVYER no longer adorn legal circles; and Professor SIEMENS, the electrician, has joined the great majority. The ranks of the nobility have been thinned by the deaths of the Duke of MARL- BOROUGH, Lord STAMFORD, and others; and the turf has to deplore the sudden demise of Prince BATTHYANY. The QUEEN Of MADA- GASCAR and the PRINCESS of the NETHER- LANDS died this year; and so did Prince GORTSCHAKOFF, Russia's greatest Statesman. The number of deaths has not been so high as in former years among persons of note.

A TRANSFER.—SamueI Spann applied to the magistrates at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, for permission to sell at the Royal Oak Inn, Trinity-street.--His application was granted. THE SY ILL-PDX OIIIBP4II AT WIDNES.—There DOW only remains one patient in the Small-pox Hospital, two having been discharged this week. We are glad to say that Mr. Higginson is fast becoming convalescent. The Runcorn Parish Church Dividing Club and Axsur- ance Society has lust brought its year's operations to a close, a dividend of £1 2s 6.1 per member being declared. Mr. John Littler was re-appointed secreta-y, and Mr. Wil- liam Sutton hon. treasurer for the ensuing year.

THE RECENT FATALITY AT MESSRS. HUTCHINSON AND CO.'S WORKS, WIDNES.—The, parents of the young man John Walker, who Wa3 killed at Messrs. Hutchinson's works on the 7th inst. will receive about LSO from the firm, the deceased being insured in one of the Employers' Lia- bility Associations. WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS.—At these sessions, on Wednes- day, nine persons were fined for being drunk, and Daniel May and Miles Tumulty were each sentenced to seven days' hard labour for sleeping out. Walter Bushell was brought up on remand charged with neglecting his family, but having paid the money due to the Guardians, he was discharged. ASSAULT ON A WIDNES GIRL.—At Runcorn Petty Ses- sions, on Monday, Hugh Goldrich, a labourer, surrendered to his bail charged with havinx, on the Bch December, as- saulted Elizabeth Webster, of Widnes.—The circumstances of the case have been previously reported, and after hearing the evidence the Bench fined the defendant 10s. and costs.

PROPOSED GYMNASIUM FOR RUNCORN. At the last meeting of the Young Men's Christian Association it was decided that the members of the Runcorn Football Club and Cricket Club be invited to meet the committee to consider the advisability of calling a public meeting with the object of forming a gym- nasium club in connection with the Association. SHOCKING RkILWAY ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—About six o'clock on Wednesday evening a painter, named Frederick Gough, was found lying on the London and North-Western Railway, near the Ann-street level crossing. His leg was fearfully mutilated, and he was conveyed to the Accident Hospital, where it was found necessary to amputate the injured limb. He was yesterday still in a very critical con- dition. We understand that Gough had no right to be on the particular spot where he was found, and it is conjectured that he was knocked down by a passing train. NELSON-STREET WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL.—The chil- dren attending this school were on Monday afternoon pro- vided with a tea at the expense of Mr. Peter Pendlebury. There were about 200 children present, besides the teachers, and the proceedings were of a very interesting character. Subsequently a public meeting WAS held in the schoolroom, the chair being taken by Mr. T. Norman. There was a crowded attendance. The children who took part in the entertainment were each presented with a medal and badge of the Band of Hope. An address was given by Mr. S. C. Beckett, and the Rev. J. F. Collier presided at the piano. WIDNES CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE TONTINE SOCIETY.—The balance sheet just issued shows an income of £257 6s 10d, and an expenditure of £BO 15s 9d, including payments for sick, burials, and management expenses. The Rev. J. Wright-Williams has been elected president; Mr. L. Kilcross, vice-president; Mr. R. Walker, chairman; Mr. F. Beattie, deputy-chairman; Mr. J. Hankinson and Mr. H. Handley, stewards; and' Mr. W. Glover, sick visitor. Mr. Job Hartland is treasurer, and Mr. W. Dwerryhouss and Mr. W. Hunt, auditors. The committee of management consists of Messrs. T. Bruce. T. Glinton, J. Seddon, T. Hughes, William Dixon, C. Watson, and J. Birkhill.

CHRISTMAS TREE AT WIDNES NATIONAL SCHOOL.—On Thursday afternoon a Christmas tree was held in Widnes National Schools, in aid of the building fund of St. Paul's Church. The project had been entirely promoted by the following children connected with the Sunday School : Mary Kilcross, Edith Lord, Fanny White, Maud Mather, Edith Pemberton, Kate Annie, and Alice Jones, and Minnie and Gertie Balmer. fn disposing of the many articles which depended from the branches of the tree, the children were assisted by Mrs. Lord, Mrs. White, Mrs. Kilcross. Miss Wrench, Mrs. Captain Jonas, Mrs. C. Jones, Miss Kirkham, and Mrs. Pemberton. The refreshment stall was presided over by Mrs. and Miss Thomas. A small charge was made for admission, and during the day about 380 persons visited the sale of work, nearly all the stock being disposed of. CAPTAIN RIGBY, OF RUNCORN, AT CAPRTOWN.—Tke voyage of the Dunbar Castle, of which celebrated vessel Captain Rigby, of Runcorn, has command, was com- pleted at Capetown, South Africa, on the 28th November. The South African newspapers contain accounts of a highly interesting event which took place to celebrate the departure of the vessel. The Dunbar Castle had to take in a quantity of powder at Simon's Town after leaving Capetown, and Messrs. Anderson and Munson, the owners' agents., took ad- vantage of the opportunity to offer a trip to the people of Capetown. Some 350 persons accepted the invitation, and the trip was very successful, the courtesy of Captain Rigby and his officers being warmly commended. The vessel sailed with great speed and steadiness and gave complete satisfaction to all on board, who heartily thanked our towns- ' man for the pleasure he bad been instrumental in giving. PRESENTATION TO THE REV. D. LLEWELLYN, OF RUN- CORN.—The Rev. D. Llewellyn, curate of Holy Trinity Church, having accepted a living in Wales, a presentatieu, consisting of two elegantly bound copies of Canon Farrar's works, was made to him on Friday evening last week, in behalf of the Holy Trinity and Ragged Sunday schools, with the teachers and members of the Young Men's Associa- tion. On handing the volumes to the re6pient, the Rev. W. Preston, M.A., incumbent, said he deeply regretted that they were going to lose Mr. Llewellyn, who was about en- tering upon a new and important sphere of labour, which he had advised him to aceept, and gave him permission to do sa at once if necessary. He had besides written a strong letter of commendation to his new bishop and archdeacon. The way Mr. Llewellyn had done his work and visited the poor had given him (the speaker) much satisfaction, and they had worked together amicably and harmoniously.— Mr. Llewellyn feelingly responded, observing that his as- sociations in Runcorn had been of the pleasantest descrip- tion. He had experienced the greatest kindness from Mr. Preston, and they had ever worked cordially, agreeably, and happily together. (Applause.)—Congratulatory addresses were delivered by Messrs. Hankinson, Rogerson, Yates, Goodwill, Cunningham, and H. Hankinson. RUNCORN YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION.—At the last meeting of the committee of this association Mr. K. Evans, bon. sec., submitted his resignation owing to his intended departure for Australia in the course of a few day's. Regret was expressed that the associati na was losing Mr. Evans's services, and a vote of thanks was unanimously accorded to him. On Monday Mr. Evans was presented by Mr. W. Shaw, on behalf of the committee, with -Canon Farrar's "Life of Christ" in five volumes, inscribed as ' follows :—" Presented to Mr. Kirkham Evans, late hon. en- retar-v by the committee of the Young Men's Christian i Association on his leaving Runcorn for Australia, as a token of their regard.—Mat. Steele, president." In the course of some remarks which Mr. Shaw, Mr. Coventry, and Mr. Smith addressed, wishes were expressed for the future welfare of Mr. Evans, and that gentleman suitably responded. On Wednesday Mr. Evans left Runcorn for London to join the steamer Lusitania. which was expected to sail for Adelaide on the following /day. On the platform had assembled many friends of Mr. Evans, including representatives of the Young Men's Chris- tian Association and Camden Wesleyan Sunday school, where for nearly two years he was a teacher. Mr. Evans carried with him many tokens of the esteem in which he was held while in Runcorn, and the best wishes were ex- ; eressed for his future success, and as the train passed out of ~he station hearty parting cheers were raised. Mr. W. Pownall has been appointed secretary of the association pro. tern.

A very clever little Pa;liamentary 6.kiit has jast come out under the title of "TER? Pao, tora'i L 2:.'l it is a .31 of the Ulster campaign, showing kov.• it was arraneze, Le 7.• it was conducted, and how it \1719 cono.uded. The epe-ellnt; chapter is laid at the Carlton, where names tarq d.iffieult decipher as Cross, Rowton, Beach, L)wther, Crani.re.,!i-, George Hamilton, awl Chaplin constitute tht' ineetin4. •At this Council the Ulster campaign is planned, and a deputation sent to Sir Stafford. Then follows the inei!ement, the pursuing, and the adoption of the p:1fl, with a. very biting account of its disastrous progresh and issue. The cleverest thing in the handling of t:ie satire is that the individuality of the speakers is thro.ughout well kept up. It must have been written by someone who well understood Parliamentary life, and had intimate knc.'w- ledge of the Conservative chiefs. Mr. Marion Crawford's new novel "To Leeward," of whick so much has been expected, turns out a failure after all. He is to be added to the list, to the long list of the single speech Hamilton's of English story writers. Like Shorthouse, and like Anstey, he struck a new vein with his first work, and charmed by his fancy, his feeling, and his directness. "To Leeward" misses its point just where "Mr. Isaac's" made it. Mr. Crawford has nothing to say, and so he resorts to the tricks of the manufacturing novelist. We have the morbid analysis of unhealthy characters, a style we have taken over from the French fiction writers, and which the Englis'a novelist seems always to adopt when he has nothing original or healthy of his own to give us. Mr. Crawford's first work had so much chivalry and poetry about it that his best friends will regard this last work as a sad faliirg off.

div.head: VOLUNTEER PRIZE DISTRIBUIION AT WIDNES.
div.p: VOLUNTEER PRIZE DISTRIBUIION AT WIDNES.

The annual distribution of Christmas prizes to the suc- cessful volunteers in the Widnes Coma of the 21st Lanca- shire Rifle Volunteers took place on Christmas Eve in the Drill Hall. The following officers were present :-Captain Brunner, Lieutenants Lewis, Foster, and W. W. Gossage, and Sergeant. Instructor Colebrook. Before distributing the prizes Captain Brunner addressed the men, remarking that they had, he was glad to say, a better average in the shoot- ing this year than last. The highest scores were not quite so high as last year, but the average was considerably better. He was glad to see that 89 men had fired altogether, and only four had failed to make the number of points qualifying them to receive a prize. The number of those who took an interest in shooting and practiced shooting was increasing, and would increase ; and he warned those men who were neglecting the shooting that if the prizes were limited in number and increased in volume, as was contemplated, there wou'd be nothing at all left for those who did not take an interest in the shooting. Perseverance and attention to the instructor was all that was required to make a good marksman. He knew there Were complaints that some of the rifles did not shoot well. The rifles which they had had been in use a great number of years,-some of them he supposed 20 years-and anybody knew that an old rifle worn in the grooves could not be depended upon to shoot accurately at the longer ranges. At the shorter ranges almost any of their rifles would do. The rifle might not be a good one, but if they practiced with it they knew the exact allowance to make. After a few other observa- tions, Captain Brunner expressed his sorrow at the fact that Captain Wareing had been taken home ill, and had not, ' therefore, been able to help them that evening. Before he concluded he would ask them to join him in a hearty vote of thanks to the donors of the prizes. They had come for- ward v€ry kindly, and he thought they had a handsome prize list.-Three hearty cheers were then given for the donors. The prizes were then distributed according to the follow- ing list. Five shots each were fired at 150 yards. THE SEQUEL TO A DOG FIGHT AT
RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Knowles, a young man, was summoned to answer a charge of having, on the 15th December, unlawfully assaulted Henry Crowther, of Halton-road.—Mr. Hitchin appeared for the complainant, and Mr. Percy Davies, of Warrington, defended.—lt ap- peared' from the statement of Mr. Hitchin that the com- plainant was the foreman at the tannery of Messrs. Ockleston and Sons, Halton-road, and the defendant and his father were some time ago employed at the same works.- Mr. o,laleston trusted to Mr. Crowther's care a valuable dog of the Scotch terrier bleed. The defendant was als3 the pos- sessor of a dog which he considered to be very good in the fighting line, and he had set this animal upon the complainant's. The Scotch terrier was victorious. Shortly afterwards the complainant had occasion to d;scharge both the al, fendant and his father from the works. On the night of the 15th inst. the complainant, according to cw,tom, turned the dog loose in the yard, from which,it could not escape, and into which no dog could enter unless placed over the wall. About 11 o'clock he heard a great noise in the yard, and found the defendant there, and his dog fight- ing. He ordered the defendant to leave the premises. The defendant left the yard, and the door was shut. The com- plainant then told his son to fetch a policeman, when de- fendant said, "I don't want any bother about this; let me go fetch my dog • and I will take him away." Agreeing to this suggestion, the complainant opened the door, when the defendant rushed at him, struck him in the face with his fist, kicked him savagely on the shins, and then knocked him to the ground, crushing his foot in such a way that the nail of one of his toes was split. His foot was so severely injured that he could not get his boot on for several days.—The complainant, his two daughters, and his son corroborated this account—For the defence, Mr. Davies contended that the assault had been first committed by the complainant, and stated that when the defendant and two companions were passing along Halton-road, the complain- an'.'s dog appeared and commenced to fight with the defen- dant's, and the door of the yard being open they went in there. Defendant attempted to separate the animals, but Crowther assaulted him in a violent manner.—The Bench we satisfied an assault had been committed and fined the defendant 203. and costs.

Mn. MORRIS ON THE WESTPHALIAN IRONWORKERS.— lie other evening, Mr. T. Morris, F.G.S , read a paper be'ore the members of the South Staffordshire Institute of Iron and Steel Works Managers on "Four days in the iron wire manufacturing district of Westphalia, Germany." At e outset the writer stated that the object of his mission to Westphalia was to ascertain how it was that in the iron-rod trade they were being completely ousted by the Germans, who are underselling us to a very large extent in both the home and foreign markets. During his four days' sojourn he found that the men worked longer hours, and that their earnings were very low when comp Iced with wages paid in England. It was a perfect marvel to him to find that pud- dlers stood six shifts per week, and sometimes seven, of twelve hours each. They worked at inferior iron, and turned it out in a clean condition without being allowed fet- tling, and the managers had no waste, for they used up un- satisfactory rods in their nail and hoop factories. Whilst in England it cost £6 13s. 7d. to draw No. 4 wire-rod to 20 wire gauge, it cost the German manufacturer £3 10s. sd. only. The men had wages which appeared to be starvation earnings, but still the purchasing power of them exceeded ours very much, owing to the mode and cost of living, as well as the lower cuts. The Westphalian was satisfied with brown bread; he could get cheap milk, butter, eggs, fruit, working cloth- ing for his back, shoes for his feet, all wood, a miserable itnitat;on of the Lancashire clog, but requiring skill in their manufacture; whilst the common necessaries of life with us, plus the luxuries of white bread, a home the workman can call his own, fewer shifts per week, &e.; all tended to bring the receipts on a pay-day of no more value than the receipts of the Westphalian piece-man. Another matter he might mention was that the directors of the works had every day samples of the iron produced hammered and tested, and any red-short or cold-short was at once stopped, and the reason investigated. This care, aid the fact that the cost o' labour from the crude metal to the finished wire rod was some 50 to 60 per cent. below the rates paid in similar forges and mills in England formed another part of the answer to the oft-repeated question—how is it done? In conclusion, wi;ter urged that in order to meet German competition better machinery should be here provided, a little less profit I should be sought by manufacturers, and each wire drawer should mind two blocks with an assistant.—A vote of thanks having been passed to Mr. Morris, the meeting closed.

div.head: CHRISTMAS FESTIVITIES.
div.p: CHRISTMAS FESTIVITIES.
RUNCORN.

, On Christmas riO.V services were held in many of the clitirnes and chapels io Runcorn. At the Parish Church the Rev. T. M. Armson preached a sermon, and the choir sung music appropriate to the occasion. The interior of the sacred edifice had been beautifully decorated with a variety of mottoes, flowers, and evergreens. Holy Trinity Church had also been decorated with much taste and skill under the superintendence of the churchwardens, Messrs. Buckley and Fisher, the following ladies and gentlemen also taking part :—Mesdames Preston, Fisher, Buckley, and Martin; Misses Preston, Smith, Tyrie, Stubbs, Cooley-, Swim, Hitchmough, Leathwood, Lea, and Dennis; Messrs. Martin, Hulse, and West. A tea party, arranged by Mr. Robert Harrop, who undertook to pay the cost should it not be successful, was held in St. John's school-room. Subse- quently a large audience gathered to listen to a musical entertainment by the choir, who were assisted by Mr. J. Clough and Miss M. Ainsworth. Social games were also engaged in. Mr. Harrop has presented the balance in hand to the Sunday school library. Mr. and Mrs. Henry Row. land gave a substantial tea to the scholars of the Primitive Methodist Sunday school, Rocksavage. The treat was much eojoyed.

E:LLESMERE-STREET Scitoor..,-A sacred concert was given in Ehlesmere-street Schoolroom, Runcorn, on the evening of ChristxTlas Day by the chapel choir, and it is gratifying to note thl, t it was patronized by a large and appreciative' au- dience. Miss Curzon gave a pleasing rendering of two songs, " Hc doeth all things well," and "Under the-shadow of Thy win,-r," receiving an encore for both pieces. The quart.ts," LiOht at evening time," " In the cross," and "It is Jesus," were given by Miss S. Kalov?, Miss Jones, and Messrs. F. Parr And A. Fox. Mr. Holford gave a pleasing delivery of "I will give you rest," and in response to an encore repeated part of the song. In the second part of the programme he gave a spirited rendering of "Soun,l an alarm," from Handel's "Judas Macabant-," which was received by the audience with loud applautea and persistently re- demanded. Mr. Holford declined (owing, we believe, to indisposition) to repeat the solo. Miss Jones gave an artistic rendering of the ever welcome air from Meralelssohn's "Elijah," "Oh rest in the Lord," and received an enthus- iastic encore, to which she responded by repeating the solo. The anthems were Henry Wilson's " iise, shine," Caryl Florio's "Cry out and shout," and E. F. Wilson's "Glory to God." The programme also contained, two choruses from Handel's "Messiah," viz , "And the glory of the Lord and " Hallelujah." We missed several well-known faces from the ranks of the choir, as a consequence of which the balance of parts was interfered with, but the aopranos and contraltos, although few. did their work well, the chorus singing well together and giving very fair justice to the con- certed pieces which fell to their share in the programme. Miss Clough officiated as accompoinist in an efficient manner, and Mr. John Holford conducted the choir with his usual ability and good taste.

div.head: WIDNES.
div.p: WIDNES.

Christmas was ushered in, as usual, by the glad voices of he wait singers, who early commenced their peregrinations throughout the town, notwithstanding the chilling damp atmosphere. The "unseasonable" weather which has been la- mented very extensively has enabled many persons to spend a merrier Christmas than would otherwise have been possible, for with frost or snow the wretchedness of many a wretched home, of which there are sadly too many in Widnes, would have been immeasurably increased. The chemical trade is on the whole in a better state than it was twelve months ago, the workmen are receiving good wages, and there were few who could not look forward to the Christmas holidays with some degree of joyousness. With few exceptiows the works stopped operations from Saturday noon to Thursday morning, Christmas-day and bank holiday thus being ob- served. On both these days the town presented a quiet Sabbath-like appearance, considerable numbers of persons having left the town for the neighbouring city and the surrounding places.

THE PAPISH Cringcrt.—On Christmas morning the Rev. J. W. Williams) preached a sermon to a large congregation in Widnes Parish Church, his text being part of the 10th verse of the second chapter of St. Luke. The sacred edifice had been beautifully decorated by Mrs. Williams, Mrs. Imison, Mrs. Kilcross, Mrs. Thomas, Miss Lord, and Miss Walker. Over the reading desk was a vermillion-coloured shield, with a border of evergreens, bearing the text, "Unto us this day is born a Saviour." Cunningly formed in rice a similar shield with the motto "Son of the Highest" wrought upon it, occupied a place over the pulpit. These were the work of Mrs. Fred. Neild. From the pulpit there was suspended a banner, with the monogram " 1.H.5." worked with berries by Mrs. King Hague. A font cover, having an octagonal spire with eight gothic arches, had been made and presented by Mr. F. Starkey, while the framework in the chancel had been com- pleted by Messrs. Lea and Son, of Farnworth, under the superintendence of Mr. J. B. Imison. A variety of mottoes occupied positions in the sacred edifice, which presented a bright and pleasing appearance.

THE BLUE RIBBON ARMY. On Christmas Day the Widnes corps of this army held a tea party, to which about 200 persons sat down, tha tables being presided over by Staff Captain Mrs. Ebines, Captain Miss Boast, Miss Bold, Mrs. Adams, Miss Farmer, Mrs. Tomlinson, Miss Hobson, Miss Lasley, Mrs. Pierce, and Mrs. Leach. Subsequently, a crowded meeting was held under the presidency of Mr. Hudson. An isteresting entertainment was given by the Misses Horrabin, Miss Blease, Miss Jones, Mr. Hill and party, and Mr. Glover. On the roilowto day- I,M;ris.y) Christinas tree and sale of work took place in the Public:Hall, Hutchinson-street. The st dl was presided over by Staff Captain Mrs. Ebines and Captain Miss Boast, while the refreshment stall was in charge of Brkhers Leach and Emery. The whole of the articles for sale had been con- tributed by the members and friends of the army in the town. The proceeds are to be devoted to the funds of the local corps. A t mtine saciety has recently been formed in c,nnection with the army, and it 1.13 W possesses twenty-two in bers.

f.ACEY-STREET SUNDAY SCHOOL—In connection with ti school, a tea party took place on Wednesday. About tw., hundred persons sat down to tea, the tables being pre- over by Mrs. Stringer, Mrs. Hothersall, M's. Swale, Mrs. Charles Brown, Mrs. Stead, 1%.1:s Poulson, Mrs. Cooper, Mrs. Spencer, Mrs. Sadler, and Mrs. Booth. Subsequently a public meet- ing and entertainment was held under the presidency of Mr. I'. S. Sir-ales, the senior superintendent, who was supported by the Revs. J. Harper, J. Hothersall, Mr. B. Brown, and Mr. Ormroyde. Under the leadership of Mr. Joe. Robinson, the choir rendered in an efficient manner several selections from the cantata the " Lion of Judah." Miss Toft, of War- rington, delighted the audience with skilful performances on the harp. The Chairman delivered a short introductory address, in which he observed that the object of the meet- ing was the truly Methodist one of raising funds with which to carry on the work of the Sunday school for the next six months, as the money collected at the annual sermons had been spent in adding to the efficiency of the school. air. Joseph Robinson, the secretary, made a short statement with regard to the condition of the school. There were 31 officers, of whom 28 were members of society—(hear, hear)—on the books. He thought this was a very good proportion of members of society, and would compare favourably with any school. The average attendance was 20 in the morning, and 27 in the afternoon. Them were 426 scholars on the books, of whom 70 were members of society, and the average attendance in the morning was 133, and in the afternoon 245. The attendance had been greatly irwreased through the introduction of the "star system." During the year the committee had anxiously del:berated on the best means of keeping the elder scholars in the school, and in order to aid in attaining this end 100 excellent books had been added to the library, which now contained 470 volumes. A cricket club, which it was thought would be a useful adjunct to the school, had been formed; but the Sunday school organisation could not be considered complete until a reading room, or an institu- tion of that description, was established. He should be glad if such a movement could be inaugurated and carried through successfully—( hear, hear)—as it would have a good effect in keeping young people to- gether. The Chairman expressed himself strongly in favour of such an institutieu. A reading, room ought to he established at once. There was not a room in Widnes where a respectable young man could go and read the papers and magazinelhat he could not afford to buy, and he did not see why the trust in connection with that school should not set apart one of the corner rooms for that purpose. It could be opened each evening, ( xcept when public worship was taking place. He thought they ought to have a place where yonire men could read the best literature of the day, in- cluding the daily and weekly newspapers.—Mr. Ormreyde, the Rev. J. Harper, the Rev. J. Hothersall, and Mr. B. Brown also delivered addresses.

DAMAGING PLATE-GLASS WINDOWS AT WARRINGTON.— At the Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, a man named Thomas Watts, glass worker, last from Manchester, and who said he was a native of Dublin, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, and refusing to quit the licensed premises of William Humphreys, the Lower Angel, Butter- market-street ; and further, with doing damage to the plate- glass windows therein to the amount of £4 15s.—According to the statement of the Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt), prisoner was in Warrington on Saturday, hawking. He entered the Lower Angel public-house kept by William Humphreys, and called for beer. Tne landlord re-fused to serve him, be- , cause his would-be customer was drunk. Prisoner there- upon beeline very insolent and turbulent, but Humphreys was exceedingly patient with him. Ultimately, however, in the absence of a policeman or anybody else, he had to de the ' best he could in ejecting prisoner, and in this he was suc- cessful. The landlord closed the door on putting prisoner out, but a minute or two afterwards he heard a fearful smash of glass. On going outside he found that a man named William Skelton had detained prisoner, having seen the latter throw one of his boots at the plate-glass windows, and was pulling off the other to hurl it. The damage amounted to £4 153, Prisoner was kept in the back yard of the Lower Angel until the arrival of a policeman, when he was taken to the lock-up. There were two persons cut through the falling glass.—Prisoner pleaded guilty, and in reply to the magisteates, said he had been a teetotaller for three years, but on the day in question he took a little drink, and did not know what he was doing.—The police produced a heavy block of glass found on plisonor, who said be intended that for a present to a friend.—The lench ,I characterised the offence as an outrageous one, and sentenced 'I prisoner to two months' hard labour-.

The nig.b: Previous he had been employed opening mussels for Mr. le:onsas Shuttle- bothers), in the Market-place, and a little before 12 o'clock he left with two or three other lads having purchased a pint of rum or whiskey at some public-house in the town. He did not like to say anything harsh in the absence of the person who supplied the liquor, but he did not think it WaS a proper thing to sell spirits to boys of such tender age. AS' he understood the rum or whiskey was drank neat, deceased having three drinks, and which affected hint very much. He went home quite tipsy, and was put to bed. About eight o'clock on the following morning his brother, on see- ing whether deceased meant to get up to light the fire as usual, he found him dead. Those were the facts, and he (the coroner) had no doubt the lad died from the effects of the strong drink. H 3 would not direct a post-nsortein examination of the body to be made without it was absolutely essential in leading the jury to arrive at a decision. In his own mind he thought the drink had produced congestion of the brain. He then called the mother of deceased, Catherine ONVCD, wife of John Owen, who is at present in Areerica, and who said she lived at 56, Foundry-street. Witness brought bins home, hiving found him with three other Soys in a pigeon cete. They had been drinking what she- thought to. be whiskey. She heard the rattle of bottles, Let did not cee the drink. Deceased ran into Foundry-strecee and then into Dallarn-lane, where he fell. She picked him np and took him hems. He said he had been drinking, and asked her not to- beat him. He went upstairs and lay across the bed. It was then about 20 minutes past ene o'clock. She then wen: and un- dressed deceased and put him to bed with his brother. She was not disturbed daring the night. On the fcilowing morning, ore telling him to get up she Sound him dead: She asked her other boy where they obtained the drink and he said at the Rodney public-house. He was not asked for who the liquor was required. His companiona were waiting for him in Tanner's-lane. They then went and secreted the Honor in the straw of a pigeon-cote in Bay Horse Yard, off Winwick-street. When deceased had finished his work they all adjourned to the pigeon-cote, and having obtained an egg-cup the spirit which they imbibed raw went round twice. Deceaseed, however, managed to get three "pulls," and had a great deal snore than: the rest. Witness had never dranlc epirits before, and A made him so tipsy that he was falling down every minute. Iris • mother took deceased home, and else then came and " copped " witness coming out of a coffee house.—The Coroner facetiously remarked that he supposed the witness wantadsome coffee to sober him.—ln reply to a juror, witness said they paid 2s for the liquor.— John Dickenson, 14 years- of age, and James Massey, 13, gave similar evidence, but nene of the witnesses cauld say whether it was runs or whiskey which was supplied them. The bottle was labelled "Irish inalt."—The manager of the Rodney, who was present, said the barman whom the lad John Owen said served thedrink, could not remember anything of the occurrence. It was a usual thing for adults to send their youngsters for grog on such nights.— Dr. Spinks said he had ex salines' the body externally, but could find no sn srks of violence, or any indication of a fall. There would be 20oze. of alcohol in a pint of rum, and di- vided into four (sozs.) would be qoite sufficient to cause al- cohol poisoning. His opinion was that death in this case was due to alcoholic poisoning.—A Juror: That is a very com— mon occurrence at Christmas time.—The Coroner : Too common, perhaps.—ln addressing the Jury, the Coroner thought there was now no necessity for a post-ntort on exami- nation after the evidence of Dr. Spinks, whose opinion as to the cause of death corroborated his own. The caoe was certainly a very sad and shocking oue. It struck him as being very improper to serve young lads with spirits, but then it should be considered that at such a, time of the year it was customary for parents to send their children for drink, and those serving it would think that it was required by adults and would .not be drunk as these boys had taken it.—The jury returned a verdict of "Death from alcoholic poisoni lg."
THE WARRINGTON CHEMICAL EX- PLOSION CASE.

The adjourned inquiry into the circumstances connected with the death of William Turley, a " shinglerr aged 51 years, lately residing at No. 49, Gladstone-street; Warring- ton, was held on Wednesday by the Deputy Coroner for .the city of Manchester, Mr. S. Smelt. The evidence previously given showed that on the 12th inst. the deceased purchased q..natr,- of quick3ilver and aquafortis from mr. J. H. Woods, a chemist at Warrington. Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, of Warrington, represented Mr. Woods, the chemist concerned. Mr. Woods placed the two substances together in a bottle, whl2h he corked and handed to the deceased, who left the shop with it. Subse- quently the bottle burst, and part of the contents burnt the deceased severely. He was taken to the War- rington Infirmary and afterwards removed to the Manchester Eye Hospital, where he died on Thursday week. A son of the deceased, who is employed as an errand boy by Mr. Woods, stated that when Mr. Woods gave the bottle con- taining the mixture to the deceasel the latter asked whether it was safe, and Mr. Woods replied that it was. Medical evidence was also given to show that it was extremely dangerous to place aquafortis and quicksilver together in one bottle and then cork it. On Wednesday Mr. Woods' assis- tant, a youth named Nicol, who was in the shop at the time the deceased was served with the nquafortis and quicksilver, said that the deceased never asked whether it was safe to have the articles mixed in one bottle, nor did his master say

that it was " all right." He had seen the deceased served wall the same articles on a previous occasion, and at that time Mr. Woods cautioned the deceased about the dangerous character of the chemicals. Mr. A. H. Griffith, house surgeon at the Manchester Eye Hospital, said he had made a post-mortem examination of the de- ceased. After describing the results of that 'examination he said that death was undoubtedly caused by collapse due to extensive ulceration of the intestines. How that ulcera- tion was caused he could not say, but ulceration generally occurred in a case of burns such as the deceased was suffer- ir.g from.—Mr. Smelt said the fi at question the jury would have to consider was whether there was prima facie evid- ence that the deceased died in consequence of the burns ho received. The doctor's evidence showed that death was the result of the ulceration of the bowels, which might hare been caused by the burns, or might have been due to other causes. The next thing they had to consider was whether anybody was to blame. The law said that every person using dangerous drugs should exercise care, and if any per- son whose business it was to understand the peculiarities of those drugs was grossly ignorant, and did not understand them, and thus caused the death of another person, then his gross. ignorance would make him guilty of the manslaughter of that person. They would have to consider whether Mr. Woods had been guilty of criminil negligence in giving the de- ceased the drugs, mixed in one bottle and corked up. The public must be protected, and it was a very scrious.matter for the public that their lives should be in jeopardy at any time in consequence of the carelessness of chemists, or doctors, or anybody in the like position. If they thought there was prima facie evidence that Mr. Woods had been guilty of criminal negligence it would be their duty to say so, and he would be committed for trial on the charge of manslaughter.—The jury retired for a few minutes to con- sider their verdict. On returning into the room the foreman said the jury were not satisfied that the death of the deceased was owing to the injuries receive" from the burns. At the same time they thought therE• hal been a little negligence on the part of Mr. Woods and that he ought to be censured.—Mr. Smelt then called Mr. Woods forward, and told him he must remember that he occupied a very important position in regard to the safety of the He frequently had the lives of people in his hands, and if he was guilty of negligence it might 1)1 a very serious matter both for himself and the public. lie (Mr. Smelt) did not think anyone who had heard the evidence could doubt for a moment that he (Mr. Woods), a member of the Pharmaceutical Society, and knowing, as he must: have done, the danger of mixing aquafortis and quick- silver, had been guilty of negligence in acting in the way he had done. He honed that Mr. Woods would take the matter into consideration and would be more careful in the future.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (I,ldermin J. Harrison), Alder- man Joseph Davies, and Major Cartwright. The ca.se3 of interest are reported in another column. WsDNEsDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman J. Harrison)
and Isfr. John Fairclough. The cases of interest are reported in another column. THUESDAY.—Before Captain Litton (in the chair), and

Alderman Webster. ASSAULTINII A POLICEMAN.—James Connor, labourer. was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st. on the previous night, and with assaulting P.C. McLaren. Pri- soner was with others creating a disturbance, and when the officer requested him to go away he struck him twice and " butted" him.—Prisoner pleaded guilty to drunkenness but not to the assault, and as the latter charge was not pressed he was let off with a fine of 58 and costs. FRlDAY.—Before the Mayor (kideeman J. Harrison) and Mr. John White. A VIOLENT WlYE.—Catherine Ball was summoned by her father-in-law, George Ball, for damaging windows to the value of 2s.—Mr. Percy Davies appeared for complabant.—lt seemed that defendant's husband bad been obliged to leave his borne owing to his wile's violent eonduct, and bad lately been residing at his father's hou,e. The husband was in the em- ploy of 31r. Peter Stubs. Mrs. Ball had pawned almost everything in the house, and yet she would not let her husband alone. At midnight, a few days ago, she went to Geo. Ball's house and told her son, who she brought with her, to knock at the door and ask for the father. The complainant came to the door and said he was not there, and told the boy to go away. Defendant then came from her hiding place, and picking up some stones deliberately smashed four squares of glass in the house, and for which 28. was charged.—Defendant was fined Ri and costs, and ordered to pay the damage, or a month's impris mment.

THE TIEFT OF A HEARTITEUG.—Edward Alfred Molyneux, of Thatto Heath, was charged, on remand, with having stolen a heart/wog, the property of Wiliam Coppell, of Portico, under the circumstances narrated in our last issue.—He was sent to gaol for 14 days. MONDAY.—Before the Mayer (Mr. H. Baxter), Mr. H. Hall, and Alderman Cook. BREACH OF TIE PEACE.—Thomas Ithody and James Rhody, young men, were each bound over to keep the peace for three months for having oommitted a breach of the peace on the 16th last.
SUSPICIOUS DEVII AT BURTON- WOOD, ALLEGED FATAL BEATING OF A BOY BY A SCHOOLMASTER.

Owing to the sudden death of a lad named Ned Travers, son of Joseph Travers, of Chapel-lane, Burtonwood, under circumstances of a peculiar character, the greatest possible excitement has been occasioned throughout the township. So far as the facts of the case can be ascertained, it seems that the deceased, who was nine years of age, attended the Burtonwood National School, of which Mr. William Thos. Jones is the master, and was present in school on the morn- ing of the 17th inst.—last Monday week. Whilst the mas- ter was marking the register he saw Um boy Travers and a number of others playing and laughing. Travers was there- upon called out and was flogged by the master with a stick. Whilst flogging the deceased the master, it is said, leaned the boy's breast against one of the writing desks, the correr of which, it is alleged, was pressing against the lower part of the boy's stomach, on the right side. On getting home from school tha„boy complained of being ill and sore at the spot where the desk had pressed against him. However, he went to school on the following day (Tuesday), but partook of very little food. He went to bed at his u3ual time, but shortly after midnight he commenced vomiting, and was very ill. He continued ill for two days, and on the Friday Dr. Foulson, assistant to Dr. Handyside, of Earlestown, was sent for, and he attended in the afternoon. The poor lad rapidly grew worse, and expired about three o'clock on Sunday afternoon last. The doctor refused to give a certifi- cate as to the cause of death. ffe stated that the deceased had died from inflammation of the bowels, but declined to state the cause of the inflammation. There were no external marks of violence on the bowels, but there were three or four marks upon the buttocks. The lad had previously been very healthy. Mr. L. Rowbottom, the deputy-coroner opened an inquest upon the body at the Chapel House Inn, Burtouwood, on Wednesday afternoon, when there were also present—Mr. H. L. Riley, solicitor, St. Helens, representing the deceased's father; and Mr. J. 0. Swift, solicitor, of St. Helens, who appeared on behalf of the schoolmaster. The only witness called was the father, Joseph Travers, who gave formal evidena of identification, after which the inquiry was adjourned for a week so that a post-mortem examination of the bath, might be made. We understand that Dr. Garton.; of St. Helene, made the poff- naorterta examination yesterday afternoon (Thursday).

Lowe, E. Syder, W. Birch&ll, S. Marsh, .1. G. Buckley, Wm. Gerrard, W. Swift, J. Griffith, J. Kenwright, Wm. Gilbody, J. Leatherbarrow ; the Rev. T. Chambers and J. Barnacle; and Mr. H. div.head: MASTER'S REPORT.
div.p: MASTER'S REPORT.

The WORKHOUSE MASTER reported that there were 463 inmates in the workhouse this week as compared with 464 last week, and 523 in the corresponding week of last year. There were 173 boys and girls in Kirkdale Schools, Forty vagrants had been relieved as compared with 136 in the cor- responding period of last year. There were a total of 286 patients in the hospital. The master also reported that a number of presents to the inmates of the workhouse had been received from various persons. A vote of thanks was ac- corded to the donors. THE ALTERATIONS AT THE WORKHOUSE.

Mr. HARTLBY read a letter from the Local Government Board approving of the proposed expenditure of £3OO by the Guardians for the purpose of improving the means of escape at the workhouse in case of fire.

The School Attendance Committee reported that they had expended for the quarter just ended £56 9s (M. The com- mittee estimated that their expenditure for the quarter end- ing 28th March, 1884, would amount to X. 58 15s.

Mr. NEWSOME asked for permission to allow his motion, as to the appointment of a treasurer to the Union, to stand over for a for a fortnight.—This permission was granted.
THE INDUSTRIAL SCHOOL CHILDREN.

On the motion of the Rev. T. CHAMBERS, it was resolved that the members of the Board should make their annual visit to the Industrial School, Liverpool, so as to acquaint themselves with the condition of the children connected with the Union there.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF NURSE.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF NURSE.
A number of applications for the post lf nurse in the in- fectious hospital at the Union were considered, and Miss May Jennings, of Rochdale Infirmary, was appointed.—This concluded the business.
