div.p: ROBBING PETER TO s PAY PAUL.
BY JOHN SAUNDERS, Author of "IllEtEl!L OIL, LOVE BORN OF STRIFE," "AL Dam's WIFE," " ISRAEL MORT, OVERILAN," IC., IC.
CHAPTER LVI.-I HANN LOST ILL THROUGH THE FOLLY-THE MADNESS-OF A MOMENT.

For some time after the arrest Stephen's mental state can be described by no other word than that of stupefaction. The incidents that leel:to it had fallen so suddenly—so unexpectedly—as to confound him for the time. Mut still there was hope the Sergeant might, on reflection, accept his apology; and to avoid discovery of his own breach of the rule, let the matter drop. And then the affair was all but driven from his mind by the appearance of Miss Vandeleur with the Earl; and by the all-absorbiog conversation he had held with her, ending in his promise to go to his mother in a short time in obedience to her urgent summons, if he could. And now that was settled for him! He was a prisoner, and on his way to the Guard-room. Is it any wonder if his brain seemed. te reel at the chaos of wild agonising thought in which he was plunged; and that to repel the incoming of madness he accepted nature's kindly anodyne—dulled sensibility—and tried not to think as the best way not to feel. Yet even in the brief journey to the Guard-room hew every object he met or passed seemed to have changed its character, and like the sky itself to have put on a sort of angry 'lurid aspect. He sat down in the Guard-room and waited mechanically for what was to happen next. He glanced round at the soldiers there, but shunned notice of any particular face ; and then crossing his arms upon his breast, and letting his eyes rest on the door, he summed up the position in the words "I have lost all through the folly—the madness of a moment!" Presently he was conducted to his room and ordered to consider himself a prisoner there among his usual com- panions, who included a sergeant and tea privates. The respect thus paid to him as a non-commissioned officer, brought a rueia of fearful emotion; as once mere reminding him of how hard had been his fight to achieve that first step, which foretokeneal all the rest of the steps by which he was to work out his redemption; and it was some time before he could again cover himself with the pall of oblivion that he now courted as his only remaining method ef escape from self-torture. But courted in vain for any length of time. Remem- brances he was striving to keep off, would not be so dealt with. Again he heard the drummers at their work, aeon the day of his quarrel with the sergeant; again he was asking Gentleman Jack the meaning of their strange unearthly noises; again he received the reply, they were preparing to dog some miserable wretch; and again he had to remind himself the man's offence resembled his own; and that the merciless character ef the commander as a "flogging colonel," which Gentleman Jack described, rendered his • escape as unlikely as that of the men for whom the drum- mers had been preparing, and who had passed through their hands, reeking with his blood. The thought was horrible Death itself a soldier may cheerfully face, but not punishment so cruel and so irre- deemably infamous. Again the words were in his heart and almost on his lips, but with an addition —"I: have lest all through the folly— the madness ef a moment—why then not accept the fact as irrevocable; and stifle as it springs every thought of the past, every hope of the future, and seek that way the only possible rest."

div.head: CHAPTER LXVII.—Taz SERGEANT'S CHARGE.
div.p: CHAPTER LXVII.—Taz SERGEANT'S CHARGE.

on and fraish it; but woe stopped, confused by the multi- plicity of details that even so comparatively simple a case in outline premed upon his attention. Abandoning this effort, and tearing up the paper, he now began to jot down those details, heedkes of any logical suc- cession but that of the actual order of their oceurrenc,e in his mind.

Of coarse the result was that all the salient points were soon on the paper before him, needing only to be methodi- cally arranged. In that business of arrangement he stopped every now and then to put into worde a thought that struck him; so that when the entire mechanical process had been got through he was pleased to see he had really made consi- derable progress towards the actual and final defence. Interruptioas unfortunately were many in the one room, by the gossip of his comrades, who in their kindly feeling for Stephen in tde it a point to report to him any anecdotes of the !minas of the day that were likely to interest him; while he on his part could not but put a good face on the mAtter, and listen, and bear in patient goad humour the delays they caused. But the moment they were gone he hurried back to his little table and his papers, and did his best to resume with- out loss the theme they had interrupted. • And so at list a rough version .was completed of all he had

Stephen's crime having been duly put into official form by Sergeant Grablee, as that of "wilfully striking him in the face with his clenched fist, and so knocking him down," the prisoner was next morning marched by the Regimental Orderly Sergeant before his Colonel. There the crime, as officialised, was read out to him, and then the Colonel asked him what he had to say to the charge. Stephen acknowledged, with the deepest regret, it was true; adding he had instantly done all he could to satisfy the Sergeant that it was entirely unpremeditated, and to humbly apologise for the deed. " Hum ! Ha!" ejaculated the Colonel, giving Stephen one of those furtive half-aside glances that told those who knew him the prisoner need look for no favour at his hands.

Stephen saw that glance, remembered his first impressions of the Colonel when he had seen and heard him that night on the packet, when they were both on their way from Holyhead to Dublin, and took it as a fresh monition to abandon hope, and cherish blank, dull despair. The interview closed with the remand of the prisoner, to be tried by a district court-martial; the authority for which had to be obtained from the General commanding the Cur- ragh Brigade. This was duly given in the next four days, and the Col- onel was then free to act. Accordingly next day there appeared in the regimental orders a statement to the effect that by order of the General Commanding the Curragh Brigade, Stephen Shand would be tried by a district court martial assembled in the Court Martial Room, F square, at eleven a.m., on the 9th of Janu- ary, 18137, for his trial, and for the trial of such other pri- soners as might be brought before it. While events were thus htarrying on to their natural or unnatural conclusion, Stephen, the uahappy prisoner, whom they so deeply concerned, was no longer in the state of passive misery which at first so overwhelmed him. That look of the Colonel—which, for the moment increased Stephen's own sense of the hopelessness of any efforts for safety—in the end aided greatly to restore him to himself— to his fortitude, to his courage; to, in a word, a determined purpose to fight manfully this new combat imposed upon him; and If he must fail, do something in the process which should make the future one to incline men to thiak he ought to have succeeded. Yes, that would be something. And as to the process it- self—would not that be better a thousand times than simply sitting in a corner staring blankly at the ceiling of his reom, when his comrades were on parade; or stalking to and fro in frames of mind that sometimes brought home to him in an odd mixture of humour and anguish, the thought—he was about to walk away from all his difficulties. 13ut the stupor had thoroughly passed away, even before the OCaurrefide ot a new incident that certainly was quite sufficient to prevent its return. This was a visit from Major Etheredge. And the two being presently left alone, the Major shook Stephen by the hand, before speaking a word. The act was magical. Tears sprang into the young man's face. _

"Come," said the Major, "let us sit down, and have a little talk together. Have you begun your defence?" "No," said Stephen, half ashamed. "How is that?' asked the Major, gravely. should be lost in such matters." "I must confess to a most unmanly and prolonged mood," said Stephen. "But it was ended before you came. lam spared that shame," he said witk a smile. "Glad to hear you say so. But I think I understand how you have been overwhelmed, and I cannot wonder. But let all that pass." The Major then got Stepen to narrate in the minutest detail the particulars of the quarrel with the Sergeant ; and so became acqaainted with the Sergeant's breach of rules, which seemed to interest him greatly. "I almost wonder that that fact and your instantaneous apology did not induce the Sergeant to be silent." "That was my hope, after he had left me; but as you see a fallacious one," responded Stephen. "There is a vindictiveness in some men that no sense of what is prudent, no wise selfishness can moderate, till it has, been satisfied in its own ferocious way," said the Major thoughtfully. "Yes," said Stephen. "that is the danger with the Ser- geant. Bosides, I doubt not he can find ways to gloss over his fault if it does get known." "You will want ma as a witness, of course," continued the Major, after a few moments of silence. "It is an honour I greatly covet, and I fear as greatly need."
"No time

"You are entitled to it in every way. I shall testify to ye ur character both as a soldier and a man ever since you joined the camp. I shall point to your services with the flying column; and lastly to my own individual debt to you in the affair of the treacherous spies." '1 shall be most grateful, Major, whatever may subse- quently happen." " "By the bye, bring all this out by questions to ma. Don't let me play too much the part of a volunteer." "I understand, Major, and will take care to do so," said Stephen. "Would it not be well to inform your friends?" "That is the one thing in the world I desire should not be done," exclaimed Stephen passionately. "I may escape, or with but that kind of punishment which will leave no stigma behind. But if the worse were to come, there could be for me one only consolation—the infamy would be un- known to them, and would for ever remain unknown; for at the earliest possible period, I would obtain my discharge; and then seek in external exile some possibilities of for- getfulness of such a past, and of hope for a better future!" "Well, I regret your determination; I cannot think it wise, but neither can I wonder at it. Well, now, far a couple of suggestions: "Prepare a written defence, as powerful as you can, but not long. Avoid, if you possibly can, compelling Sergeant Grabbe to own that late night-gossip with the woman. If he denies giving you the lie, you will have no choice. You must then show his motive for anger, and for so falling foul on you. Bat short of that, I would keep as well with him as You can ; his testimony may be more or less strong just as he sees you spare him or press him on that point." "I will certainly do, Major, exactly what you advise. It is counsel which entirely commends itself to my own judg. anent." - -
thought to say, But not until this had been re-written, al- ways with add.tions and corrections and improvements, some six times, did he feel his work was done.
And then, rentembring tha Major's injunction about brevity, he saw with dismay that much of what he had done he bad mow to undo.

Cutting out recaoreeleAly " lang passages that led to nothing" but the expression of his own individual feeling, to begin with; ha did not stop there. Choice phrases, tell- ing passages, forcible displays of fact, had now all to be subjected to a severe revision. And only when these things were done did ho make a fair copy—one, indeed, that was so beautifully written as to suggest, apart from the internal evidence of the matter, that only a gentleman could have wrltten it. He recognised that fact with a certain satisfaction; be- lieving that his judgos could not be so destitute of feeling for ono of their own social rank originally, as not to be a little influenced to kindly consideration of his act, and there- fore to merciful treatment.
He put the document, carefully folded to an offici 11 shape, in his pocket; and from that moment waited with a sense of growing hope and confilence he had not been able to feel before.

Now, then, to say good-bye !" And the Major rose,ani again shook hands with Stephen; whose heart was so pain- fully fall of grateful feeling that he could not let it venture to let it try to express itself in any other shape than by the warm, retentive clasp, and the reluctant resignation of the Major's fingers at the door.

CHAPTER LVIII.—PREPARING THE DEFENCE. Not one moment did Stephen lose after the departure of the Major before beginning the study of his defence. He began to write as if he thought at once to go straight
THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, DECEMBER 29, 1883.

"Well, sir, the Sergeant's charge against me was not really a matter of military duty at all; it was simply the repetition of a tale told to him by a contemptible go-between, who wanted to create bad blood. I would prefer to say no- thing about it. The Sergeant acknowledges in effect all I wanted to prove—that no neglect of my duties c iused the Sergeant to question me; that the informer who misled him was Tommy Atkins; that the Sergeant did call me a liar; and I, in the anger of the moment, responded by the offence that has unhappily brought me here. I have nothing more to ask of the Sergeant, who has given his evidence fairly." There was something in the low buzz of conversation amongst the members of the Court Martial, and in the look of their faces, that told of a success being scored. The Sergeant perfectly understood what Stephen was do- ing; aucl.though he did not by look or sign manifest the relief he felt at finding he was not to be exposed, he took care to run no risk by farther speaking; and withdrew the moment he was permitted to do so.

To Stephen's great surprise, and still more serious alarm the President closed the court, before any examination of the witnesses for the prisener, the latter being marched out, and only the members of the Court-Zartial left.

Nor in answer to his anxious and harried questions from the Orderly under whose charge he was, could he feel much reassured in being told his witnesses would 6e heard; but only after the Court-Martial had decided the question whether he was or was not guilty of the crime charged against him. Once more the sense of injastios burned fiercely in Ste- phen's heart. Assuming the witnesses yet to be heard were only witnesses to character, was not character in Stephen's case an all important element in determining the amount and quality of his crime? But he could only wait and summon up whatever of la- tent fortitude there might be in his sou', to bear the im- pending verdict, which he began seriously to fear would be a fatal one.
On the re-opening of the Court, the President called upon St:phen to say whatever he wished to say in defence or extenuation of his behaviour.
Stephen saw now the whole position. If they had found him "Not guilty," of course the proceedings would have ended there and then.
They had then found him guilty, he and his witnesses alike unheard!

Revolting at what he conceived to be the monstrous in- justice of such a method of trial, he determined to throw overboard the defence he had so laboriously prepared, and speak freshly, as he felt, without note or paper to aid

Rash as the step may seem, he had stilled glanced at that aspect of it and satisfied himself. As they had already found him "Guilty," he had little or nothing to fear in that direction; while a few manly, outspoken words might, with the aid of his witnesses, seriously affect the character of the sentence. Not caring to inquire or speculate any farther, he made his plunge boldly. "I could have wished, sir, you and the members of this honourable Court could have heard what my witnesses had t 9 say before entering on the—to me—momentous question Gf my guilt, or my freedom from it. "For, sir, I think, when you do hear tbeir evidence, you will find convincing proof that the very essence of the charge against me—wilful malice—is contradicted by the whole tenor of my life in the camp. "I must own that this procedure, which I did not know of beforehand, and which I had never thought to inquire about, disarranges all my plans of defence. "I hold here, sir, in my hand, a paper prepared with the greatest bare, but written throughout in the belief that I was appealing to still unpledged judges ; and was, therefore, shaping my course so to influence them by appeals to their judgment derived from a dispassionate review of the facts that I might hope, at least, to be understood; and that point gained, I felr I ought leave all to your honourable Court in quiet confidence. " That paper is now. useless for the purpose for which it was written. But I venture humbly but most earnestly to ask that it be taken by you, to be preserved with the other records of this trial, as my only sufficient and deliberate de- fence. It may be a satisfaction to my friends, to be able at some future time, to see my own statement of my case, side by side, with your judgment." . _ _ . _
Therewith be banded the document to the nearest of the
officers. a subaltern, who after a moment's hesitation handed it to his neighbour, who placed it before the Pre- sident. He glanced at it carelessly, laid it down, and then
said,— - "yrisoner," said the President in his harshest, most dis-
cordant tones, "Do you ask this as a veiled threat to the court, on account of what you imagine the court will do, or not do 2"

" God forbid, sir! There was no such thought in my heart. lam separated by my own act from my friends, who are not without influence. But I have kept all know- ledge of my position from them. I shall still do the same. See then, sir, what that has involved, my putting all trust in a fair trial here!

"But can this trial be so called if I am first found guilty of wilful and malicious intention on the evidence of a single man—and that the man who received the offence, white I be- lieve after hearing my witnesses you will see how strong is the presumption that I could not have premeditated any kind of 'violence; and how contradictory the proofs will ap- pear as to my having felt anything approaching to malice when I struck in defence of outraged honour. "'Outraged honour ! ' These are perhaps unwise words, but they reveal a truth. lam a gentleman by birth, by education, by culture, by everything that could tend to mike such an outrage on me as the being called a liar one to be resented without forethought, without time for any kind of prudent or wise reflection to interpose a restraining force.

"That, sir, is and must b 3 my essential defence. If you, as gentlemen c moot listen to that after hearing my wit- nesses, it will be useless for me to sty more." "Thanking you all gratefully for the indulgence you have shown to one who is painfully conscious he has not been able to speak as he so earnestly desired, in harmony with the customs and traditions of the Court, I have now only to call my witnesses." The Adjutant having first testified to Stephen's length of service and to his good character, the next to give evidence was the Sergeant-Major. "Do you remember," so ran Stephen's question to him, "that I have on any occasion told on my own authority, or repeated tales to you from others, likely to prejudice Ser- geant Grabbe in your estimate of him ? " "Never! And speaking from ample knowledge I can only say that I know no man in the regiment so unlikely to do anything of the kind to injure a comrade." "And yet I believe Sergeant Grabbe has allowed you to see he had got impression of you ?" "Yes, I think so. I cannot else understand varioui re- marks that have at different times dropped from him." "That is all I wish to ask you, Sergeant-Major." Eut here the inquisitive captain again interposed a little paper; in cons,quence of which the President asked the Sergeant-Major, "Can you tell U 3 the nature of the charge made by Ser- geant Grabbe to the prisoner which led to the lie being given as alleged by the prisoner, add to the subsequent vio- lence which is not, and cannot be, denied ?" "No, sir, I know nothing abut it." And then the Ser- geant-Major was allowed to go away; and Major Etheredge proffered himself for examination. .
"Have I, Mak)r, been a fairly good soldier, and subjected to no punishments since I first came under your com- mand ?"

"You have never been punishe I. A better soldier in all respects, up to this sad business, I never expect to see." "Had I thci good fortune to be of servica in the riots of last autumn when I went out under your command ?" "Your services were of that character that I thought it _ _ _ _

advisable to call you out on your return home before all the men, and publicly compliment and thank you. The Presi- dent will find a full account in my report, presented next day, to the Colonel, his predecessor." "I know not," Mid Stephen, turning towards the Presi- dent, 4 if the forms of this honourable court permit ins to thank the Major for evidence so dear to me—as a soldier— so precious to me as a man—but if they do, I beg to tender him my most grateful thanks. If anything could lessen the pain—the humiliation of my position, the Major has done that for me. Again I thank him." These last words ' were so broken by emotion that every one in court felt them. _ _

"As I find," said the Major 'recovering his equanimity and presence of mind, for Stephen's sake, "that the prisoner does not intend to elicit a fact that redounds greatly to his credit as a soldier, I must myself mention it to the court." He then described briefly but picturesquely the incidents previously shown in connection with the treachery of the scouts; but so described them as to make the result bear rather upon Stephen's skill and decision of character as a soldier at a critical moment than upon the fact that he owed his own life in all probability to the qualities illustrated. This fact he did not even refer to as a matter affecting him- self, knowing the use that might be made of it to weaken his own previ'ms evidence, as that of an uncommonly grate- ful ma'!

Stephen was now ordered back to his room, there to ruminate on the business the Court had yet to perform—the determination of the sentence, and the sending of the find- ing of the Conrt to the General in command of the Brigade for approval.

div.head: CHAPTER LIX.-THE COURT NI _ARTIAL.
div.p: CHAPTER LIX.-THE COURT NI _ARTIAL.

The very next day Stephen was summoned before his judges. About 10-45 of the clock he was marched to the Court- Martial room, wearing his usual dress, and a shako, but without belts. The Sergeant, his accuser, entered with bins.

At the head of a long table sat the Colonel as President having two other officers of the regiment sitting on each side, equally divided between Captains and Subalterns. The Adjutant, who acted as prosecutor, stood a little apart; while the Major stood by the window. Stephen and the Sergeant took their places, standing at the bottom of the table.

After a respectful salute at his entrance, Stephen ven- tured to glance at the faces of his judges; two only being of his regiment. These were of course known to him, but now invested with a new and terrible interest in his eyes, as being the men selected for this dread tribunal.

He had indulged in frequent speculations beforehand on this critical point, and had hoped that certain men would of his regiment, and other certain men would not be chosen; but now he knew, and the knowledge was to the last degree unsatisfactory.

fiovreyer, lie could not afford to dwell on such a topi4 and he did not. But strove by calmness—careful thought —slow considerate speaking when lse should have to speak, so to pass through the ordeal as to hare nothing where- with to reproach himself hereafter. Diverting his thoughts to the Court, and its forms, he was struck by one peculiarity, the entire absence of any display of the tremendous force in the backgrounds. He himself was in no way personally degraded. No file of men had brought him hither, only the Orderly-Sergeant of the regiment. He was not handcuffed. No ssntry was on guard. The officers wore their swords as a part of their uniform, and there was present a single Court-Orderly. That was well.
The proceedings began by the President reading the for- mrl orders, which gave the Court authority to act in Cie case of Stephen Shand; and then, addressing the prisoner, he said—
"Do you object to be tried by me, or by any other mem- ber of the Court ?"
No, sir," was Stephen's reply, in a clear distinci voice. _ _

. Then the four members took the Bible in their right hands across the table, and were sworn in by the President to duly try the prisoner now before them, without favour, partiality, or effection, according to the evidence brought before them, aid in accordance with the custom of War.

Stephen, be it observed parenthetically, could not but notice how carefully the words chosen—" without favour, partiality, or affection," b)re all against the prisoner; while none accompanied them, as a safeguard against the opposite tendencies of official bias, personal dislike, or the many forms in which oppression on the part of a superior might have created the crime charged against an inferior. The words indeed seemed precisely fitted to injure a case like his own—where some such feelings might be expected to rise in the breast of the judges when they had the whole fairly before them; and which they were thus warned not to give way to.. . _ .

Stephen tried to disc)ver the equity of this, but was not successful. What favour, partiality, or affection could be expected in the heart of an officer, on the trial of a man, so far below him, with whom he had nothing in common but the yocation, unless such feelings had been doe to what they knew of his character—and conduct in the regiment. And in that case should they not have been esteemed as per- fectly legitimate elements in the final result? While these thoughts were passing through Stephen's mind, the President was being similarly sworn in by the senior Captain. That done, the Major, Sargeant Grabbe, and other pos- sible witnesses retired, and the President reed out the charge against Stephen, which was to the effect, That be, to the prejudice and good order of military dis- cipline, at the Curragh Camp on the let of January, 1860, did wilfully and maliciously strike in the face with his clenched fist Sergeant Grabbe, the earns being his superior officer.
"Are you guilty or not guilty " Stephen 1933 novr asked.

"lain guilty of the act; I am not guilty of all that is im- plied in the words "wilfully and maliciously." "You must plead one way or the other. The words are not at your disposal to add or to alter" Then, after a pause, the Colonel added, in a seemingly kinder spirit, "I advise you to plead not guilty.'" "Then, sir, I thankfully accept! " Therewith he pleaded " Not guilty." And the President recorded the fact.

The one and only witness f6r the prosscution was then called in—the Sergeant who had been struck. He walked up the long room awl placed himself at the right of the Pre- sident, and was by him duly sworn. He then—in very few words—but in a hard unsympa- thetic voice, narrated his story in this fashion. He was standing in conversation with the prisoner, complaining of matters that he thought tended to disturb the peace of the regiment, when suddenly he was struck with such violence that he fell to the ground. He rose, and then the prisoner expressed his sorrow, and the Sargeant left him to call the Guard.

All this was duly written down by the President, and read out to the Sergeant to have the correctness of the record duly verified. "Have you any questions to put to the witness ?" asked the President.
" Yes, sir," replied Stephen, and began at once his cross- examination.

"I think, Sergeant, it was thnugh your advice, I entered the regiment when you found me wandering in the camp "Yes," said the Sergeant. "Have we, prior to the last few weeks, ever htd a single quarrel or anything approaching to one ?" "Not that I remember."

"Bat within these few weeks have you not changed in your manner to me, Ido not say without occasion—l simply ask as to the fact of the change ?" "Perhaps my opinion may have somewhat changed." "And that is due, is it not, to the secret incitements of Tommy Atkins ?" "I have talked with him, as well as to other soldiers, as a part of my duty." ' "Bet in listening to him sould you not have remembered that in consequence of my having twice defeated him in , wrestling, he had not disguised from his comrades his hatred of me, and his wish to do me an ill turn? And now, Ser- geant, to what all this leads: Has he not done me this ill turn, in bringing reports to you from time to time which you believed, to my discredit • and which led up to the conver- sation you spoke of; when for the first time you gave me the opportunity to challenge one of these reports, and I gave it an indignant denial. Is not that true?" "You did deny something or other that I had to say to you." "And then you told me I lied ? " "I don't think I used so strong an expression, but some- thing equivalent I dare say was say was said." "And on the instant of the utterance of the phrase, which was, It's a d---d lie ! ' the blow was struck ? " "The blow was struck—that was enough for me!"
"I think so too," said the President: "Prisoner, you will hardly benefit yourself by entering into these small de- tails.

"But, sir, I entreat you to observe," said Stephen, with earnest but respectful manner, " it is only by these small details I can show how the S3rgeant was provoked against (as [firmly believe) his own better nature, to ell( me a liar, and so to give the provocation which led to the blow."

One of the captains here handed to the President a paper, containing no doubt a suggested question; for the latter, after a naDmmtary pause, asked Stephen— " What was the nature of the complaint or charge made by the Sergeant which you sty you so indignantly repu- diated ?" That wag a critical monvnt for our hero. Could he avoid frankly repeating what tha Sergeant had said when the mat- ter was so put to him? And yet the Major's advice was per- hops morn necespiry than ever to be acted on. He took a medium course:

div.head: CHAPTER LL-MAJOR ETREREDGE'S LETTER.
div.p: CHAPTER LL-MAJOR ETREREDGE'S LETTER.
Awful, indeed, were the days following, in their agonising suspense, and in the fear fast growing to a con- viction in Stephen's mind, that he must prepare for the worst.

What he might have done to anticipate the worst may be guessed rather than told. But there were two restraining influences. The first was that the very circumstances of his position which made suicide possible—the indulgence shown to him as a non-commisiioned officer—made him also think of the consequences thereafter to other unfortunates, if such an act as he dimly meditated were seen to be duc to the consideration shown. A sudden stop would certainly be put at once and for ever, to any and every indulgence that could be abused.
The other influence was a letter from Major Etheredge, which ran thus:—

"I have just had an interview with the Colonel on two subjects: the one to tell him that I have succeeded in effec- ting an exchange into a regiment in which I have a brother, and other personal friends; news as pleasing to him to hear as I to narrate, for in truth no two m3n I think ever more cordially disliked each other, and were more glad of a separa- tion.
"The other matter related to you. lam supposed not to know the decision of the Court; but these things do ooze out somehow, where there is any special desire to know. So

div.head: DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.
ASHTON.

HRATH-ROAD SCHOOLS, ASIITON.—Last evening (Thurs- day) the children connected with the Rectory Schools, Downall Green, gave an entertainment consisting of an operetta, entitled " C;nderella, or the fairy glass slipper," in the Heath-road schools, Ashton. The same piece was suc- cessfully given in the Downall Green schools a week or two , ago, and its repetition in the Heath-road schools last even- ing gave great satisfaction to those present. The children were attired in appropriate dresses ',rigs, &c., and in every respect the performance was enjoyed. ENTERTAINMENT AT ASHTON CATHOLIC SCHOOL.—There was a large attendance at St. Oswald's Catholic School, Ashton. on Wednesday evening, when the school children gave a very pleasing entertainment. The first part of the programme consisted of a 'Scene from the life of King Alfred," whde the second and principal part was a represen- tation of the popular piece "Puss in Boots, or a good deed rewarded." The characters were well sustained throughout, and those present were highly delighted with tha acting, The entertainment was repeated last evening (Thursday). ASHTON CONGREGATIONAL SCHOOL : ANNUAL TEA PARTY AND PRESENTATIONS.—The annual tea meeting in connec- tion with the Ashton Congregational Sunday School was held in that building on Christmas Day, when about 200 sat down to an excellent tea. The room was very prettily decorated with evergreens and seasonable mottoes, the latter being splendidly painted-by Mr. Thomas Rigby. Messrs. Ashton, Corless, and others assisted in decorating the room. After tea the annual public meeting was held, and Mr. Charles Latham presided. After prayer by the Rev. H. Wilson, the Chairman gave an introductory address, after which an interesting programme was gone through. The church choir, conducted by Mr. J. Turton, capitally ren- dered several anthems; and Mr. Richard Latham ably presided at the harmonium. The Sunday school children occupied seats on the platform, and in a pleasing manner they sang several melodies, and nicely gave various recita- tions and dialogues. In the course of the evening Mrs. Wilson presented a copy of her portrait to Miss Sarah Winstanley and Miss Fanny Cook, two of her scholars, , who have only been absent from school once each during the past year; and three other scholars who have become teachers were presented with beautiful pictures. The scholars in Mr. Latham's class presented that gentleman with a copy of Canon Farrar's "Life of St. Paul" and Thompson's "The Land and the Book" as a mark of their respect and esteem; while Mr. Samuel Hope presented to the adult members of his class handscme volumes. The proceedings were of an interesting character, and, on the , motion of the Rev. IL Wilson, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman, choir, decorators, &c. GOLBORNE. I GOLEORNE PARISH CHURCH.—At a special service held in this Church en Christmas Day there was a pretty large congregation, the preacher being the Rev. W. Thorpe (cu- rate.) For the occasion numerous sprigs of holly and other greens were tastefully displayed about the church. _

I ANN-UAL TEA PARTY AT GOLDORNE —The Golborne In- dependent Methodists held their annual tea meeting on Christmas Day, when about 170 sat down in the school- room. The subsequent proceedings took place in the chapel, about 300 persons being present. Mr. James Unsworth (president of the church) occupied the chair. An excellent programme of songs, recitations, &c, was gone through, the choir being conducted by Mr. John Open- shaw, and Mr. Joseph Openshaw presided at the liar- , monium. YOUNG MEN'S TEA FARTY.—AbJUt 21 of the members of the young men's class at Golborne Church Sauday School partook of an excellent knife and fork tea in the school-room, on Friday evening last. Among those present were—The Rev. W. Thorpe (curate), Mr. Fearns, and Mr. Woolacott ; while the Rev. W. Thorpe read a letter from the Rector (Rev. C. T. Quirk), expressing regret at his in- ability to attend on account of ill-health. The evening was spent in a social and enjoyable manner; Mr. Woolacott in the course of the proceedings giving an excellent address. 00LBOUNE CONGREGATIONAL SCHOOL TEA PARTY. The scholars and friends of the Golborne Congregational Sunday and Day 5ch0.,13 sat cluwn to their annual tea, which was held in the schoolcoonr on Christmas Day. About 200 persons attended, and all sealed to be well pleased with the , nice tea provided. Mr. Roger Yates presided at the subse- quent meeting, and gave a capital opening address. Selec- tions of music were given by the choir, under the leadership of Mr. Twist, and Mr. Travis ably accompanied on the American organ. Recitations and songs were nicely given by the scholars, and a very pleasant evening was spent. HAYD 0 CS. ST. JAMES'S CHURCH, HAYDOClC.—Comparatively little decoration was carried out in this church in celebration of Christmas. A few sprigs of holly and berries were taste- fully arrayed about the building, and the font was a little bedecked with flowers, but beyond these nothing was to be seen 0.1 any attempt at adornment. A special service was held on Christmas Day forenoon, when the Rev. H. Mason (curate) preached an excellent sermon.

• , HAYDO&S WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE —The annual tea party in connection with the Haydock Wesleyan Band of Hope was held in the Haydock Wesleyan School on Cnrist- mas Eve, when a goodly numbor of persons partook of an excellent tea. The schoolroom was very prettily decorated by some of the teachers and scholars, a prominent feature being a Christmas tree (presented by Miss L. Evans). At the subsequent meeting the chair was occupied by Mr. H. L. Riley, of St. Helens, who gave in address. The Rev. G. Smith, of St. Helens, and Mr John Fairhurst, of Haydock, ale° gave addresses. The members of the Band of Hope and choir went through a nice programme of recitations, songs, &c. SALE OF WORK AT HAYDaCK.—For the purpose of rais- ing funds to liquidate the debt upon the Haydock Primitive Methodist Chapel, a sale of work was held in that building on Friday afternoon last. Among those who actively be- stirred themselves in the movement were Mrs. James Livesley, Mrs. Barrow, Mrs. David Livesley, Miss Barrow, Mrs. Littler, and Mrs. Henry Harrison, and the result of their labours was very pleasing and gratifying. In formally opening the sale, the Rev. F. N. Shimmin, of Earlestown, alluded to the nice collection of articles that had been brought together by the ladies, considering the short time they had been at work. It was very satisfactory, and he expressed a hope that that effort would tend to the reduc- tion of the debt, and be only the beginning of efforts to place them in a better position. (Applause.)—Attractions in the shape of a "fishing tank" and "dip tub" were pro- vided, while a stall was set apart for refreshments. The sale of work was again opened on Saturday, and we under- stand that a fair sum was realised.

ASSOCIATION FOOTBALL.—The second team of the Hay- dock Temperance Football club journeyed to Skelmersdale on Saturday last to try conclusions with the first team of the club, which is held in connection with the Wesleyan school in that place. The captains elected to play half an hour each way, the ball being kicked off at half-past three o'clock. A very high wind blew throughout the game; but as the second team of the Temperance appear in excel- lent form this year, a very animated and pleasant game was played by both sides, resulting in a victory, for Haydock by two goals to nil, the play being almost within the pre- cincts of the Skelmersdale goal during the whole of the game. After the game was over all proceeded to the Wes- leyan schools, where the first annual tea meeting in connec- tion with the home club was to be held. After tea had been partaken of a public entertainment was clmmenced, in which the visiting team, with a few friends, took part, Mr. James Blackey reciting two pieces, Miss Hockley re- citing two pieces, and the company singing three melodies in a very creditable manner, accompanied by the harmo- nium.

div.head: HUYTON.
div.p: HUYTON.

SIR THOMAS BIRCH'S CHARITY.—The above was dis- tributed on Wednesday last in the vestry of Huyton Parish Church, to the aged poor of the parish, to the number of thirty-eight, twenty reeeived six yards of flannel, and eighteen a pair of blankets each. The charity amounts to £l5 per annum, this year ten shillings was added. The Revs. W. T. Southward and H. D. A. Hubbard, and Messrs. W. Busby, janr., and W. H. Crook, churchwardens, took part in the distribution. -A letter from the Rev. Canon Penrhyr was read, to the effect that those receiving the charity were not to expect it every year, as it was intended for the most deserving cases in the parish.- A further legacy has just been left to the poor of Huyton by the late :dr. Willmk, a former resident. The interest on £5O is to be given to the poor annually.

HUTTON TEMPERANCE MUTUAL BENEFIT CLUB—The above, which is a kind of fireside club connected with the Huyton Temperance Association, held its annual meeting on Friday last in the Huyton Park School, for the purpose of passing the accounts, dividing the surplus, and election of officers for the ensuing year. From the report, it appears the club numbered 45 members, but during the year, 13 had lapsed. The sick calls have been very heavy, £2l having been disbursed in meeting them, out of the total income of £26 Bs. 6d. There being ne working expenses incurred, a dividend of two shillings and five pence per member remained, when the usual levy for reserve fund was also deducted —The following officers were re-elected: presideat, E. S. Eccles; treasurer, W. D. Stober ; secretary, T. Oliver. Messrs. G. Lester and J. Davies were appointed stewards.

CHRISTMAS AT THE HUYTON POST-OFFICE.—There may be an impression abroad that the work of a country post- office is a very small affair. Had any person of that way of thinking paid a visit to the Huyton office on Christmas morning, any time between six and eleven o'clock, they would have had their ideas very much altered: Letters, cards, and missives of every description were literally knee deep. When it is stated that 9,891 letters passed through the bands of the small staff employed, and having to be counted, sorted, bundled, and delivered on that day, the labour and care required will be recognised—handcarts, wheelbarrows, and clothes baskets were pressed into service. 818 letters, tic., were posted on Christmas Eve in Hayton for delivery in the Huyton and Roby district alone. The parcels post also brought a considerable addition to the busi- , nets.

NEW STAINED GLASS WINDOW.—A "stained glass window, for which a faculty was recently obtained, has jest been placed in the south wall of St. Michael's Church, Huyton, by Mrs. Ihler, in memory of her husband, the late George Francis Ihler. The subject of the illumination is "The raising of Lazarus," designed by Halliday, in a two light window with tracery. Six figures are represented, the colours are rich, the drawing all that art can accomplish, and a feature not often seen is that, the design not occupy- ing the whole of the space, a flood of light ,is introduced, which brings the picture into more prominent relief than would otherwise be the case. In the upper portion of the tracery is a representation of our Saviour sitting in majesty surrounded by angels. The following inscription is added in the margin :—'To the glory of God, and in loving mem- ory of George Francis Ihler, died October, 1882, aged 46 years." The work has been executed by Messrs. James Powell and Sons, Whitefriars. London. CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY CHRISTMAS CLEM--The proceeds of the Christmas or Goose Club were distributed to the members in the infant school, on Saturday evening last. Each member received a goose, or fifths. of beef, mutton, or pork, and a quantity of groceries. Ten members took their subscriptions back. Messrs. E. B. Williams, J. J. Dawson, and J. Webster (upon whom the major portion of the work of the club devolved) were present. The good things provided presented a fine show, and gave general satisfaction, except in one instance a lady bearing a not uncommon name gave very expressive objec- ' tion to her goose, preferring mutton, and going the length of throwing the biped into the middle of the street, the good offices of P.C. Rutherford having to be exercised to persuade her to resume ownership. We have reason to believe that the lady has since given another illustration of the old adage, "The proof of the goose (?) is in the eating," and is perfectly satisfied. The meat was supplied by Mr. Doran and Mr. J. Turner, the geese (18) by Mrs. Birchall, and the groceries by Mr. Flint, of Huyton Quarry. HUYTON CHURCEL—The church on Christmas morning presented a pleasant appearance to the large congregation of worshippers, and reflected credit to the taste and industry of the several ladies who had taken part in the work during the short time at their disposal. At the base of the font choice plants were embedded in moss ; evergreens and flowers en- circled it, the basin was full of water, a cross of white cry- saathemums and ferns floated in the centre. The pillars were wreathed with evergreen, the carved oak screen taste- fully ornamented with holly and ivy was surmounted by the text "Glory to God in the highest, on earth peace, good-will toward men," in illuminated letters on a white ground and fringed with holly, a cross of white cry- santhemums occupying the centre, shields with monograms finishing the ends. The text, "The mighty God, Prince of Peace," was worked in white on crimson ground, as was also" Unto us a Child is born, unto us a Son is given," on the steps leading to the choir. A large cross, composed of splendid white chrysanthemums, adorned the table, with vases containing the same flower in different colours. The pulpit was dressed in holly, a cross of the same in yellow being in front. The ancient font by the eastern door was trailed with ivy and other evergreens, and filled with choice plants, the windows, gas brackets and cornices were also decorated with evergreens. The following ladies took their several parts in the work :—Mrs. Astley, the reredos and choir; the Misses Fieldwick, the screen; the Misses Caw, the pulpit; the Misses Busby, the font by the west door ; Mrs. Ihler, the ancient font and windows ; Mrs. Fishwick, the pillars ; Mr. Newry, and Mr. Webster assisted. The services were conducted by the vicar, the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, assisted by the senior curate, the Rev. W. T. Southward, M' .A. who preached the sermon in the morning from Isaiah IX., sth and 6th verses. The vicar took for his text in the evening, "Of such is the kingdom of heaven." The offertory for the day realised £7 2s. The musical portion of the services were well ren- deied by the very carefully trained choir; theaccompanying in the organ by Mr. Hodgson was beyond praise. IRLA IVE.

The annual Wesleyan School festival was held in the schoolroom, Irlam, on Wednesday evening. The tea was well patronised. The decoration of the room with flowers, p.ctures, and mottoes, was chaste and beautiful. The char was occupied at the after meeting by the minister of the circuit. Efficient addresses were delivered by friends, more or less connected with Sunday school work. The meeting was charmed by a little boy, who gave a recitation with wonderful correctness, emphasis and pronounciation truly surprising. We are sorry that we cannot say much in praise of the two dialogues which followed. The several pieces of music were well rendered by the choir. Prizes, in the shape of books, including Bibles and hymn books, were presented by the Rev. R. Dillon to those boys and girls who had made good attendances during the year at Sunday school. Special mention was made of a boy who had made 104 attendances. A very pleasing incident iii connection with the meeting was the presentation of a beautiful clock and Bible to a mar- ried lady who had b3en a member of the choir for 16 years —from a little girl. The meeting was closed with the usual vote of thanks.

div.head: RAINHILL.
div.p: RAINHILL.

RAINHILL CREWEL—The decorations of this church for the Christmas services was, as usual, very handsome and effective. The following ladies and gentlemen undertook the work, and completed their task in a manner that, for expedition and completeness, could not easily be excelled. Mrs. Barton, Miss F. Hooking, Miss Heagen Gibbs, Miss G. Lewis, Miss A. Martin, Miss R. Martin, Mr. S. Hooking, and Master W. Eyre. The services were well rendered, the only addition being the anthem "Behold I bring you good tidings." The Rev. .J. Barton officiated.

div.head: RLXTON,
div.p: RLXTON,

The Wesleyan Sunday School tea meeting was held in comtection with this place of worship on Christmas even- ing. There was a large attendance. The chapel was taste- fully decorated. After the tea a public meeting was held, which was addressed by the Rev. R. Dillon, and Messrs. Horrocks, Holland, and Birchall. There were several ex- cellent recitations by the children. The choir rendered very efficient service. The minister occupied the chair. The meeting was pleasant and profitable. ROBY.

Our readers will be pleased to hear that the Rev. Frederick G. Nott, 8.A., who has for some time resided in Roby, and assisted in the service of St. Bartholomew's Chnrch, under the Rev. G. J. Banner, has been appointed to the curacy of St. Andrew's, Southport, of which the Rev. Prebendary Cross is the vicar.

CONCERT AND BALL.—The annual social gathering took place on Christmas Eve in the large entertaining room attached to the Stanley Arms Hotel. The party numbered about 60. The programme consisted of songs, reci,tations, Ltc., finishing with a dance, led by a string band under the conductorship of Mr. J. Fisher. Mr. Cook presided at, the piano. The whole arrangements were ably carried out by Mr. J. Pinnington, who acted as master of ceremonies. A very pleasant evening was spent. The Christmas decorations in St. Bartholomew's Church, Roby, were of an exceedingly tasteful character, the font and lectern being richly ornamented with rare and splendid white chrysanthemums, and other hothouse flowers and ferns. The pulpit was dressed with variegated ivy and a cross of chrysanthemums. The reredos was wreathed with evergreens and flowers, and vases with fine flowers stood on the communion table. The windows were laid with moss and crosses and other devices, formed with flowers and berries. Hyacinths and other plants were ranged on either side of the choir. The vicar, the Rev. G. J. Banner, con- ducted the service.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

CURISTMAS FESTIVITIES.—The different religious sects have endeavoured to supply something for the general good during this Christmas time. The Church of England, by the ordinary service held at each church, and amid decora- tions more or less chaste and graceful, have kept up the great festival of the year. The Primitives have had teas and entertainments. That in the Station-road, presided over by Mr. T. Gibson, was well attended, and, as usual, a good programme led to an enjoyable meeting. After the opening hymn' dec., the choir rendered "Good tidings," an anthem which took well; as also did "Glory to God" and "Mes- siah reigns." The songs "The bells in the belfry ringing," by Mr. Percival; The dying child," by Miss lomlinson ; "Christmas greeting," by Mr. Plant; "Hark, I hear an angel whisper," by Mr. Johnson; "A happy new year," by Mr. Mellor, were well rendered. Other songs were given by Mr. Rowlinson, Mr. Pimlett, Miss Tomlinson, and the Messrs. Hickson; Mr. Thomas played a violin solo excel- lently; Mr. G. Hamlett gave a solo on the flute; and Mr. Kennerley one on the cornet. Collections for the trust fund were made. The Wesleyans had a gathering in the interests of thoir Sunday school, when the chapel was crowded. The young people gave recitations, and the choir under their leader rendered good service so that the affair passed off very well. The Free Methodists had their Christmas tree and sale of work in favour of the trust fund, when the choir proved as effective as previously. ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.

A SERVANT GIRL'S ADVENTURES WITH A. £2O Nara Priscilla Jones is in custody of the Cheshire police, at Nes- ton, charged on remand with stealing a £2O note under extraordinary circumstances. Early this week the prisoner called on Mr. Wood, jeweller Neston, and said she wanted to purchase a gold watch. She selected one, valued at £3

153, and then also purchased a gold guard chain, a silver bracelet, a set of earrings, and a brooch, tendering in pay- ment a £2O note. Mr. Wood, regarding such a large sum. with suspicion, questioned the girl, who replied that her father gave it her to procure the goods, that he had been, engaged in a coalmine in Wales, that the proprietors had, failed, and that Mr. Gladstone had bought the mine and paid up the men's wages, £2O being her father's arrears. So plausible was the girl's story that Mr. Wood let her have the jewellery, cashing the note for her. The prisoner then went to other shops in the town, buying three pairs of fashionable high-heeled boots, a fur tippet, a pair of fancy gloves, and other articles of lady's dress, when Mr. Wood, becoming suspicious, went to see the prisoner, who is servant with two ladies at Parkgate. She boldly denied ever being in Mr. Wood's shop. She was arrested, and then confessed the whole of her adventures with the £2O note, which she said she picked up in her mistress's bed-- room.

SALE OF WORK AT RUNCORN. In aid of the building fund of the new church, the erec- tion of which will shortly be proceeded with on a site in, Crreenway-road, given by Major J. Cavendish Orred, of Maidwell Hall, a sale of work was held in the National In- fant School, Church-street, on Thursday afternoon. We • may state that plans have been prepared for a church cipable of accommodating 600 worshippers, but it is only intended at present to build the nave at an estimated cost of £3,000. Since 1866 the spiritual necessities of the neigh- bourhood have been ministered to in Newtown Mission Church, which is now under the charge of tbe Rev. E. M. Armson, but the population having greatly increased during recent years, a proper church has become requisite. Towards the cost of its erection upwards of £1,500 has been raised, and the sale of work, which con- sisted entirely of goods unsold at the bazaar held in 1882, when nearly £l,lOO was obtained towards Ole same object, was intended to still further increase this amount. Numerous beautiful articles were displayed on the three stalls, which were arranged on both sides of the room. The first was under the superintendence of Mrs. Barclay, Mrs. John• Brundrit, Mrs. Bryant, and Miss Barclay; No. 2, Mrs. Steele ; No. 3, Mrs. Lightburn, Mrs. Crosby, Mrs. Barker, Mrs. Whittaker, Mrs. Summerfield, Mrs. Parnell and Miss Booth. There was also a refreshment stall, over which presided Mrs. Joule, Mrs. P. Wright, and Mies I% ilson. An important feature in the decorated room was the splendid Christmas trea in the centre. This, a fine fir, was the gift of Mr. S. B. Chadwick, J.P., and from its frosted branches depended a large number of articles likely to give pleasure to the juvenile mind. The tree was fixed in a rockery of frosted coals, and the general effect was exceedingly pleasant. Mr. Tonks, of Lord- street, had kindly frosted the tree and the coals. In a brief speech the Vicar, the Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A., declared the sale of work open, wishing the enterprise every success. In the evening the Christmas tree was brilliantly lighted with 100 wax candles, and a series of musical entertainments were given by Mr. Harry Roberts, while the Parish Church Band played a number of selections of music with their usual proficiency. There was also an exhibition of wax candles which had been lent by Mr. James Stubbs, of Percival-lane.

TWO MEN DROWNED AT ST. HELENS. DRINK AND ITS CONSEQUENCES. On Wednesday Mr. Barker, county coroner, held an inquest at the Princess Royal public-house, Parr, touching the death of Thomas Murphy. The deceased was a collier, 37 years of age. and lodged with a Mrs. Ellidge, at Double Locks, Haydock. On Sunday night he had been in a, drunken condition, and was being assisted home by a young man named James Webster. As they were going along the banks of the Sankey canal they overtook another man, who was also in an intoxicated condition, and Webster attempted to assist him also on his way home. In doing this, however, the deceased either slipped or jerked himself out of Webster'e• grasp and fell into the canal. Before he could be rescued he was almost dead, only living three or four minutes on the banks.—The Coroner said the affair was evidently a pure accident. It was a case of drink again.— A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.---At the same place, and on the same day, Mr. Barker held another inquest re- specting the death of a married man named James Devlin. Devlin was a labourer, living in York-street, and engaged at Mr. Walker's chemical works, Parr. On Christmas Eve, about a quarter-past eleven o'clock, he was seen in a drunken state going towards the canal near the Princess Royal public-house, and a short time after two or three men, who were going to the Christmas Eve service at the Catholic Chapel, Blackbrook, beard a scream, apparently coming from the canal. They went along the bank some distance till they came to a point where they saw the deceased in the water. At this point the canal is deep, and the bank rises perpendicularly some seven or eight feet above the water. The deceased, by grasping at the sides of the canal, was managing to keep his head above the water. The men who had been attracted to the spot tied their handker- chiefs together and held one end down to deceased. He got hold of it with his teeth, but the handkerchiefs tore, and he fell back beneath the water, and before any effectual aid coeld lad' procured he was drowned.—A verdict of " Acci. dental death" was returned.
DEATH OF MRS. M. STAPLETON BRETHERTON. OF RAINHILL.

The death of Mrs. M. Stapleton Bretherton, Marchioness of Romana, took place at.ltainhill Hall on Friday morning, the 21st inst. At the time of her death the deceased lady was 75 years of age. She was the daughter of the late Mr. Bartholomew Bretherton, in his time the largest and molt popular mail-coach proprietor in the kiegdom. The great wealth he amassed was left to the deceased lady, and by her judicious management has so increased that at the pre- sent time the family estate and other property is said to be worth upwards of a million pounds. The deceased lady was a zealous adherent and firm supporter of the Roman Catholic Church, of which she was a member. Her father erected the noble chapel at Rainhill Stoops, and she, for her part, has recently added a most ornate entrance, which, though not adding to the grand architectural arrangements of the main building, still shows her attachment to the place of worship she generally attended. At the time ot the expulsion of the Jesuit Fathers from Germany she provided a home for a large number of th4in at Ditton, placing at their disposal her house and furniture, and even- tually building, at her sole expense, a handsome church for the conduct of their religious ceremonies. On account of her munificence and zeal in the cause of her religion she received from the Pope the title of Marchioness of Roman& At Rainhill, her native place, the deeeased lady was greatly respected. Although ostensibly holding aloof from all par- ticipation in the passing events of the place, she still took a great personal interest in anything that benefited the neigh- bourhood, and privately did much to alleviate the wants of her poorer neighbours, and support any move- ment she thought conducive to the public good. At four p.m. on Wednesday afternoon the remains of the Marchioness were removed from the Hall to the neighbours ing Church of St. Bartholomew's. The tenants, emplaves, servants, and school children, considering the occasion a fitting oppoitunity to show their sincere respect and esteem, assembled at the Hall, and forming into prooessional.order escorted the body to the church • Mr. F. Bretherton, Mr. Wood, of Warrington, and Mr. T. Heald, of Rainhill, with the chief tenants and friends being present as mourners. A special funeral service was conducted by the Very Rev. Dean Kierman, assisted by the Rev. Father Henry, of Por- tico. The musical portion of the service was beautifully rendered by a choir of German Jesuit Fathers from Ditton great credit being due to the school children and teachers for the pathetic manner in which their part of the choral arrangements was carried out. The chapel, bearing no special mark of the solemn occasion, was crowded.

GOOD TEMPaRISM AT EARLESrOWN.—TIIO usual weekly meeting of the Hope of Earlestown lodge of Good Templars ws held on Monday evening in the lodge-room, Bridge- street. There WAS a good attendance of members, and Bro. John Taylor, NV.O T., presided. The only business of any interest was the making of further arrangements for the annual new year's tea party. Refreshments in the shape of coffee, tarts, were afterwards handed round, an I the members pleasantly spent the evening singing. EARLESTOWN BAPIIST CHAPEL.—A portion of the choir and a few friends connected with the Baptist Chapel, EarleS- town, met at the school on Christmas Ere, and under the leadership of Mr. J. Houldsworth proceeded to the resid.nces of several members of the congregation, where appro- priate hyms and cards were sung in celebration,of the ad- vent of Christmas. Mr. Houldsworth accompanied the sing- ing on his clarionette. Among the houses visited were those occupied by Mr. J. Eckersley (Regent-street), Mr. W. H. Adams (Queen-street), Miss Swann (Bridge-street). and Mr. Cooper (Market-street). At the house of Mr. Houlds- worth, Lawrence-street, the singers partook of an enjoyable tapper, and the party separated abut four o'clock. The sum of money realised is to be devoted towards the liquida- tion of the chapel debt. --- FIRS AT GLASGOW.—A serious fire occurred shortly after one o'clock on t"aturdiy morning in a block of business premises. at the corner of 3t. Vincent-street and Renfield- street. Glasgow. WIIITECROS6 RANGERS V. ST. PAUL'S (2ND TEAMS).—Thi• match was played on the ground of the latter on Saturday and resulted in a win for the Hangers. LYRIC V. CHEETHAM HILL (SECOND TEAM).—This match was played on Saturday at Lymm, ant resulted in a win for the latter by two tries and five minors to Lymm one miner point. RUNCORN VICTORIA V. RUNCORN WHITE STAR —This match was played on Saturday, and resulted in a win for the Victoria by two tries and five minor points to three minor points. Jolly obtained the first try and Woodward got the second, but the goals failed. BY. PAUL'S CHOIR V. ORFORD EXCELSIOR—This Match was playei on the ground of the latter, on Saturday, and resulted in a victory for the visitors by one try (disallowed), one dead ball, two touchdowns, and one touch-in-goal to one touch-in- goal. All the St. Paul's team played well. Howtiv TRUE BLUES V. SOAFERY (A TEAM).—This match was played between the above clubs, on the ground of the for- mer, on Saturday, before a fair number of spectators, the game. A very noisy and unpleasant one, ending in a win for the for- mer by one try, one disputed try, and two minor points, to seven minor points. By. HELENS V. WIGAN (2ND TEAMS).—The second team of the St. Helens Club visited Wigan on Saturday last, but only with half a team, but were ably assisted by several p-omineat members of a strong Wigan local club, who kindly volunteered their services; therefore, with the two clubs combined, a. strong fifteen were put on the field. From the very com- mencement of the game it was plainly seen that the visitors were simply not in it, the Wigan youngsters easily adding their eleventh consecutive victory, as at the call of "no aide" the score stood, Wigan, four goals, five tries' and ten minor points, to nil. WIDNES V. BALL—This match was playel at Sale, and re- sulted ie a victory for Sale by two goals, one try, and four minor points to one try and two minor points. B, Macfarlane obtained two tries and Hargreaves dropped a goal from field for Bale. Corns obtained a try for Widnes. Teams :—Sale: W. Macfarlane, back; It. Macfarlane, H. Smith, and F. Warburton, three-auerter backs; H. Alexander and B. Hargreaves, halt backs: T. Hardy (captain), E. Lings, T Lings, H. Cookson, H. Marsland, E. Marsiand, H. Vipond, H. Chambers; and 8. Price, forwards. Widnes: J. Briggs. back; J. Goulden. H. eliirrua, and S. Kendrick, three-quarter backs; T. Laws and J. Rid) ard, half-backs ; W. Mather, J. Corns, P. Perrin, T. Fogg, J. Sampson, H. Smith, W. Leche, A. Brown, and T. Killen, forwards. WARRINGTON WANDERERS V. BUTTON IST—This match be- tween the above teams took place on the ground of the latter. The home team were a heavy lot towards the Wanderers, who, howevsr, nonplussed them by their smartness. The game had not proceeded long when one of the Wanderers' beet backs re- ceived a mishap which prevented him from further taking part in the game. Two more of the visitors received slight accidents owing to the rough and severe game, but, nothing daunted, the visitors played well to a man. Appleton kicked a goal from the field. and the home captain objecting, the visitors reluc- tantly gave way. The ball being grounded over the line and the home team again objecting. the Wanderers gave way Eventually C. Uusworth secured a try, which proved the winning point. Score: Wanderers, I try. 3 minors, to 1 minor. EARLESTOWN (A TEAM) V. B. WILLIAMS' Cn Christ* roes Day morning a strong "A team" of the Earlestown club met a scratch team of players captained by B. Williams, the noted and popular Rugby footballer, the gams b sing played at Wargmve Moss in the presence of a goodly number of specta- tors. The play throughout was pretty even, some of the adepts at the Rugby game making a fair attempt to play under Association rules. The Earlestown Club team were found plenty of work by their opponents, and the latter—among whom were several well-known gentlemen—were much ap- p auded by the onlookers. The game resulted in a win for Earlestown by three goals to two, the goals for Williams' team being scored by B. Williams and M. Birkhead. W. Moses kept goal very well for the losers, and S. Williams (captain) also played well. OUGHTRINGTON V. LEVENSHULME WANDERERS.—This match was played at Heatley on Saturday before a meagre crowd of spectators. The home team defended the station goal, and kicked eft against the wind. The game was of a very even cha- racter until half-time, the score being one try each and several minor points. It was thought after the change of ends the home team would:win, but the wind ceased to blow; neverthe- less they still held their own. J. Parkinson made a splendid bid for goal, the ball falling about two yards short. The home team gained two tries in the second half, but they were disal- lowed. P. Holt made some very good runs for the home team, as did the other three-quarter backs. B. Davies and J. Shaw played splendidly at half-back, the most prominent forwarde being W. Clarke (captain). Woods, Perrin, and Leigh. The fol lowing is the score :—Oughtrington, one try, one touch in goal and two touchdowns. Wanderers, one try, one touch in goal. one touchdown, and one dead ball. EIRLESTOWN V. EVERTOR (O. M. LINDSAY'S TEAM).—The Earlestown Club had arranged a fixture for Wednesday after- noon last with the first team of the Everton Club, but, unfor- tunately, the latter turned up with only six men. Good sub- stitutes were found, and a goecisp.d exciting game was the re,ult. Notwithstanding the thick fog, through which the players could searcely be distinguished across the field, th-re was again a very large attendance of spectators. The home , team won the toss, and Richards started the leather for the ' visitors, who commenced very well, and slightly pressed their opponents. After five minutes' play Richards scored the first gest by a splendid shot, which elicited much applause. On the game being resumed the Earlestonians were not long in equalising the score, Duxbury rotching the first point for the home team. In quick succession Simm scored two other goals, said ends were changed at half time with the score three goals 'to one in favour or Boriewtown. The second half was very even, and both sides played well. Each goal was unsuocess- fully attacked up to within a few minutes of the finish, when Duxbury kicked the leather against the crossbar. As it dropped down in front of the goal. Dwell rushed up and headed it through amid considerable cheers. The match thus resul. ed in a victory for Earlestown by four goals to one. The followitigyere the teams :—Earlestown—J. Appleton, goal; R. Green and F. Emmett, backs; J. Whalley and J. Green, half-backs; W. Rich and J. Duxbury, right wing; A. Dagnall, centre; Simm and R. Bowker, left wing. C. M. Lindsay's team—J. Mean), goal; H Richards and J. Guinness, backs; A. E. Welsh and C. Birkhead (Earlestown), half-backs; 0. M. Lindsay and W. Noble (Earlestown). right wirg ; W. Richards, centre; J. Mather (Earlestown) and J. Ellison (Earlestown), left wing. Referee, Mr. P. Hestia. The players and a few friends afterwards sat down to an excellent dinner at the Sunbeam Inn. Wargmve Moss. The " spread " reflected much credit upon the host and hostess (Mr. and Mrs. Morris), and to them hearty votes of thanks were accorded. EARtEsTOWN V. OOLBORNE.—The return match between the Earlestown and Golborne first teams was played ai, Wargrave Moss, Earlestown, on Saturday afternoon, Red as the greatest possible rivalry exists between the two teams, a considerable number of spectators put in an aLpearance. The captain of the home eleven won the toss, and chose to play with the wind and ground in their favour during the first half. Cottam started the leather for Golborne, and for about a quarter of an hour ti e play was fast and exciting. After that time, however, the Earlestonians had matters all their own way, and the Gol- bornites were very severely pressed. ITu to half time no point was scored, though the home team met with many hard lines. On the change of ends the Earlistonians set to work with renewed vigour, and the forwards time after time ran the leather in front of the Golborne uprights. Ten minutes after the resumption of play the ball was nicely centred from the left wing, and Duxbury securing it about lb yards from the Gol- borne goal screwed it against one of the uprights, from which it glanced through the posts amid leud cheers Encouraged by the shouts of their supporters the home team warmed to their work, and five minutes later, after a scrimmage in frent of the goal. Duxbury again secured the downfall of the Golborae colours by a capital shot. Up to within a few minutes of the call of time the play was very one-sided, the ball never leaving the Golborne quarters. Just before the expiration of time Jenkinsen, the Golborne goal-keeper, wilfully and al' ogether needlessly jumped upon Simm—one of the home players—and after some strong words had passed between them the visitors left the field amid groans and hisses—the game thus resulting in a win for Earlestown by two goals to none. It must be said that the home team displayed much forbear- ance, especiallrin the second half, when every disputed point was given in to the visitors—some of whom appeared to have no other object in view but creating &disturbance. The teams were :—Earlestown: J. Appleton, goal; R. Green and F. Emmett, backs; J. Whalley and R. Bowkor, half-backs I J. Duxbury and W. Rich, right wing; A. Dagnall and J. Mather, centre; J. Slam and J. Cameron, left wing. Golborne Jea- kinson goal; J. Bate and Waddington, backs; Fanning and T. Kay, half-backs;: A. Allen and Se Morris, right wing; B. Cot- tam. centre; Leyland and Clarke, left wing. EARLESTOWN V. PRESTON OLYMPIC—This match was played on the ground of the former, at Earlestown, on the afternoon of Christmas Day, when there was an exceedingly large attend- ance of spectators, who were interested In witnessing a well- contested game. The Earlestonians won the toss, and for the first half chose to play from the end nearest Earlestown. Hodgkinson started the leather for the visitors, who ran the ball towards the home goal, but Bowker and J. Green easily returned it. The home team quickly asserted their superiority, and after tea minutes exciting play Simm sent the ball through the Preston posts, but the goal was disallowed for off-side play. Some nice passing by Rich, Simm, and Dagnall resulted in an attack upon the visitors pal, and Duxbury centreing the leather in front of the goal. Dagnall headed it through amid considerable en- thusiasm. On the game being resumed the home backs were I pressed, and in five minutes the score was equalised by Gar- slang, owing to R. Green missing the leather and alowing it to roll between the posts. Shortly afterwards another good run was made by the home forwards, and a short struggle in tto Preston quarters resulted in Duxbury shooting the leather through the posts, thus scoring a second goal for Earlestown amje loud cheers This defeat impelled the Prestonians to further efforts, and they again met with success. Hodgkinson once more equalising the score by a splendid f• screw" kick. No other time was register.d up to half time when ends were changed. The subsequent play was very ex- citing, as both elevens strove hard for victory. The play however, was mostly in favour of the Eartestoniang, who made several good attempts te score- At last Dagnall ran the leather up the field and a neat " pass " to Duxbury enabled the latter to score a third goal with a good shot. Immediately afterwards Bowker made a splendid kick from mid-field, send- ing the leather just over the oress-bar, while Duxbury after a nice corner-kick by Simm, nearly scored once more by a. " header," but the ball skimmed past the corner of the goal No other point was registered, however, and the match re- suited in a victory for Earlestown by three goals to two, Teams:—Earlestown: C. Birkhead. goal; ii. Greeu and J. Green, becks; R. Bowker and J. Whaley, bait-backs; J. Dux- bury and W. Rich, right wing ; A Dagnall and J. James, cen- tre; J. Sinun and J. Cameron, left wing Preston Olympic: M. Hart, goal ;R. Holmes and J Sanderson, backs; C Land- less, W. Hardman and J Bayman, half-hacks; J. Heade and J. Rinlook, right wing; J. Hodgkinson, centre; T. Lembo and T. Gerstang, left wing. The utnpires were Messrs. P. Hustle (Earlestown) and G. taighfield (Preston).

As we have previously stated, our townsman, Sir Andrew Barclay Walker, has purchaeed the Osmaston Moor estate in Derbyshire, and intends to reside there. The estate has been for many years in the hands of the Wright family, who assumed the name of Osmaston. The property may be aptly described as a "residential domain," and Is remarkable for the fertility of its soil, the picturesque beauty of its rural features, and the grandeur of the central mansion. This mansion is one of the principal country houses in England, stately in exterior form and richly decorated internally; it is seated within a well-timbered park, diversi- fied with hanging woods, lakes of water, and' avenues. The grounds and gardens are extensive; the estate comprises about 3,400 acres, and is nearly all old pasture, renowned for its milk-producing and cheese- making quality, and produces an annual income of more than £6,000 per annum (without estimating the value of the mansion, which is stated to have been built by the ancestors of the late owner, at a cost of upwards of £200,000) and surroundings, the woods and plantations in band and the sporting. The designs of the mansion is in the "early Italian style," with a large central tower, and so much attention has been paid to comfort and convenience that the house is warmed and ventilated throughout arti- ficially, and hot and sold water (both hard and soft) are conducted all over the premises. One of the most interest- ing features is the hydraulic service; advantage has been taken of the differencP between the levels of three lakes in the park, and two large overshot wheels have been fixed, which drive pumps forcing water into a large reservoir en one of the hills, and so by gravitation serving the mansion, the grounds, the fountains, the waterfalls in the rockery and Italian garden, the house, farm, buildings, and the reservoir driving the wheel which works the various domestic machinery in the house, while the drinking water is conveyed by iron pipes, over a mile in length, from springs in Shirley Woods and across the valley. The situation of the estate is advan- tageous in the extreme, being about three miles from the pleasant old town of Ashbourne, at the south end of romantic Dovedale. The estate includes the model village of Osmaston, the manor and manorial rights of Osmaston, part of the village of Shirley, and cottages in Wyaston, about thirteen homesteads, also a subordinate mansion called Wyaston Grove. The purchase also comprises the whole of the decorations in the mansion, including the oak and chest- nut carvings and all the furniture and decorative objects,l estimated te be worth many thousands of pounds.
