SOCIAL GATHEIIING AT TLIE WAR- RINGTON LIBERAL CLUB. SPEECaEs BY J. G. McMINNIES, ESQ., M.P., AND MR. COUNCILLOR BROADBENT. A Crist'flS gatnering of a thoroughly s)cial and con- 1 vival character took place at the Liberal Club, Bewsey- street, on Thursday evening, to celebrate the recent billiard handicap in connection with the Club. About sixty sat down to a capital knife and fork tea provided by Mr. andl Mrs. Cassidy, who were assiduous in their attention to the guests. The large upstairs room in which the proceedings took place was neatly decorated with bannerettes, and the following inscriptions arranged by Mr. Dell:—" Welcome to old friends and new ;" "A merry Christmas to you all;' "Long life and health to our worthy member, John Gordon McMinnies ;" " Success to Lord Ripon ;" "Equal franchise icrEneland and Ireland." The chair was taken by J. G. McMinnies, Esq., the member for the borough, Mr. Thomas Morris being in the vice-chair. Amongst others present were Councillor Charles Broadbent, Messrs Thomas Jones, S. Barlow, Thomas Fairclough, Perry, James Strange, L. S. Kenyon, Joseph Garner, Gandy, 'William .Roberts, Alcherd Rolneee and Dr. Gomel!, After teel ;tar, having been filled, The CHAIRMAN (WllO Was loudly cheered) proceejed to give "The Queen,' and in doing so observed that they dis- puted any aseartion that the Liberal Party was not a loyal party. (Hear, hear.) They believed that the Liberal party was as loyal as any other in the kingdom, and the measures they had been instrumental in passing had estab- lished the Queen's throne in a way it would not have been established else. (Cheers.) They all admired the Queen as a constitutional monarch; in every private relationshid as a wife and a mother she had been most admirable, and her fame i that respect had gone through tho whole world. (Cheers.) The toast having been loyally received, The CIitIRMAN gave "The health of the Prince and Prin- cess of Wales." There was no doubt, he said, that the Princess was a most charming woman and His Royal High- ness was a very good young man. (Hear, hear.) They wished them long life and health—they could not say that they wished they would soon come to the throne, but when they did he hoped the Prince and Princess of Wales would have a long and prosperous reign. (Cheers.) Song : Mr. Scarisbrick. The CHAIRMAN then said: The next toast is that of the Liberal Party, which I suppose is very much like what used to be called the Mayor of Wigan's toast, "Oar noble selves." (Hear, hear, and laughter.) I for my part have no doubt about the success of the Libeial Party, but it is an undoubted fact that the success of the Liberal Party de- pends on its own exertions. (Hear, hear.). There is not another influence in town that can interfere with the suc- cess of our Party if we are true to ourselves. (Hear, hear.) I have known the Liberal Party for many years, and I never knew a time when it apparently was so united and had such a promise of success. (Cheers.) I believe, when I seer "apparently," that the Liberal party is undoubtedly well united—(hear, hear)—and I do not see myself a pros- pect of anything but union amongst us, and if that be so there is no prospect but success before us. (Cheers.) I have great pleasure in calling upon my friend, Mr. Broad- bent, to respond to this toast. He has been for a long time a very earnest supporter of the party. (Cheers.) Hs is a gentleman who CAC do us a great deal of good, who has done a great deal of good, and who I believe will continue to do us a great deal of good. (Cheers.) We are proud of his support, we are happy to see him here, and I beg to give this toast, coupling with it the health of our friend, Mr. Broadbent. (Cheers.) Councillor Beloammere (who was cordially greeted) ob- served that he had no idea he should have been called upon to respond to such a toast. He came there at Mr. Cassidy's invitation, and he was very pleased to attend, because he thought amongst other good purposes that that club exer- cised as well as its political attainments, it ought to encour- age sociability. (Hear, hear.) He must heartily agree with what Mr. McMinnies said about the Liberal party. He believed they had great and true principles to support, they had a magnificent past to look back open, and they might congratulate themselves upon their party haying passed measure after measure which had maintained the advancement and prosperity of this country, and that if they had not succeeded in passing those measures their country would have suffered revolu- tion, and he believed many ether evils. (Hear, hear.) The Liberal party had saved the prosperity of the country from time to time, and especially—to refer to the chairman's open- ing remarks—had helped to establish the Throne. (Cheers.) Well, it had been found from time to time that the English people were so constituted that they could not depend alto- gether on abstract matters however good and right they might be, but they required other elements in the political party. They required that which had been referred to just *ow, viz, the social element, so that they could meet to- gether in a friendly way and support one another; and they required also, what, to use a word, they had got rather sick of,the " educational "element which was met in the lectures now in course of delivery in Warrington. ( Elear, hear.) He believed those were very good things, and would no doubt bear fruit. The Liberal party had passed through phase after phase of important measures. Mr. McMinnies rem- embered the time when the great corn law agitation was occupying the minds of the people. Then there were re- forms one after another, and the older members were apt to think that because those events were so imeressed on their own minds that the younger men must be equally well ac- quainted with them. It behoved the party, he thought, not only to look back on the past, but to look forward to the future and to see that the younger men were interested in politics. (Hear, hear.) ,A.s they went along he considered that there was no subject in the world m ire interesting than politics properly understood, and it should not only be their plea- sure, but it ought to be their duty to take an intelligent in- terest in politics, because the young man must bear in mind what was literally true, that upon him and his fellows not only depended the future prosperity of the Liberal patty, but the future prosperity of the country. (Cheers.) Unlers intelligent young men showed an interest in politics—bat not to the utter exclusion of billiards—(hear, hear, and laughter)—but in addition to billiards, it would be a poor thing for the future of this country. (Hear, hear.) He had great pleasure in responding to the toast of the Liberal party, and in wishing long life and success to the party, and to their own Liberal Club. (Cheers.) Song: Mr. Arthur Jones. The CHAIRMAN observed that the next toast was " Suc- cess to the Club "—(cheers)—and he had no doubt he should meet their wishes if he did what he was going to do, and that was to ask their friend, Mr. Thomas Morris, to propose that toast. (Hear, hear.) There was not a warmer friend to the club than Mr. Morris, and he thought they would all be gratified if that gentleman was the proposer of the toast. (Cheers.) Mr. Cassidy having recited "The Spanish Chieftain" with considerable elocutionary ability, Mr. MORRIS rose to propose the toast, which he said he did with all pleasure. He did not think it was the main idea of the gentlemen who promoted that club that it should be a success financially, but that it should be a success in Liberal politics, aud that men should come to think and talk on those questions uppermost in the world's affairs. (Hear, hear.) He thought they did that, but the reading-room was not so much frequented as he should like it to be. (Hear, hear.) As regarded politics, he liked reading speeches when those who made them had something to say, but not other- wise. He had a little dog who howled and yelped when the bell rang, and when it stopped he wagged his tail as if it was through his barking, and it reminded him of some People who went howling and barking about the country and thought they had stopped the bell from ringing, and they retired wagging their tails, although they were bitten again. (Laughter.) It was the same with some of their politicians; they launched out, but generally against stone walls, and he thought they must cut their hands semetimes. (Hear, bear.) If such men could not give them a little common sense, let them sit down until they could. (Hear, hear.) lie wished very cordially success to the Liberal Club, and coupled with the toast the name of Mr. S. Bar- low. (Cheers.) Mr. S. Bantow, in reply, said he had great pleasure in responding to the toast of the Liberal Club, inasmuch as the club was a place where they loved to dwell above all others. (Hear, hear.) There was no other club in the town with which he was associated, and he did all he could for the prosperity of that club. It was an unmistakable fact that the club was prosperous, and mere so than it appeared on the surface. There was more strength in the club thin there had ever been since it was established, and that arose because in the first place they had an honourable president —(cheers)—a secretary who was unsurpassed by any he knew—(cheers)—and a committee, all of whom, excepting himself—("No, no")—were indefatigable in their efforts to promote the prosperity of every member. (Hear, bear.) In addition, for their social enjoyment there was no man' equal to their manager, Mr. Cassidy. (Cheers.) He admired the union and harmony which prevailed among them, and he believed that as they had now inaugurated those social gatherings it would be the one grin ;1 means of oiling the wheels of their club. (Cheers.) Mr. Morris had mentioned something in his speech about the Scotch. Now he (Mr. Barlow) had been across the borders just recently, and at one of the local clubs in Ayr- shire he got among some thorough Radicals. One man said, " You hail from Warrington ?" and he replied he hailed from the Warrington Club. His interrogator said, "I think your member comes from this very spot." In the course of the evening the health of the member for Warrington was drunk. (Cheers.) He said the chairman of that club had not exceeded in geniality the chairman of his own club, and he told them that their president emanated from that dis- trict, and was worthy of the place and the Ayrshire men. (Cheers.) Mr. McMinnies was known all over Ayrshire, the people loved him, and seemed to enjoy to hear about him. (Hear, hear.) Although they did not often hear his voice in the House of Commons, he believed Mr. McMinnies was very well esteemed and liked there. He used his influence in the best possible manner, although it did not appear so prominently before the public, ' and they might depend upon it that as long as they pos- sessed Mr. McKinnies as their president the club would con- tinue to prosper as it did at present. They would also work in harmony, and he sincerely hoped Mr. McMinnies would be spared to preside over them for many years. (Cheers.) Song, "The old arm chair " (encored), Mr. F. J. Dell. The CHAIRMAN, in proposing the next toast, viz, the health of the prize donors, said he was sure the club was very much indebted to them for the encouragement they had given to what he considered was a very innocent and interesting game. (Hear, hear.) For many years he spent his evenings in playing billiards, and he did not know that it way much interfered with that kind of

industry which it had been his lot to exercise. In the to further victory the flag that te, e have carried. (Cheers.) club, of which he was a member, they had not a I don't know that I have - what foe . reading room, so they spent their evenings entirely in beyend this, that dit alea aaything to say about myself playing billiards. He was never anything but what was o I can .vs .. gives me very great pleasure to my Party and for my friends. I feel termed a fifth-rate player, but he enjoyed it very much, and towards there_ a sincere friendship and I have never seen for what he knew those he played with enjoyed it also. At any rate, bered with great pleasure the evenings he spent—and he either in one capacity or another, you will never find me spent every evening—in playing billiards. (Hear, hear.) wanting. (Cheers.) I cannot say in what capacity I can Now they were very much indebted, as he had said, to the best serve you; perhaps I shall have to judge for myself, prizedonors for the encouragement they had thus given to but in whatsoever capacity I can serve you I will serve yor. . the young gentlemen playing billiards, and whosoever had (Hear, hear.) I don't think I have anything further to arranged the present entertainment in connection with the say, except to congratulate you upon the very pleasant 'billiard playing had done a very good service to the party and upon the very pleasant occasion that we have social life of the club. (Hear, bear.) The very spent to-night, and to hope you have had -r, very merry essence of a club was the sociality of if members, and as Christmas, and to hope still more that you will have a very long as they were cordial to one another, forbeering to one happy New Ye tr. Morris presiding on the departure of Mr. aila:corini js. mrA (Cheers.) He had not before him the list of prizes, but he I Most enjoyable rime was sneut by the mombets. rather fancied they wets both valuable and useful. In any ..---- Case there could be no doubt that the giving of those prizes would be a great encouragement to what he had already called an innocent and interesting game. (Cheers.)—Song : Mr. Feirclougla—The toast was enthusiastically drunk. Mr. WILLIAM ROBERTS, in proposing the health of the prize winners, sail he should state the nature of the prizes and name the winners of the first four [prizes. No. 1 consisted of a dinner service and roand of beef, value 355., which was won by Mr. Oldfleld. The second prize was half-a- dozen table knives and forks, with carvers to match, and a leg of mutton, of the value of 253, woo by Mr. Charnock, the third consisting of a copper kettle and two rabbits, value 17s CI, was won by Mr. Jeffreys, and the fourth, a vary fine &Jose, won by Mr. Walker. Then there were ten other prizes. It was gratifying to notice that the prizes which had been given were both useful and ornamental, and were such as could be participated in by the families of the respective gentlemen who had obtained them. (Hear, hear.) He was exceedingly proud at so many prizes being given, and it was also very pleasing to observe that seine of their younger members especially hail been successful in winning them. They were greatly indebted to the gentle- men whose liberality had enabled the committee to give such valuable prizes. (Hear, hear.) In doing so they had done a great service t) the Club. A. billiard handicap was not only useful as a means of enjoyment to the members, but he believed it was to a very large extent instrumental in keeping a spirit of unanimity and good feeling among them, which as a Party was so desirable should exist. (Hear, hear.) He was glad to hear the remarks of their worthy Chairman, that the Liberal party were thoroughly united, and he honestly hoped they would continue so until the next general election, because they might depend ape it they would have their work to do, but in unanimity they would have nothing to fear. (Hear, hear.) He rejoiced in the fact that there was every prospect of success for the Warrington Liberal Chile. and he trusted their honoured president would be long spared to coma among them, and add dignity to their proceedings by his genial presence, which caused them so rimy times to rejoice. (Cheers.) In conclusion he wished the prize- winners long life, and hoped they would be able to compete for prizes ,of equal value in the future. (Cheers.) Songs having been given by Mr. C. Oldfield, Mr. Young, and Mr. Manoghue, Mr. MORRIS rose to propose the health of the Chairman, which he did in complimentary terms. He rejoiced to lie in company with Mr. McMinnies, and he had no doubt all around him entertained the same feelings to- wards their member. (Eeer, hear.) He hoped they would assemble in that room ur "er the chairmanship of their pre- sident, and if the time should come when Mr. McMinnies would have to go to the poll again, he trusted that the 529 would be 1,053. (Cheers.) That would be so if a certein party kept talking twaddle, and the party they (the Liberals) belonged to spoke commoe sense and promoted measures for the good of old England. (Hear, hear.) Let them hope that *their young men would always have someone to preside aver ' them who would give them sound advice and words ot cern- mon sense. When they heard Mr. McMinnies there was always something worth listening to which made them love and admire him. (Cheers.) Mr. PERRY supported the toast, and expressed the hope ' that Mr. McMinnies would represent Warrington for many years. Personally he was a comparative stranger amongst them having been in the town only about six months. When he first Came to Warr:ngton he did not take much interest in politics, but he was a constant reader of both Tory and Liberal papers and thought over in his own mind what one speaker and another said on public affairs until he came to the conclusion that the Liberal Party were the common-sense party. (Cheers.) It was always his prac- tice in business or anything else to well weigh a matter be- fore arriving at a decision, and to look at both sides of the question. T' -1; was what he did before he joined that club. (Hear, Ar.) He firmly believed that the efforts of the Liberal Party were for the interests of the people of this country. They might title for instance the recent Conservative meeting which took place in the Public Hall, and the laage gathering of Liberals held last week—any impartial person comparing the speeches delivered at those two meetings would be bound to say that the last meeting was the most successful. (Cheers.) Having thus come to the firm conviction that the Liberal Party was what he would call the best party—(hear, heir)—in the interests of the people of the country he hoped when an election came that he would be able to do his little duty towards their Chairman, and that the Liberal party would be the reign- ing party in this country. Song: Mr. Gandy. The CEFtIRMAN, who was again received with load cheers, said: Gentlemen, I can't ray I am unaccustomed to public speaking in response to a toast like this, and in acknow- ledgment of the great kindness received from my party and from my friends on all occasions. (Hear, 'hear.) lam very much obliged to Mr. Morris for the kind terms in which he has proposed this toast, and to our new friend, who has seconded it, for the equally kind terms in which he has per- formed that ditty. (Hear' hear.) As regards our friend Mr. Morris, we know him well. (Cheers.) He is a very old friend of ours, a very valued friend of ours, and on an occasion like this I should say he is invaluable. (Cheers.) As regards our new friend I can only say we are all delighted to find he has cast in his lot with us and I sincerely hope, and I have no doubt that every min in this room hopes, that he will never have any reason to regret it, and that he will spend a long and very prosperous life amongst us. (Hear, hear.) I have great sympathy with what Mr. Morris said about the pleasure of these social meetings. I agree entirely with him, and I can say, as tee has said, that I do not know anything that gives me more pleasure than to take part in them. (Cheers.) He said something about the refreshing Lifluencee of a drop of cold water. Ido not know whether he expected I should throw cold water on this meting—(laughter)--if he did he was entirely mistaken. (Cheers.) I should like, on the con- trary, to warm it up to the utmost extent of my Malay, and upon my word I don't think there is very much to com- plain of as to the warmth of this meeting. (Heerkkear.) Well, we are getting old Some of us, and I sympathW cor- dially also with what Mr. Morris said about the young men. (Hear, hear.) Instead of the fathers, we must have the help of the children in the natural course of events, and I shall be very glad if we find that the young men belonging to our party are as anxious as their fathers have been to promote the best interests of the Liberal party in this district. (Hear, hear.) I can look back myself upon some fifty years of Liberal measures, and upon nearly as long a time as that in which I have taken an interest in Liberal politics. (Cheers.) I beg to assure the young men that in looking back upon my career there is nothing I regard with more pleasure and gratification than the interest I have taken in Politics. (Cheers.) It is a great thing to have a retrospect in po'itics, and I am thankful that my retrospect in politics has not been that of opposing every good measure that has been passed in the interests of this country—every measure which has been admitted to be for the good of the country —but on the contrary, I am glad to think that I took my part in supporting those measures which have been calcu- lated to promote the best interests of the party during the last 50 years. (Cheers.) I remember measures that were passed for the eafrauchisement of those centres in connection with the Corporations of this country. There was a time , when no Dissenter in this town or in this country could have taken part in the corporate management of the towns. ilf a man was a Dissenter he was ex laded from the man- agement of corporate matters. (Hear, hear.) I remember also the time when if a man was a Catholic he could not sit in Parliament. I remember the time when 1 the trade of this country was crippled, cribbed, and con- fined by protectionist laws. (Hear, hear.) I remember the . time also when the Corporations to which I have referred were sinks of iniquity and corruption—(hear, hear) , —and those of you who have weighed the proceedings of the corporations of this country since their reform in 1831 must have been convinced that that great reform was of great importance for the welfare of the boroughs that have been incorporated, and you may go further and say with me that to meet the grievances which are complained of in London at the present time with regard to the East End, and the various sanitary reforms needed there, that the first reform should be the reform of the Corporation of London. ([tear, hear.) There may be some things to this day which are doubted as to their good effects upon the country. It may be doubted whether the abolition of the Established Church in , thing.lreland (wasH e goodaar,h ehear.) thing..) tiy b nli thinke te d 0 ui it is dwhether altogethereterb ee Trish goodis 1 ILand Act—passed by Mr. Gladstene in 1881—'8 altogether a good thing. I think it is a very good thing—(hear, hear) —but I say it may be doubted. Daring my lifetime, all the Liberal measures which I have supported are now admitted to be good, and the time will come when even those measures which I have referred to, which have been thought doubtful, will be generally admitted to have been for the prosperity of the country—(eheers)—and I should not be surprised if the Tories before I die were the people to lay claim to having carried those measures. (Loud laughter.) Mr. Morris said something about my going to Heaven, and I think be rather expressed the wish that I should go there. Well, I might go to a worse place. (Laughter.) I hope, however, th tt when the good tirno. comes I shall see rising up to fill the places of those elder ones of us who have gone before, a number of young men who will carry out the measures that still remain to be carried out and that a multitude of young people will be carrying

CHRISTMAS CELEBRATIONS AT WARRINGTON, Christmastide, despite the depreseeeag ana nuseasenahle weather with which it was attendee, was celebrated in War- rington in the customary joyo,as spirit, and in a manrer befitting the great festival. Our tradesmen seemed to be reaping quite a little harvest en Saturday and Monday, the public not being sparin-g le their purchases, whilst on both days, especially in tlee evenings, the streets were thronged. Buttermarket-street and Bridge-street particularly were at times almost impassable. An additional market was held on Monday, and proved a very good one, there being a fine and ample display of turkeys, geese, and all kinds of game, the best of which were soon disposed of. During the evea- ing the carol parties paid their usual visits, and Christmas morning was ushered in with their singing of suitable hymns. On Christmas Eve, too, in addition, a brass band composed of a numerous company of local musicians paraded the principal streets, so that from a musical point of view the inhabitants had plenty to remind them of the approach of the glad Christmastide. Christmas morning broke out foggy and mirky, and continued so throughout the whole of the day. The streets were consequently com- paratively deserted, although in the morning a large number of persons were to be seen wending their way to the various churches and chapels. The Parish Church especially, and most of the other sacred edifices were artistically decorated, but the scarcity of berries this year made the embellish- ments in several instances considerably shorn of that bright effect they would otherwise have had. At the Roman Catholic Churches there were the usual Christmas decora- tions. The chief feature at St. Albans is the Crib on the Gospel side of the altar. There is a beautiful group of three figures representing the Infant Saviour, St. Joseph, and the Virgin Mary, the whole calling to mind most vividly the scene of the stable of Bethlehem narrated by the Evangelist. The High Altar has also been tastefully and I artistically decorated with evergreen and flowers for the festival. On Christmas Eve the preacher, the rev. Father Beauvoisits, took his text from the Gospel of the Day, and after explaining how the Christmas Festival was different from all the other High Festivals of the year, he showed some very practical les- sons to be learnt from the Feast, chiefly d welling on the advan- tages to Christmas of lowliness of mind and christien joy, suet!, as was seen in the lives of the Shepherds of Bethle- hem. There was a good congregation, whose interest and and devotion seemed very earnest during the whole of the ceremony. High mass was celebrated, the rev. Father Feeney officiating as celebrant, Father Beauvoisin being deacon, and Father Furnise sub-deacon. The musical portion of the services was very impressive, Mozart's 12th Mass with orchestral accompaniment being rendered in a most praise- worthy style. The solos were taken by Miss Cavanagh, treble; Miss J. Unsworth, alto; Mr. F. J. Dell, tenor; and Mr. Cotterill. bass. Herr Praeger led the band with the first violin, and Mr. Whitehead conducted. Several of the chapels in the town held tea parties and social gatherings during the day, which passed off successfully. On Boxing Day (Wednesday) most of the tradesmen closed their establishments, and the day was observed as a general holiday. The special trains to Liverpool and Man- chester, as on Christmas Day, were largely patronised. The list of Christmas " drunks " heard at the Borough Court, on Wednesday, was comparatively light, and. we are glad to say showed a falling off of the number in preceding years. CHRISTMAS AT THE Wonnerousn. Christmas Day at the Workhouse is al ways eagerly looked forward to by the inmates of that well-managed institution, and the good things which it brings to them makes the pro- ceedings of the day a welcome departure from their ordinary dull routine. The Guardians behaved liberally, and pro- vided them with roast beef and plum pudding, the beef be- ing from prime points supplied by Mr. Gill, whilst Mr. Bolton's treble X imparted an additional enjoyment to the repast. The respected master and matron, Mr. and Mrs. Mackey, were assiduous to those under their care, and the happy and contented looks of the inmates were a sefficient proof that the efforts made for their pleasure were appreciated. The number who sat down to dinner was 315. In addition to the requirements of "the inner man" being well looked after by our parochial authorities the surroundings of the inmates were by no means forgotten. Tne large dining hall was most taste- fully ornamented for the occasion with scrolls and mottoes appropriate to the season, this being the work of the Misses Barlow, Mackey, Pugh, Watkins, and ecot, and the whole was surmeunted n. evergreens sent by Sir Gilbert Greenall and Mr. Lyons, of Appleton Hall. Miss Dakin generously sent each inmate a Cnristmes card besides several mottoes for the rooms. This lady, we are informed, devotes a day a week to visiting the sick in the hospital, a very thoughtful consideration on her pact, and which others of her ssx would do well to imitate. After dinnsr the weed and snuff was indulgee in, a quantity of tobacco having been sent by Miss Woolstencroft of the Patten Arms. Mr. Robert Heaton and Mr. Lawless sent a box of oranges each, and Mr. Thomas Jolley a large number of illustrated and comic papers. In the evening the time was pleasantly passed in songs, recitations, esc., and all retired at nine o'clock well satisfied with the day they had spent. It is always a pleasure to know that the wants of our poorer aid indigent brethren are carefully attended to on all joyous festivals of the year, and Werrington is particularly strict, and rightly so, on this point. Thanks to the liberality of a number of gentlemen of the town, the matron has prepared a beautiful Christmas tree for the children, and the toys will be distributed on the 4th January. The tree this year has been presented by*Mr. John White. PRIMITIVE METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL, LEGE-STREET. —A public tea messing wee held in the schoolroom on Christmas day, when about 70 persons sat down to tea. The tables were presided over by the following ladies Mrs. Morton, Miss L. Morton, Mrs. Morriss, Miss Morriss, Mrs. Jones, Miss P. Cook and Miss C. Cook. After tea an enter- tainment was given, the chair being taken by the esteemed 1 minister, Rev. J. Morton, assisted by Mr. J. Hall, Mr. Jones, IMr. Bissen, the res,eected superintendent, and Mr. W. Miller, , assistant saperintendent. The following programme was given in a very excellent manner r—Chairman's address; I recitation, "God upon the ocsan," Miss Florence Morton; anthem, choir; 53rd chapter of Isaiah, Miss Emma Morriss; • address, Mr. Jones; anthem, choir; recitation, "The old Saxon name for mince pie," Mister Joseph Buckley ; recita- tion, ." Trust in mother," Miss Emma Conway; anthem, choir; recitation, "The gospel engine," Master Charles Morriss ; quartette for strings, " The serenade "—Mozart, Misses Borrows, Meredith, Littlewood, and Podatere. Miss , Beatrice Thornton presided at the harmonium and Mr. H. Thornton conducted the choir. WORKINGMEN'S MIsSION SUNDAY SCHOOL, BANK QUAY. —ln this school there are 214 male and 180 temale scholars —total 394, with an average morning attendance of 152, and 300 in the afternoon. Mr. Thomas Ashley and Mr. Thomas Dale are the superintendents ; Mr. W. Ford, secretary ; Mr. J. Monks, visitor; and there are 12 male and 9 female I teachers for the ensuing year. There is also worked here a Band of Hope with 200 members by the teachers. The scholars annual treat took place the day after Christmas, when the children were plentifully supplied with tea, cur- rant bread, seed bread, buns. At the close each scholar re- ceived an orange, for which the teachers feel very thankful to the patron of the Mission, John Crosfield Esq., J.P. After tea a very interesting programme was gone through of reci- tations, songs, dialogues, rte. CHRISTMAS AT THE BARRACKS. Nowhere was Christ- mas celebrated in a more jovial and thoroughly English character than at Orford Barnacles, where special prepara- tions had been made by the soldiers. Quite a transforma- tion was effected in the appearance of the various rooms, and it was really wonderful to ebserve the artistic taste and finish displayed in the adornments. A good number of the men have only been at the Barracks a short time, yet every- body worked with thorough zest and earnestness, and the result of the whole, as we have said, was an unqualified success. On being shown over the Barracks by our res- pectee) guide, Sergeant Caurbedge,—an "old saldier " in every sense of the word—we were first conducted to No 1 room, of K Company Ist Battalion eouth Lancashire Regi- ment, better known as the famous XL Regiment. This was in the Princes block of buildings. On the walls were the words smartly arranged, " Peace and happiness to Colonel Bell and family," "A hearty welcome to Lieutenant Man- son," Long life and success to Lieutenant O'Brien," " Long life to Major Ball and family," "A long and happy life to Captain Mansel," Sze , whilst a graceful tribute to brave colleagues was expressed in the sentiment " May prosperity descend and health attend all our comrades who fought at the Egyptian War." There were several excellent Christmas paintings all the work of the men ; whilst like the thoroughly loyal fellows that they are, they showed their reepect for the Throne by a portrait Her Majesty with the Royal Standard, etc., and the words God save the Queen and iloyel Family." eet the far end of the room was a shield of leeyonete, and in the centre the words "Defence net defence" being a memento of the battle of Meharajpore in 1843, and the anniversary of which is celebrated to-slay (Saturday.) On each side ef this was an 1 interesting relic in the shape of a flintlock used by the Grenadier Company of the 40th (XL.) Regiment in Egypt ia 1790. The general aspect of the apartment was set oil with smart festoons and garlands of ever- , greens, of which there wee aei abundance. • In thisj the Christmas tree was placed, and over eighty children re- I ceived toys oF all descriptions from it on Christmas Day. j

Afterwards, I through the kind permission of the Colonel, friends were I allowed in, and a right merry time was spent in dancing and singing up to eleven o'clock. Boxing Day was spent in the same happy style. CHRISTMAS AT THE INFIRMARY. The patients at the Infirmary spent a very pleasaat day, thanks to the generosity of the committee and the kind attention they received from the officials of the institution. Indeed the inmates for the time appeared to forget their ills, so happy were their sur- roundings. There was the usual bountiful cheer of roast beef and plum pudding, and during the day the Ladies' Committee visited the patients and distributed a quantity of Christmas cards, which were gratefully accepted. The wards were neatly decorated with evergreens, flowers, and mottoes appropriate to the season, this being the work of the matron (Miss O'Neill) and Nurses Chipman and Bram- wood, who may be congratulated upon the pleasing effee produced

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
The St. Jamess Gazette learns that Professor Owen is to be made a K.C.B. in acknowledgment of the important services he has rendered to science during a period of 60 years.
The Central News is informed that Lord Headley has been elected a representative peer for Ireland in the room of the late Earl Mount Castlell. He will take his seat when Parliament meets.

The Pall Mall Gazette states that the title by which Mr. Tennyson is to be raised to the peerage, and which has been approved by Her Majesty, is Baron Tennyson, of Aldworth, in the county of Sussex anol of Freshwater in the Isle of Wight. Writing in answer to correspondents, Mr. Bradlaugh says he proposes to go to the House of Commons on February. sth. alone, and do his best to take his seat. He does not in- tend to organise a solitary public meeting before the meet- ing of Parliament. or obtain a single petition, as petitions have been disregarded and public meetings ignorei.

AN UNEXPECTED FORTUNE A CLERIC TO BECOME A BARONET.—A young man engaged as clerk in an auc- tioneer's office at Huntingdon has unexpectedly become a baronet by succeeding to the title and estates of the Blackistones of Staffordshire. The whilom clerk is now Sir Horace Blackistone, Bart., with mansion and extensive estates in Staffordshire.

It appears that Cetewayo complains of being insufficiently supplied with food. Mr. William Grant, in writing on this subject in a letter dated November 27th, says the King is not receiving anything like the amount of food which he ought to receive. He adds that the people are anxious to send him supplies of cattle and grain, but the police will not allow them to do so. FATHER AND DAUGHTER DROWNED.—Late on Wednes- day night, as a man named George Lockwood and his wife, with their daughter, aged 16 years, were walking homeward along the bank of the canal, near 111irfield, the girl, owing to the fog, stumbled and fell into the water. The father jumped into the canal with the object of saving his daughter, but not being able to swim he was drowned, as was the girl._ _

SERIOUS COLLISION AT SEA: NARROW ESCAPE OF A STEAMER'S CREW.—lntelligence was received yesterday at Great Yarmouth of the loss of the steamer Gainsborough belonging to the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company, by collision 30 miles off the Spurn light, with the steamer Collier Wear, belonging to Sunder- land, and bound thence to London.with coal. The Gains. borough was a regular trader between Grimsby and Ham- burg, with a general cargo, a crew of 23 men, and four saloon and three steerage passengers, among the former being an actress named Lilla De Vere and her husband, who were on their way to America via Grimsby and Liverpool. The Gainsborough under ordinary circumstances should have arrived at Grimsby on Wednesday morning, but she hld to proceed with such caution owing to the prevalence of fogs that sbe did not arrive off Spurn Head until neon on Thursday. At one o'clock, on Thursday afternoon,

when about 30 miles off the Spurn Lighthouse, those on board the vessel Gainsborough heard through the thick fog the sound of a steamer's whistle on the starboard bow, and two minutes afterwards they saw the dim outlines of a steamer approaching. The engines were at once reversed, but nothing could be done to prevent the collision, and the Gainsborough was struck amidships and cut down to the waters edge. The crew and passengers, with the exception of two of the lat- ter, together with Captain Hawkins, the second engineer, and the fireman, scrambled on board the Wear, the others being conveyed from the sinking steamer to the Wear by one of her boats. They had only just time to save them- selves when the Gainsborough went down. The crew and passengers lost all their personal effects. Miss De Vere had some valuable dresses, &c., with her. It was found that the Wear was very much damaged, and she han to return to the Tyne, the passengers and crew being Soon after the Cc.ilieien transferred to the Franklin belonging lo Sunderland and bound f!;;a1 that Dort to Lon- don' with coalet On arriVlng in 'Yarmouth Roads they were I tag'ene tonrci a tug, which steamed them into thelbarbour I and they were conducted to the Sailors' Home. 1" 'ln the afternoon most of the crew were frankedl to their homes by the secretary of the Sailors Home.— I The Grimsby correspondent of the Central News tele- graphs :—The Wear, which collided with and sunk the Gainsborough, is lying in the Royal Dock Basin. Besides a large hole in the centre of the how, she has sustained serious damage below the water line, and her forehold is full of water. The Gainsborough was valued at between £30,000 and £40,000, exclusive of cargo, and the loss will fall upon her owners, they being their own underwritors. The last vessel lost by the company was the Leeds, which foundered off the North Pier of the Maas Sluis, in 1880, and the Halifax, which was wrecked on Heligoland in Feb. of-the same year.

div.head: REPORM OF THE HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: REPORM OF THE HOUSE OF LORDS.

• Speaking late on Thursday night at the Mayor ia banquet at Chester, which was attended by the Duke and Duchess of Westminster and Mr. and Mrs. Henry Gladstone, the Duke of Westminster, in responding to the toast of the House of Lords, raade a most important speech on the re-- form of that institution. His Grace said that members of that august institution had been told they ought to clear out of the way altogether. He lid not believe that the House of Lords would stand upon the hereditary element alone in its constitution. The times was changing, and though the hereditary element had worked well on the whole, he believed that the House could not have existed but for very liberal additions which had been made to it. What they wanted was same reform in the House of Lords itself, enabling that House to take a larger share in the public business of the country, and bringing it more within the range and spitit of the age and of the public opinion. (Ap- plause.)
PUBLIC-HOUSE STORMED BY 300 SOLDIERS. FLIGHT OF THE INKEEPER : HIS STOCK CONSUMED.

The Central News Canterbury correspondent telegraphs : —A. scene of the wildest confusion prevailed for about four hours in this city on Thursday night. A body of cavalry soldiers, numbering nearly 300, broke into and completly wrecked a public-house known as the City Arms. The origin of the riot, which lasted until past two o'clock on Fri- day morning, was the non-receipt of a silver watch won by a soldier at a recent " Sing-song party." Enraged at its being kept from .them, the soldiers stormed the house shortly before closing time, possession being taken by the soldiers, who drank the whole of the liquor in the place, smashed the furniture and windows' and completely wrecked the premises. The landlord and his wife succeeded in making their escape. Fearing to make matters worse the authorities declined to send troops to quell the disturb- ance And the picket was totally unable to cope with the rioter'. About six hundred of the men left on Friday morn- ing for Portsmouth en route to India.

div.head: DRUIDS' FESTIVAL AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: DRUIDS' FESTIVAL AT WAR- RINGTON.

A public tea party and ball took place at the Public Hall, on .Wednesday evening, in connection with the Widow and Orphans Fund Society of Druids, Warrington district. About 300 sat down to tea, after which the Mayor (Alder- man J. Harrison) took the chair, and he was warn-tly welcomed. He said he was very pleased to attend that eveniag. and was glad to see everybody looking so happy. He was particularly pleased to see them at that festive sea- son of the year. They knew that Christmas came but once a year, and it brought with it many joys and festivities, but they knew that unfortunately it frequently brought its sorrows also. People gave themselves up to enjoyment, and they did not always follow that sensible maxim which said "Be merry and wise." (Hear, hear.) It was all very well to be merry, but if they were merry without being wise it did not avail them much. His Worship then referred to the shocking death of a lad in Warrington through drinking raw spirits on Christmas Eve and observed that that was brought about by the season of the year. No doubt that lad and his companions had had some money given to them and they sought to be :merry without being wise. (Hear, hear.) He hoped those present that 'evening would be as merry as their hearts would let them, but they must not forget to be wise as wed. He trusted they would not have the painful reflection on the morrow that they had ms-spent the night. It was perfectly proper to enjoy a dance; their legs were made to walk and to dance, and they could enjoy the pleasures of a good dance, but still be wise, which was in regulating their conduct in such a way as to produce no misgiving when to-morrow morning came. (Hear, hear.) He should like to make a remark or two upon the nature of the institution, the anniversary of which they were met to- gether to celebrate. From what he knew of it he s..aid say it was an institution that every workin.gm in should identify himself witb, for it would be productive of blessings to himself and family. Institntions of that kind always were so, and he thought the Druids' society having existed so long hi Warrington its reputation and good cha- racter were beyond reproach. (Hear, hear.) He observed that by the payment of the small sum of 21 per month would secure to the member taken ill 103 per week as long as he was disabled, and that he received for the first six months. After that period, if he was still incapable of working, he would then be entitled to receive 5s per week for six months longer, and should it happen that at the end of 12 months he was disabled, as they knew unfortunately such was the case at times, he wouli be entitled to 4s per week for the rest of his life. (Applause.) Those were very great ad- vantages, and a hich every working man who was able to pay the small subscription, should secure for himself. The best and strongest of them could not tell when they might be laid on a bed of sickness aud contract a disease which might strike to them for life, and it was, therefore, a prudent thing for them to provide for a little self-dependence which would be an advantage, not only to the members themselves, but to the persons dependent upon them. Then supposing the head of the family died his widow was entitled to a paynaenf of £lO. He might tell them that the fund out of which the payments were made at present amounted to £5,000. That was a substantial sum, and he thought it was sufficient to make everybody feel pretty secure who joined the society. The bulk was in- vested in the Warrington Corporation bonds, which were as secure as the Bank of England. The fund connected with the widows' and orphans' branch amounted to £6OO 178 id, being an increase of £Bl Os 5d on the previous year. During 1883, the year which was drawing to a close,there had been seven widows recieved with £5 each and ten children with lOs each. In conclusion the Mayor expressed the hope that the company would spend a happy but temperate evening, reminding them of Shakespeare's words that "Every inor- dinate cup contains an ingredient, and that ingredient is a devil." (Applause.)—P. A. DAVID HoucuaroN, having read the balance sheet, he asked them to accord a hearty vote of thanks to their worthy and respected Mayor for honouring them with his presence that evening. If there was one thing more than another which encouraged Friendly Societies to work with renewed stimulus it was when that work was backed up by such a gentleman as their Mayor. (Applause.) He was sure they would all join with him in cordially thanking the Mayor for his patrenage, and wish his Worship and the Mayoress a very happy new year. kAp- plause.)—The MAYOR, in reply, remarked that he was there that evening as a duty as well as a pleasure, because he thought, having been placed in the proud position he was a short time since, it was his duty to make himself as use- ful as he could in assisting and encouraging every institu- tion which was for the benefit of the people among whom he lived. (Applause.)—Dancing shortly afterwardr com- menced to the strains of Mr. Manning's quadrille band, and was vigorously kept up until the early hours of the morn- ing. R.A. Wm. Bibby acted as M.C., the stewards being P.A. Josseph Berry, and P.D. G M. S. Hankey.

RUNCORN POLICE COURT.—Yesterday afternoon, Kate Lancaster, Elizabeth Doyle, John Murray, and Ann Murray were brought up at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. G. L. Davies, charged with stealing a pair of boots, of the value of 10s., the property of Henry Stone, shoe dealer, Church- street.—On the evidence of the prosecutor, who identifiod the boots, and P.S. Whalley, who apprehended the prisoners, the prisoners were remanded till Monday. PENKETH MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION: ANNUAL CONVERSAZIONE.—The annual conversazione in connection with the Penketh Mutual Improvement Association was held on Thursday evening in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, which had been tastefully and effectively decorated for the occasion with evergreens: pictures, and mottoes, &c, promi- nent among the latter being one, "God bless our president and his wife." The remainder of the mottoes consisted of familiar quotations from the writings of Robert Burns. The evergreens, ctz.., were kindly supplied by Mr. R. Garnett. There was a goodly number of persons present, and everyone seemed to be thoroughly well pleased with the entertainment provided for them. In the course of. the evening the Rev. Thomas Rippon. of Warrington, gave an earnest address on the benefits to be derived from such societies as that. The programme of the evening's proceedings was as follows :—Glee, Mr D Garnett and others; pianoforte duet, the Misses Boyd ; reading, Mr R Hobson; song, Mr C H Parkes; recitation, Mr P Davies; cornet solo, Mr G Guest; song, Miss Annie Boyd; reading, Mr C E Parker; song, Mr R E Garrett; pianoforte solo. Miss Nellie Garnett; song, Mr D Garnett; local duet, Messrs Cobson and Gaudy; reading, the president; song, Miss Annie Moses ; song, Mr C H Parkes; local duet, Miss Annie Boyd and Mr D Gar- nett; reading, Mr R E Garnett; song, Miss Briscoe. The party broke up about eleven o'clock after singing the National Anthem.

CHRISTMAS TREE AT PENlCETR.—Yesterday afternoon a Christmas tree and sale of work was opened in the Penketh Wesleyan schoolroom, in aid of the chapel alteration and extension fund. The sale had been looked forward to with some interest in the neighbourhood, and the members of the ladies' committee, comprising Mrs. Robert Garnett, Mrs. Wilkinson, Mrs. Picton, Mrs. Mainley, Mrs. Seed, Mrs. Soderland, Mrs. David Garnett, Mrs. John Jackson, Miss Reswick (treasurer), and Miss Dodd (secretary), worked zealously in order to make it a success. There is every reason to hope that their efforts will be rewarded with this desired result. The schoolroom presented a very cheering and lively appearance, the three stalls bein well filled with a choice assort- ment of useful and fancy articles; while in the centre of the room was a large Christmas tree stocked with children's toys; the . latter having been adorned uy Moses, Miss Cook. Miss Nelly Garnett, and Miss Hobson. There was a well-laden refreshment stall at one end, and this was in charge of Mrs. Seed, Miss Boyd, and Mrs. John Jackson, while Mrs. David Garnett, Mrs. Robert Cook, Mrs. Wilkinson, Mies Jones, Miss Garnett, and Miss Bestwick looked after the " general " stalls. The walls of the room were neatly decorated with pictures, mottoes, and sprigs of holly and other greens, and altogether the rows and its contents were a pleasing sight. It was intended that Mrs. Coupe, of Southport, should have de- clared the sate open, but as that lady fowarded a telegram expressing her inability to attend, the duty in question was kindly accepted by Mrs. Robert Garnett. There was a fair attendance at the opening ceremony, including Mr. R. Gar. nett, Mr. P. Johnson, Mr. Thomas Seed, Mr. John Mainley, Mr. Thomas Watson, drc. Mc. Robert Cook briefly intro- duced Mrs. Garnett, who, in a few well chosen and appro- priate words, declared the sale open. She remarked that she did so with the greatest pleasure because it was for a good cause, and she hoped all who attended would buy willingly and freely so that it would be successful. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. Robert Cook said they were much indebted to Mrs. Garnett, and also to Mr. and Mrs. Beswick for :heir kindness in allowing their house to be used by the !adies' committee as they pleased.— The sales were then proceeded with. In the evening the room was well filled, and selec- tions of music were nicely rendered at intervals.

I went. I pressed upon him all the points that I thought ought to convince him that while yours was undoubtedly a case for some punishment, it should be of such a nature that when once pressed through would leave no rankling thoughts it feelings behind. 'Punish, but don't ruin,' I said, in effect. "Curiously enough my strongest arguments were those he caught the fastest hold of, but simply to 1139 against me. When I spoke, for example, of a vast difference a punish- ment may have upon two different men—one a rough, who when he had been penished and got over tke torture, would nearer trouble his mind by reflecting on its nature, or on his own degradation through it; the other a gentleman, to whom the physical torture, however cruel, would be less frightful than the everlasting sense of infamy that he would be sure to associate with it." "The Colonel listened attentively, smiled, and presently I found he received what I said, as proving he had then another duty to perform besides those be knew of, and that was to sho ff the humblest among his soldiers, their Colonel was indeed their father, one who wou:d show equal justice to all. That one illustration may serve for all. left Mai convinced there was but one thing to do, and that I am now on the way to London to try to accomplish. "Before you can possibly reeeive this, I shall be on the ether side of the Channel, and a few hours later I shall pre- sent myself at Harlaxton House, to take counsel with your brother. "I should not tell you this, but I fear what may be your method of escape if you see no hope in any quarter. "But no, my friend, you are made of nobler stuff than goes to the making of suicides. Bear up then. I may fail —God knows I may—but assuredly I will succeed if success be possible. Not, lam well aware by myself, lam too humble a person; no, not by myself, but by putting others on to the work, of greater, more commanding influetice. "Forgive me then my violation of your urgent—your pas- sionate demand that I should be silent. But whether you do or do not, my duty is the same; to save you if I can; or if I cannot, prove a true friend in the hour of your worst trial—and one who will hope to mitigate consequences by his brotherly sympathy afterwards. " CHARLES GORDON ETHEREDGE." (To be continued.)

Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers. 13, Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (Dec. 27th) The holidays and the fortnightl'. settlement now progressing —both occurrieg this week, a *detailed report is impossible; prices not being tested at all decisively, except in one or two instances who e special circumstances have caused extraor- elloary movements. The market for miscellaneous shares is practically neglected owing to above causes. Except a few dealings in banks, next to nothing has been passing. Mexican railways. which Immune° another large decrease of traffic this week, are again lower nearly 5 per cent. Home railways, though quiet, are, with slight exceptions, a trifle harder. Scotch stccks also little better. In Cauadians' trunks have had a drouping market all week. The traffic return to-day shewing a large decrease (212,190) did not further depress prices a great deal, it having been carl.:ent,:y anticipated in soma quarters, but latest figures are about worst or very little above worst of the week.
